Every other library keeps the upstream flags, except aom on x64, which entry 121 builds as a Release at `-O3`. Only `libvips-cpp.so.8.18.7` replaces the copy of the npm package; the addon, the versions and the notices of the package stay as they are, since the library versions are the release's own (`versions.properties`).
  - **One stage serves both architectures.** The stage takes the platform of the build, as every stage does (`docker compose build` on the host, so arm64 on the Ampere A1 host and amd64 in CI), and `docker/sharp-libvips/env.sh` picks the settings of the upstream `platforms/linux-x64` or `platforms/linux-arm64v8` Dockerfile by `uname -m`.
  - **Every download the build script makes with curl is pinned, and its other ways to fetch are closed.** The upstream archive by SHA-256; each of the 32 files `posix.sh` downloads for Linux (27 source archives and 5 patches; it asks for the freetype archive twice) by the SHA-256 of its bytes (`sources.sha256`), served through `fetch-pinned.sh`, which stands in for `curl` while the script runs and downloads over HTTPS only, redirects included (`--proto-redir '=https'`); the notices file from the pinned archive instead of the upstream `main` branch (`pinned-notices.patch`); `rustup-init` by SHA-256 and the Rust nightly by date (`nightly-2026-10-23`); cargo-c by version with its lock file; meson and ninja by wheel digest; gcc-toolset-15 by release. A download that is not pinned, or whose bytes differ, fails the build, and so does a pin the build no longer asks for. The tarballs the script unpacks carry Meson wrap files that clone from the network when a dependency is missing (the `wrap-git` files of pango 1.58.2 for glib, harfbuzz, cairo, fribidi and fontconfig name a branch, not a commit, and fontconfig's `freetype2.wrap` does too), and the toolchain installs `git`, as the upstream build container does; every `meson setup` therefore runs with `--wrap-mode=nodownload` (`MESON` in `env.sh`), which lets a wrap use only a subproject that is already unpacked, and `git-local-only.sh` stands in for `git` while the script runs. `posix.sh` never calls git, and leaving the program out fails the build (libxml2's `meson.build` requires it). The sources ask it for three versions, `git --version` (CMake's `find_package(Git)`), `git describe` (libxml2) and `git --git-dir=<dir>/.git describe --match=v[0-9]*` (aom), which read no network and find no repository in an unpacked archive; the stand-in passes exactly those to the real git and refuses every other call, such as a clone, and records it in the file `build.sh` checks after the script, so a tool that swallows the error still stops the build. A stand-in that refuses every call fails the build on those three queries (the first build of this change did).
  - **The build fails when the pins no longer describe it**: the upstream platform Dockerfile is not the one `toolchain.sh` mirrors (by digest), `versions.properties` names another libvips than 8.18.7, the lock file or the installed `@img/sharp-libvips-linux-<arch>` is not 1.3.4 (a sharp upgrade that brings another release), or sharp does not encode with libvips 8.18.7 mapped from the package's own `lib` directory, from a file with the SHA-256 the stage wrote beside the library (`check-sharp.sh`, run by `use-libvips.sh` in the runtime stage and in CI).
  - **CI runs on the same library.** `.github/workflows/sharp-libvips.yml` builds the `sharplibvips` stage for linux/amd64 when its key (`cache-key.sh`: the stage's lines and the files they copy) is not in the Actions cache, and saves it. The stage hands over exactly two files, `libvips-cpp.so.8.18.7` and its `.sha256`, and `check-build-output.sh` fails unless a directory holds those and nothing else, both regular files and no symlink, with the digest of the library in the second. The workflow runs it before it saves the cache entry, the `container` job before the image build mounts the restored directory, and `use-libvips.sh` before it copies anything, in CI and in the runtime stage of the image, which mounts the stage whole instead of copying a directory into `node_modules`, so a swapped `.node` file or a link in the cache would not reach `node_modules`. The jobs that convert pictures put it into `node_modules` after `npm ci` (`.github/actions/sharp-libvips`, which runs `use-libvips.sh`): `tests`, `conformance`, `parity-quality` and `parity-speed` in `ci.yml`, and `perf`, `bench`, both parity jobs, `bench-ab-speed` and `realworld` in `nightly.yml`. The `container` job builds the image with the cached stage as the `sharplibvips` build context, so the stage is built once per key. The base of a speed comparison runs on its own library (`scripts/ab-base-dependencies.sh`): it shares the head's `node_modules` only when the lock file and the key are both the same.
  - **Cache key, main and pull requests.** A key in the cache costs a lookup (the job runs on every event and the converting jobs wait for it). A missing key is built in the job, about 18 minutes on a 4-core runner. On `main` the first run after a change of the build saves it, and every pull request restores it from `main`'s scope; a pull request that changes the build builds and saves it in its own scope, so its own jobs test the library it builds and no other pull request waits for it or reads it. There is no restore key: a stale library is never used.
  - **The image speed rows time both sides on the same bytes** (`bench/families/image.ts`). A PNG source cannot be given to the reference as it is (it would apply the file's gAMA chunk, entry 22 and `bench/png-metadata.ts`), so ours is timed on the file the reference reads, the decoded pixels with the EXIF, XMP and ICC blocks; a JPEG source is read by both as it is. The quality rows still encode ours from the original.
- **Why**:
  - **Upstream builds these codecs for size.** `posix.sh` sets `-Os` for every library (lines 44 to 46, "Default optimisation level is for binary size (-Os) / Overridden to performance (-O3) for select dependencies that benefit") and overrides it for zlib-ng, lcms, libheif, libimagequant, highway, cgif, libultrahdr and libvips, but not for mozjpeg (`MinSizeRel`, line 205), libpng (line 212) or libwebp (line 225), which do the encode work of the WebP and JPEG rows.
  - **Measured on the x64 runner** (run 39984292745; base time over head time in alternating pairs of the speed rows, the prebuilt library against this build):

    | Row | Base/head | Ours against the reference, prebuilt then this build |
    |---|---|---|
    | `wm-alpha-graph.png->webp` | 1.144 | 0.936, 1.070 |
    | `screenshot.png->webp` | 1.182 | 0.960, 1.133 |
    | `wm-screen-history.png->jpg` | 1.217 | 0.882, 1.088 |
    | `lineart.png->webp` | 1.105 | 0.877, 0.971 |

    The other WebP and JPEG rows are 1.06 to 1.31 and the AVIF rows 0.99 to 1.01 (aom is unchanged). A rebuild of the same release without the patch measured 0.99 to 1.01 on every row, so the gain is the flags, not the newer toolchain.
  - **The output does not change.** 247 outputs (77 samples to WebP, AVIF and JPEG, and four quality points of the timed samples) are byte-identical to the prebuilt library's, for the rebuild without the patch and for this build; the strict quality gate of the image family passed (823 rows, none failing). On the arm64 VM the same build was byte-identical on 12 image rows and 7 to 21% faster.
  - **Pinned downloads.** The upstream script fetches its sources with `curl | tar` and five patches with `curl | patch`, with no checksum, and one file from a moving branch; the worker image pins its other downloads by SHA-256 (the 7-Zip and LibreDWG stages). The GNOME and cairo archives of the list match the checksum files those projects publish.
  - **Same bytes in the speed rows.** `wm-alpha-graph.png` is 58,819 bytes and the file the reference reads 44,013, and sharp decodes them in 2.57 and 0.86 ms; timing ours on the original charged it a decode the reference did not pay. On the 4-core arm64 VM (the npm package's library, the old and the new harness in the same pairs, 24 to 96 pairs a row) ours times 1.01 to 1.18 faster on the WebP rows of PNG sources (`wm-alpha-graph.png->webp` 0.901 to 0.974 of the reference), 0.99 to 1.01 on the AVIF rows and 0.98 to 1.00 on the JPEG rows; `photo-a.jpg` now gives the reference its JPEG too (`->webp` 1.072 to 1.223, `->avif` 1.784 to 1.807, `->jpg` 1.144 to 1.149).
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Build time.** A worker image built without its layer cache spends about 18 minutes more on a 4-core x64 runner (container 433 s, libvips 637 s in the experiment) and builds the stage natively on the arm64 host. Building arm64 on an amd64 machine under emulation would take hours; the image is not built that way.
  - **Image size.** The library is 19,550,624 bytes on x64 against 18,699,288 for the prebuilt (4.6% more), and the copy of the npm package stays in its lower layer, so the image grows by about 19.6 MB.
  - **Vulnerabilities.** A fix in libwebp, libpng, mozjpeg or any library of the build reaches the image when sharp-libvips releases it and the pins move with the sharp upgrade, as before; a fix that cannot wait can be one more patch in `docker/sharp-libvips/`.
  - **Every sharp upgrade that brings another sharp-libvips release** moves the pins in one change: `env.sh` (commit, archive digest, versions, the two platform Dockerfile digests after `toolchain.sh` is compared with the new Dockerfiles), `sources.sha256` (from the new `versions.properties`), and the two patches if their context moved. The build fails until it is done.
  - **Generated archives can change bytes.** Eleven source archives, three patches and the upstream archive are files GitHub or GitLab generate from a tag, a commit or a pull request; if a host regenerates one differently, the build fails until its digest is checked and moved.
  - **What is not pinned by digest.** The Rocky Linux packages other than the compiler (`dnf update`, signed by the distribution), the crates of librsvg (from the lock file of its release archive, with the checksums the lock file holds, through cargo's own client), and whatever a program fetches with its own client without going through `curl` on `PATH` or Meson's wraps: the build container has no network restriction, and `/usr/bin/curl` called by an absolute path would not be seen.
  - **A cache entry is trusted by its key.** The restored directory is checked for its two files and the digest of the library, but a digest file written next to a swapped library by whoever saved the entry matches it, and nothing compares it with a build of the stage. Anything that can write to the Actions cache in `main`'s scope under this key before the job that builds it (some jobs of the workflows hold `issues: write`, `pull-requests: write` or `packages: write`) would have its library loaded by the later jobs. This is the shape of the `ab-base-modules` and `bench-ref` caches, whose `node_modules` and reference build are trusted the same way. Accepted, as for those caches.
  - **CI.** One more job (a lookup when the key is cached), the 18-minute build on `main` after a change of the build and on the pull request that makes it, about 7 MB of Actions cache per key, and a copy of `node_modules` for the base of a speed comparison whose library differs. A nightly comparison with a commit whose build is no longer cached fails at its restore step.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **The distribution's libvips** (Debian 13 ships 8.16.1, built at `-O2`): sharp 0.35.5 requires libvips 8.18.7 or newer (`src/common.h` lines 20 to 23), so sharp cannot be built against it.
  - **A sharp release old enough for libvips 8.16**: gives up the fixes of every sharp release since, to change a compiler flag.
  - **The distribution's codec libraries under the upstream libvips** (libjpeg-turbo for mozjpeg, Debian's libwebp): the JPEG bytes change, and every image row would move with them.
  - **A native addon of our own around the encoders**: a C++ surface to maintain and to secure, for the same libraries.
  - **`-O3` for every library, aom included**: the AVIF rows did not move with the three codecs changed, and nothing was measured for the others.
  - **`set -o pipefail` in the upstream script instead of the refusal file**: its `readelf ... | grep -q` checks (lines 444 and 446) would then fail when `grep` exits before `readelf` has written everything.
- **Verified by**: `tests/sharp-libvips-build.test.ts` (the download check serves only pinned bytes over HTTPS and records every refusal; `MESON` carries `--wrap-mode=nodownload`; `git-local-only.sh` passes only the three version queries and refuses and records the rest; the build output check fails on an extra file, a directory, a hidden file, a symlink and a changed library or digest file, and `use-libvips.sh` leaves `node_modules` untouched when it fails; `check-sharp.sh` fails on a library whose digest is not the build's; the cache key moves with the stage and its files and not with other stages; the base of a speed comparison shares, copies or installs its dependencies as above; every converting job uses the build before it converts; the container job uses the cached stage), the updated `tests/ci-workflows.test.ts`, `tests/container-ci-job.test.ts`, `tests/ci-parity-workflow.test.ts`, `tests/runtime-baseline.test.ts` and `tests/phase-4-security-and-sandbox-hardening.test.ts`, the build of the stage itself (every download checked, `use-libvips.sh` and `check-sharp.sh` in the runtime stage), and the experiment above. A build of the stage for linux/amd64 in a VM (2026-10-24) gave the experiment's library byte for byte (SHA-256 `7f74bee5fbfc7d12c4234415fa9d07c829629564996d294f4aaac027b4062a3c`), and the image built on it encodes WebP with that file mapped. The build for linux/arm64 in a VM (2026-10-24), before and after `--wrap-mode=nodownload`, `git-local-only.sh`, HTTPS-only redirects and the two-file output, gave the same library byte for byte (SHA-256 `49031d3edff79be6e5cc73821ac6d5ccbf222d589ec4f6a896d80c098f2fc450`, 18,848,888 bytes); the amd64 build is the first run of the workflow on the pull request. A stage mounted as a build context (`RUN --mount=type=bind,from=sharplibvips`, as the runtime stage does) overrides a stage of the same name, passes `check-build-output.sh` with the two files and fails it with a third.
- **Revisit when**: upstream changes the flags of these libraries (then the patch goes), sharp is upgraded (the pins move, and the speed rows are measured again), a host regenerates a pinned archive, sharp-libvips starts publishing checksums of its sources, or the arm64 host builds the image so slowly that a prebuilt stage from CI is worth publishing.

## 85. PDF text: code 0 of a nonsymbolic simple font with no glyph name is the .notdef glyph, which has no text

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, `pdf-pdfjs-issue17333.pdf` row), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request in issue #783: follow what the reference readers print for the one glyph that maps to nothing). It narrows what entry 49 counts as a glyph without a Unicode mapping.
- **Decision**:
  - **Character code 0 of a simple TrueType or Type 1 font that is not symbolic, where the encoding names no glyph (no /Differences entry, nothing in the base encoding, or `.notdef`), is the .notdef glyph.** The in-process text reader leaves it out of the text, does not count it among the glyphs left out, and does not report it. A page that draws only such glyphs has no text, as for the reference readers, and is treated like any page without text (OCR runs when the route asks for it, an empty text or Markdown file otherwise).
  - **Everything else stays as entry 49 counts it.** Code 0 of a symbolic font, code 0 named by /Differences (`/G0` and the like), codes 1 to 31, and Type 3 fonts are still glyphs without a mapping: counted, reported, and a page of them alone is still left out or refused.
- **Why**:
  - **The standard encodings name no glyph at code 0, so the code selects glyph 0, the .notdef glyph.** pdf.js states this rule in `src/core/fonts.js` (PR 21487, "Render non-empty glyph 0 for char code 0", issue 17333): it maps code 0 to glyph 0 only when the encoding leaves it unmapped, because a symbol font may draw a checkbox there. A nonsymbolic font selects its glyphs by name (ISO 32000-1 section 9.6.6), so an unnamed code has no other glyph to reach.
  - **No reader gives the .notdef glyph a character.** For `pdf-pdfjs-issue17333.pdf` (one checkbox at code 0) `pdftotext` 26.09 prints only the form feed of the page break, pdf.js 6.3.289 `getTextContent` gives U+0000 and MuPDF 1.28.5 U+FFFD; Poppler prints nothing for the same glyphs on page 59 of `govdocs1-001045.pdf`. The file was refused with `PdfTextUnmappedError` because its one glyph counted as unmapped text, so the refusal told the caller that text could not be read where there is none.
  - **The refusal keeps its meaning.** A document whose text is in a font with no mapping draws its letters at codes other than 0, or in a symbolic font, and those are still counted; the rule takes out one code that no font can use for text.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A nonsymbolic TrueType font with no /Encoding entry may still draw a real glyph at code 0.** pdf.js then maps codes straight through the program's `cmap` (`src/core/fonts.js`, the branches after `readCmapTable`), and pdfjs does not tell the reader whether the font had an /Encoding. Such a glyph is left out without a warning where it was counted before; its text is the same (nothing, as Poppler prints it), and only a page made of nothing else would change from refused to empty. No file of the corpora below has one.
  - **The checkbox of `pdf-pdfjs-issue17333.pdf` reads as nothing.** No reader gives it a character; the drawn page keeps it.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keep counting the glyph**: refuses a document for text it does not have, which no reference reader does.
  - **Map the checkbox to a ballot box character (U+2610)**: a guess from the shape that no reader makes; entry 49 never replaces a glyph by a guess.
  - **Leave out every code 1 to 31 without a name as well**: pdf.js reaches a glyph for such a code through the program's `cmap` when the font has no /Encoding, and a symbolic or subset font uses low codes for its letters, so those are glyphs the reader cannot map; counting them is what keeps documents in unmapped fonts refused. pdf.js's own rule (PR 21487) is for code 0 only.
- **Measured**: text, Markdown and HTML of the 1,261 PDFs of the real-world corpus and of every tenth PDF of the regression corpus (950), on origin/main and on the change: 9 of the 6,633 conversions differ. `pdf-pdfjs-issue17333.pdf` converts where it was refused (empty text and Markdown, an HTML page without text). `govdocs1-001045.pdf` gives the same bytes on all three routes, and its warning counts 2 glyphs left out where it counted 4: the other two are code 0 of the nonsymbolic Type 1 font `TT175o00` on page 59, where Poppler prints nothing and MuPDF U+FFFD. `cc-2200368.pdf` is a scan without fonts whose OCR text differs from run to run on the same code (685, 700 and 703 bytes), so the change does not reach it. No other file changed.
- **Verified by**: `tests/pdf-text-notdef-glyph.test.ts` (hand-written pages: a non-embedded Helvetica with the WinAnsi encoding, the same with /Differences that name no glyph at 0, and the DejaVu Sans subset of tests/fixtures/woff2 as an embedded nonsymbolic TrueType font, each against `pdftotext`; red on origin/main for the embedded font, 2 of 2, and for the real file; the Helvetica cases held before, as pdf.js draws an unnamed code of a font it does not have as a space; controls that stay refused: code 0 named `/ornamentone`, code 0 of a symbolic font, codes 1 to 3), `tests/pdf-text-real-samples.test.ts` (`pdf-pdfjs-issue17333.pdf` to Markdown is empty, with `pdftotext` printing no text and `pdfimages` listing no image), `tests/realworld-corpus.test.ts` (the file is marked `emptyInput`, with the reason read from the file).
- **Revisit when**: a corpus file draws text at code 0 of a nonsymbolic font, or pdf.js gives code 0 of such a font a character.

## 86. libwebp's second thread for a picture with an alpha band, in the libvips of the worker image

- **Status**: Implemented (epic #759, row "libwebp `thread_level` through libvips"; #641), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request).
- **Decision**:
  - **The libvips of the worker image sets libwebp's `thread_level` to 1 when the picture it saves has four bands.** `docker/sharp-libvips/libvips-webp-thread-level.patch` changes `vips_foreign_save_webp_init_config` in `libvips/foreign/webpsave.c` (libvips 8.18.7) and adds `if (save->ready->Bands == 4) webp->config.thread_level = 1;` after the line that sets `config.pass`. A picture with one or three bands keeps libwebp's default of 0. `Bands == 4` is the test `webpsave.c` itself uses to import RGBA (`WebPPictureImportRGBA`, line 287).
  - **The build applies it with one added line in `posix.sh`.** `docker/sharp-libvips/webp-thread-level.patch` patches the upstream script, as `option-f.patch` and `pinned-notices.patch` do (`build.sh` applies the three with `patch --forward`). The line is `patch -p1 < "$SHARP_LIBVIPS_WEBP_THREAD_PATCH"`, directly after the line that applies the SONAME patch to the unpacked libvips sources, and `build.sh` exports the variable with the path of the libvips patch. Both files are in the `COPY` line of the `sharplibvips-build` stage of `Dockerfile.worker`, so the key of `cache-key.sh` moves with them, and a hunk that no longer applies fails the build (`patch` exits with a failure under `set -e`). There is no new download, so `sources.sha256` is unchanged.
  - **The rows.** `image/screenshot.png->jpg` and `image/lineart.png->webp` are removed from `bench/parity-gaps.json`: the x64 run of the pull request that made entry 84 read them at 1.137 and 1.061, and the gate listed them as at parity.
- **Why**:
  - **libvips does not set it, and sharp does not expose it.** `webpsave.c` of the v8.18.7 tag copies the options into `WebPConfig` at lines 628 to 633 (`lossless`, `exact`, `alpha_quality`, `method`, `target_size`, `pass`), and `WebPConfigInit` leaves `thread_level` at 0 (libwebp 1.6.0 `src/enc/config_enc.c`, line 58). The WebP options of sharp 0.35.5 have no thread setting, and the threads of the image library (`sharp.concurrency`) belong to the libvips pipeline, which entry 36 found slower for a WebP encode of a picture this size. The reference WebP tool has a switch for the thread (`-mt`) that the speed rows do not pass, so the reference runs on one thread.
  - **What the second thread does** (libwebp 1.6.0 `src/enc`). `VP8EncStartAlpha` (`alpha_enc.c`, lines 411 to 425) hands the compression of the alpha plane to a worker while the calling thread encodes the colour planes, and `VP8EncFinishAlpha` waits for it. `VP8EncAnalyze` (`analysis_enc.c`, lines 439 to 464) splits the segment analysis at 9/16 of the macroblock rows between two workers, and `MergeJobs` (lines 399 to 404) adds their integer counters. Lossless encodes split their crunch configurations the same way (`vp8l_enc.c`, line 1727). The merge adds integers and the alpha plane is compressed from the same input, so the bytes do not depend on the threads.
  - **Why only with an alpha band.** The alpha plane is the only part with parallel work of its own: the pictures with a transparent background gained 1.46 to 1.64 times in one encode, and the rows of pictures without a fourth band gained 0 to 9%. On two cores shared by two concurrent encodes (the worker runs `WORKER_CONCURRENCY` jobs on `cpus: 2.5`) the alpha pictures keep their throughput (0.98 to 1.03 times, CPU per encode within 3%). A first version that set the thread level for every picture read 0.91 to 0.99 times on the pictures without an alpha band in that configuration (7 to 15 pairs); the build with the band test and the same configuration read 0.997 (photo-b) and 0.985 (line art) in 25 pairs, and an identical library against itself reads 1.02 in 15 pairs, so the pictures without a band stay as they were.
  - **The output does not change.** 280 outputs (56 samples of the image sets, five of them with transparency, at qualities 30, 55, 70, 85 and 100) are byte-identical in the npm package's library, in the rebuild without the patch and in the rebuild with it (arm64 VM). The rebuild without the patch has the SHA-256 that entry 84 records for the arm64 build (`49031d3edff7...c450`), so the build is reproducible; with the patch it is `38449af5ce94...ecb`, and the size is the same, 18,848,888 bytes.
  - **Measured on the arm64 VM** (4 vCPU, `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`, the two libraries swapped between alternating processes; medians of 9 pairs of 30 encodes, one stream on four cores):

    | Picture (WebP, quality 70) | Base | Head | Base/head |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | `wm-alpha-graph.png` | 24.26 ms | 16.32 ms | 1.49 |
    | `wm-alpha-comingsoon.png` | 11.02 ms | 7.03 ms | 1.57 |
    | `wm-alpha-banner.png` | 58.60 ms | 36.97 ms | 1.59 |
    | `wm-lineart-containers.png` | 30.91 ms | 18.88 ms | 1.64 |
    | `wm-lineart-assembly.png` | 53.05 ms | 33.97 ms | 1.56 |

    The speed gate (`--parity --speed-only --family image`, head and base each on its own library): `wm-alpha-graph.png->webp` is 1.570 head against base in 24 pairs (upper bound 1.601) and 1.71 against the reference tool, where the base read 0.995 and 0.954 in two runs. The rows of pictures with an opaque fourth band moved with the analysis split: `screenshot.png->webp` 1.112, `wm-screen-history.png->webp` 1.072, `lineart.png->webp` 1.089 (head against base). The rows of pictures with three bands read 0.96 to 1.04 against the base, the spread of the harness.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **One more thread for the length of the encode** of a picture with a fourth band. CPU per encode is unchanged to +4%, the wall time of one encode on an idle machine drops by a third for a transparent picture, and a saturated worker gains nothing. The thread is created and ended inside `WebPEncode`, and none stays behind.
  - **A patch to libvips that must survive an upgrade.** A sharp release with another libvips moves the hunk's context or makes the change unnecessary, and the build fails until the patch is looked at. The change is two statements and could go to libvips as a `thread_level` choice of the saver.
  - **x64 is measured by the pull request's own jobs.** The arm64 VM measured the library and its bytes. CI builds the x64 library from the same patch, and its image quality rows and speed rows are the gate.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Every picture**: the gain in one encode of a picture without an alpha band is 0 to 9%, and the measured throughput on two shared cores was 0.91 to 0.99 times.
  - **The threads of the image library** (`sharp.concurrency`) for WebP: entry 36 measured encodes 2 to 16% slower.
  - **libwebp's default in its own build** (`config_enc.c`): it would also reach the animation encoder and every other caller of libwebp for the same effect.
  - **A native addon around libwebp**: a C++ surface to maintain for a one-line setting.
- **Verified by**: `tests/sharp-libvips-build.test.ts` (the libvips patch sets `thread_level` once, after `config.pass`, under the four-band test, and fails on a `webpsave.c` that is not the one it was written for; the posix.sh patch adds a line that applies the libvips patch from `$SHARP_LIBVIPS_WEBP_THREAD_PATCH` and fails when that file is missing; `build.sh` names the patch and `Dockerfile.worker` copies both files), the byte comparison and the timings above, and the image quality and speed rows of CI.
- **Revisit when**: libvips exposes the libwebp thread level itself, sharp is upgraded (the hunk, the byte comparison and the alpha rows are measured again), the worker runs on fewer than two cores per job, or a measurement on the x64 runner shows a row of a picture with a fourth band losing throughput.

## 87. Gzip, bzip2 and xz targets of an archive with several entries: a tar of the entries compressed with that codec

- **Status**: Implemented (area: compression; the five refusals of the nightly real-world run of 2026-10-23, commit `bccfc85a`), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request); the naming of the output amended 2026-10-24 (QA request, reference check of the first version).
- **Decision**:
  - **An archive that is not exactly one regular file becomes a tar of its entries, compressed with the codec of the target.** This holds for the targets `gz`, `gzip`, `bz2`, `bzip2` and `xz` of the native route (`package7zArchive` in `src/worker/engines.ts`) and for `gz`, `bz2`, `xz` and `zst` of the in-process route (`singleStreamPayload` in `src/lib/conversions/archive.ts`), whatever the source: ZIP, 7z, tar, or a compressed tarball. The native route reuses the branch that already wrote `tar.gz`, `tar.bz2` and `tar.xz`: `7z a -ttar` over the extracted tree, then `7z a` with the codec of the target at the product's level.
  - **Exactly one regular file at the root of the tree is compressed as that file**, as before (`7z a -tgzip out.gz .` accepts it). A single file inside a folder, an empty folder, and a tree with a link that is kept are not that shape and get a tar, so the path survives.
  - **The file is named after the tarball target of its codec**: `report.zip` to `gz` is `report.tar.gz` (`gz` and `gzip` give `.tar.gz`, `bz2`, `bz` and `bzip2` give `.tar.bz2`, `xz` gives `.tar.xz`, `zst` and `zstd` give `.tar.zst`) with the MIME type of that tarball target (`application/gzip`, `application/x-bzip-compressed-tar`, `application/x-xz-compressed-tar`, `application/x-zstd-compressed-tar`), on both engines, so the name says what the file holds. The output opens with `gzip -d`, `bzip2 -d` or `xz -d` to a tar, and with `tar -xzf` (or `-xjf`, `-xJf`) to the entries. A request for a file that names its tar (`tar.gz`, `tgz`) is unchanged, and so is a single regular file at the root, which keeps `<name>.gz` (`<source file>.gz` in process).
  - **In-process tar to gzip decides the shape as the other routes do** (`tarToGzip` in `src/lib/conversions/archive-repack.ts`): a tar of exactly one regular file at its root is gzipped as that file; a file inside a folder, or several entries, is handed to the general pipeline, which writes the tar under the `.tar.gz` name. It used to treat a lone file inside a folder as a bare file by its leaf name.
  - **The tar is built from the tree that has passed the extraction policy** (entry count, size, ratio, path depth, traversal, links, collisions: `archive-extraction-safety.ts`), so a tar written for these targets stays inside the limits of every other target. No limit was added or relaxed.
- **Why**:
  - **The references do not write several files into one stream.** 7-Zip refuses it: the gzip, bzip2 and xz handlers answer `E_INVALIDARG` when an update has any number of items other than one (`CPP/7zip/Archive/GzHandler.cpp` line 1035, `Bz2Handler.cpp` line 388, `XzHandler.cpp` line 1110, `UpdateItems`, 7-Zip repository `ip7z/7zip` at `b88c6bc0`); `7z a -tgzip` over a folder or two files exits with `E_INVALIDARG` and that is the exit code 2 the nightly run recorded. libarchive's raw writer, which writes one stream with no container, refuses the second entry ("Raw format only supports one entry per archive", `libarchive/archive_write_set_format_raw.c` lines 94 to 96, `libarchive/libarchive` at `8509b99a`). The gzip manual says to use an archiver when a file has several members: "If you wish to create a single archive file with multiple members so that members can later be extracted independently, use an archiver such as tar or zip. GNU tar supports the -z option to invoke gzip transparently" (gzip manual, chapter 4, Advanced usage); `gzip a b` writes `a.gz` and `b.gz`, two files, and a request has one output.
  - **The reference service names it `.tar.gz`.** Its archive task writes several files only as ZIP, RAR, 7Z, TAR, TAR.GZ or TAR.BZ2 and has no plain gzip, bzip2 or xz target for several files, and its zip to tar.gz and tar to tar.gz pairs are served by its `archivetool` engine (formats API and create-archives operation documentation, checked 2026-10-24). A tar inside `<name>.gz` hid what the file holds; the same tar under `<name>.tar.gz` is that product's output.
  - **The tools that write one compressed file from several write a tar.** `tar -czf out.gz dir` and `bsdtar -czf out.gz dir` (measured with bsdtar 3.5.3; libarchive `tar/bsdtar.c`, option `z`, a gzip filter on the tar writer) write a gzip stream holding a tar under the name given; the system `tar -tzf` reads it back. Python's `shutil.make_archive` has no plain gzip format: `gztar`, `bztar` and `xztar` are all tars (`Lib/shutil.py` lines 964 to 965 and 1068 to 1080, CPython 3.13 at `a737e405`), and the name gets `.tar` before the codec's extension.
  - **Refusing is the wrong answer for a lossless conversion.** The registry offers `gz` as a target of ZIP, tar and 7z. A converter that accepts the pair and fails on every archive of more than one file fails on the usual case: the nightly run refused all five multi-entry archives it converted to `gz` (a tar and a ZIP of the Tika test documents, a tar, a ZIP and a 7z of the Commons Compress test archives).
  - **The in-process route used to compress the source file.** For several entries it compressed the bytes of the uploaded archive (`foo.zip` became `foo.zip.gz`, a gzip of a ZIP), so the output listed none of the entries of the input and the same request gave a different file from the native route. Both routes now write the same tar.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The output of `gz` can be a tar.** A caller that decompresses a `gz` output of a multi-entry archive gets a tar, not a file; one entry gets the file itself. The shape follows the number of entries, as the tools do, and the file's name says which (`.tar.gz` or `.gz`). A caller that always wants a tarball asks for `tar.gz`.
  - **Two 7-Zip runs** (tar, then codec) where one failed before; the tar is written in the job's sandbox directory beside the extracted tree, the same cost as `tar.gz`.
  - **The in-process route's file name** for a single file is unchanged (`foo.zip.gz`); a tar gets `foo.tar.gz`, as the native route names it.
  - **A caller that built the output name from the target** (`<name>.gz`) now receives `<name>.tar.gz` for an archive of several entries; the result's file name is what to read.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keep the refusal.** It is what 7-Zip does, but it fails the conversion the registry advertises, and the tools that users know write the tar.
  - **A separate gzip file for every entry** (what `gzip a b` does): the request has one output, and a ZIP of gzip files is another format.
  - **Keep `<name>.gz` for a tar** (the first version of this entry): the file name is part of the API result, and a name that says gzip of a file while the stream holds a tar differs from the reference service's output and from what the tools above write when asked for a tarball.
  - **Compress the uploaded archive as it is** (what the in-process route did): a gzip of a ZIP lists none of the entries and is not a conversion of the archive.
  - **A gzip with several members** (concatenated members, which `gzip -dc` joins into one stream): the joined stream has no entry boundaries, and `gunzip` would write the entries run together.
- **Verified by**: `tests/archive-single-stream-targets.test.ts` (RED before the change, 34 of 39: ZIP, 7z and tar to `gz`, `gzip`, `bz2`, `bzip2` and `xz` on the native route, to `gz`, `bz2`, `xz` and `zst` in process, and the five real files of the nightly run; each output is decoded by `gzip`, `bzip2`, `xz` or `zstd` and unpacked by `tar`, every file is compared by SHA-256 with the tree it was made from and the real files with the `7z l -slt` listing of the source; one regular file stays a bare stream; a traversing name, a symlink entry with and without `skipLinks`, 50,001 entries and a path 1000 levels deep are refused or handled as for a ZIP target), and `tests/archive-inprocess-repack.test.ts`, whose test of a tar with several members asserted the refusal. The naming amendment is pinned by the same files (RED before it, 33 of 58: file name and MIME type per target on both engines, the five real files, and a tar whose only entry is a file inside a folder).
- **Revisit when**: 7-Zip's gzip, bzip2 or xz handler accepts several items, or the registry stops offering a single-stream target for archives.

## 88. Office rows of the nightly run: a Word document on slides with the text of its tables, a presentation whose persist id seed is too small, and an encrypted presentation refused as encrypted

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, rows "docx to pptx: no text to put on slides" and "ppt: LibreOffice could not read the file" of the nightly run of 2026-10-23), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request).
- **Decision**:
  - **A Word document becomes slides from the text its plain-text export gives**: the paragraphs of the body, the cells of its tables (a row on one line, the cells separated by a tab) and the text of its text boxes, in document order. Before, the slide builder read the paragraphs only, so a document whose text sat in tables reached it empty and was refused with "There is no text to put on slides." A document read by the structured reader (no charts or drawn shapes) gives its text through `documentToText`, the same text as `docx` to `txt`; a document with drawn shapes gives it through the drawing-aware reader's `docxBodyText`, which `docx` to `txt` also uses. Every limit of those readers stands (depth of nested tables 16, XML nesting 256, blocks, inlines, text length).
  - **Headers, footers and pictures are not body text, and a document with no other text is still refused** with the same typed answer. LibreOffice's text export gives nothing for them (`soffice --convert-to txt:Text` of `emptydocumentwithheaderfooter.docx` is empty, and so is `docx` to `txt` here); Apache POI's `XWPFWordExtractor` does return the header and footer text of that file (`blabal`, `blabla`), which is the one place the two references differ.
  - **A PowerPoint 97-2003 file whose persistIdSeed is below the largest persist id of its directory is read after the seed is corrected.** When the office suite cannot load a `.ppt` and the newest UserEditAtom has a seed below the directory, the four bytes of the seed are set to the largest persist id in a copy of the input and the suite runs once more (`repairPptPersistIdSeed`, `withPresentationRetry`). Nothing else in the file changes, and a file the suite loads is never touched.
  - **An encrypted `.ppt` the suite cannot load is refused as encrypted** (typed 422, the answer the in-process reader already gives for `txt` and `html`), not as damaged (400). The Current User stream of the file carries the encrypted header token, or its newest UserEditAtom names an encryption session.
  - **The retry reads the compound file once**, from the streams the directory tree reaches, for the encryption check, the edit history and the patch. Each of the four bytes of the seed is found through the sector chain of the stream, so a seed that spans two sectors or mini sectors is written into both, and it is written only where the bytes found equal the seed just read. A failure to read the input for the retry (a file that is gone, bytes that are no compound file) keeps the suite's own refusal.
  - **The compound file reader refuses a file that would make it copy a sector twice or hold more than the file**, for every reader of compound files (Word, Excel and PowerPoint 97-2003, HWP 5), with the typed answer for a damaged file. A sector or mini sector belongs to at most one chain (the directory, the mini FAT, the mini stream, each stream): a second chain that reaches it is refused, as a chain that returns to its own sector already was. Each FAT and DIFAT sector is read once, and the FAT sector list ends at the first sector past the file, so the FAT is never larger than the file. Before any stream is copied, the streams at or above the mini stream cutoff may declare no more bytes than the file's sectors hold, and the streams below it no more than the root entry's mini stream; the root entry's own size is read only as far as its chain goes, as before. The directory holds at most 65,536 entries (the limit the legacy reader applied after the parse), now counted while it is read. The sector shift is 9 or 12, and the mini sector shift 6 when the file has a mini stream.
  - **Three damaged files stay refused**, listed in `bench/realworld/known-refusals.json` with their evidence.
- **Why**:
  - **Reference for the text.** LibreOffice's Writer text export walks the nodes of the body and writes a table row as its cells with a tab between them (`sw/source/filter/ascii/wrtasc.cxx`, `SwASCWriter::WriteTable`, the `\t` written between boxes), and has no code for headers or footers; no proven tool writes a presentation from a text document (`soffice --convert-to pptx` of a `.docx` answers "no export filter", and POI has no `docx` to `pptx`), so the text of the document is what a slide can hold. The three nightly files with text (`testtablecellalign.docx`, `table-indent.docx`, `bug66988.docx`) give slides whose words equal the words of LibreOffice's export, in order. Four of the other five have no text in either reference (`59378`, `bug62859`, `headerPic` and `issue_51265_3` have no `w:t` in any part, and POI's text for them is blank lines and tabs), so the refusal is right; the fifth, `emptydocumentwithheaderfooter.docx`, has text only in a header and a footer, which is the case above.
  - **Reference for the seed.** [MS-PPT] 2.3.3 says the persistIdSeed is at least the largest persist id. `backgrounds.ppt` (ids 1 to 6) and `pictures.ppt` (ids 1 to 7) of Apache POI's test files carry 3. LibreOffice sizes its persist table from the seed (`filter/source/msfilter/svdfppt.cxx`, `SdrPowerPointImport` constructor: `m_nPersistPtrCnt = m_aUserEditAtom.nMaxPersistWritten + 1`, line 1344; the loop that reads the directory stops at `nOfs <= m_nPersistPtrCnt`, line 1377, and a leftover count sets `m_bOk = false`, lines 1393 to 1397; master branch of 2026-10-24), so both LibreOffice 24.2.7 and 26.8 answered "source file could not be loaded". Raising only the seed to 6 and 7 makes both load: 4 and 5 pages, the slide counts Apache POI HSLF 5.4.0 reads (HSLF reads the directory and ignores the seed).
  - **Reference for the compound file limits.** Apache POI claims every block of a chain in `BlockStore.ChainLoopDetector` and refuses one claimed twice, uses one detector for all FAT, XFAT and small-block FAT sectors (`POIFSFileSystem.readCoreContents`: "Each block should only ever be used by one of the FAT, XFAT or Property Table"), and refuses a sector shift other than 9 or 12 (`HeaderBlock`, "Expected 2^9 or 2^12"); Apache License 2.0, trunk of 2026-10-24. olefile records the first sector of every stream and flags a stream that starts where another does (`olefile.py`, `_check_duplicate_stream`, called from `OleDirectoryEntry.__init__`), and cuts the FAT to the sectors of the file (`loadfat`, `nb_sect`); BSD license, master of 2026-10-24. libgsf marks the blocks of one chain in a bitmap to stop at a cycle (`gsf-infile-msole.c`, `ole_make_bat`; LGPL, behaviour only). None of them refuses a sector that two chains share past the first one, and the parser copied each entry's chain in full, so 1,024 entries over one 512 KiB chain (a file under 1 MiB) declared 512 MiB to copy; the retry made this parse run on every `.ppt` the suite cannot load. The loop rule of the detector is applied here across all chains, and the size budget refuses such a file before the first copy. The 805 compound files of the real-world sample cache and the 9 of the test fixtures give the same outcome before and after, and the 790 of them that parse give the same bytes for every stream.
  - **The encrypted files are not damaged.** `govdocs1-002164.ppt`, `ppt_with_png_encrypted.ppt` and the three `password_protected` files throw `EncryptedPowerPointFileException` in POI and have the encrypted token; the suite also fails on them, and "damaged" told the caller the wrong thing.
  - **The three damaged files** (`2100a8d4...`, `60f557c0...`, `7ffe3cab...`) differ from intact siblings of the corpus by 2, 9,230 and 11 bytes: a slide refers to persist id 131072, a master drawing is overwritten with a record of length 0xFFFFFFFF, a SlidePersistAtom header is overwritten with text. Both versions of the suite refuse them; POI skips what it cannot follow and reads the one slide of each, and so does the in-process reader (`txt` and `html` work). Converting what a lenient reader makes of them to PDF or pictures would hand out a page the document does not have, so the refusal stands.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Headers and footers of a Word document are not on the slides.** POI would put them there; LibreOffice and this service's `docx` to `txt` do not. A document with only headers and footers is refused.
  - **A table row is one line of a slide**, as in the text export; the slide builder still makes the first line the title and splits the rest into slides of five lines, so a long table runs over many slides (30,000 rows, 6,000 slides in the test).
  - **A retry costs a second run of the suite** only for a `.ppt` it refused with a seed below the directory, and the compound file is read once more in process.
  - **The file handed to the suite is a copy with four bytes changed**, which the suite loads as it loads any file; PowerPoint's own handling of such a seed was not tested.
  - **A compound file whose chains share a sector is refused**, where olefile reads it with a warning and POI reads each stream on its own; no file of the real-world cache or the fixtures has one. A sector shared with a FAT sector is not checked, as in POI.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Reading the repaired file in process**: the in-process reader has no text for these two files (pictures only), and the suite draws their pages.
  - **Making the in-process reader answer the targets the suite refuses**: it would give a text-only page for a file the suite calls damaged.
  - **Putting headers and footers on the slides**: the one reference that does is the only one that writes a text out of a Word file without layout, and no reference writes slides.
- **Verified by**: `tests/docx-to-slides-text.test.ts` (red on the code before the change, 8 of 16: cells of a table-only document, a table between paragraphs, a document that also draws a shape, tables nested past the table depth limit, 30,000 rows; the three real files against the words of LibreOffice's export and the five others against its empty export; tables nested 3,000 deep are a typed 413) and `tests/ppt-persist-id-seed.test.ts` (red on the code before the change: the repair on files written with the compound file writer in the mini stream and in whole sectors, on an encrypted file, a looping edit history and bytes that are no compound file, the two real files as 4 and 5 page PDFs, the encrypted files as 422, the three damaged files as refusals with their text read in process). Review fixes, each red on the code before them: a seed on the last byte of a mini sector, and of a sector, whose next sector of the chain lies elsewhere in the file (the seed came out as 0xDE in place of 0xABCDE), or where the sector the seed starts in is the last of the file (a `RangeError`, an untyped 500); an unreachable entry named `PowerPoint Document` next to the reachable one (the patch went by the wrong stream); an input file that cannot be read for the retry (ENOENT in place of the suite's refusal). `tests/cfbf-parse-limits.test.ts`, red before: a stream on the chain of another, from its first sector and from inside it, a mini stream inside the mini chain of another, 1,024 entries over one 512 KiB chain (refused with under 64 MiB of new buffers), a FAT sector listed twice, and 65,537 directory entries (65,536 still read). Each rule was taken out in turn to see its tests fail; the 1,024-entry test fails only with both the shared-sector rule and the budget out, since either refuses it.
- **Revisit when**: a reference writes slides from a Word document, the suite accepts a persist id seed below its directory, PowerPoint is found to refuse a repaired file, a real compound file is found whose chains share a sector, or QA decides that headers and footers belong on slides.

## 89. HTML tables on the in-process route: the width of their content or the width they state, pages shrunk for tables wider than the paper, and MathML as its text

- **Status**: Implemented (HTML to PDF rows "Found by #840" and "Found by #845" of issue #783, epic #760), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request). It revises two trade-offs of entry 51 (tables filled their text column; MathML was refused) and adds no rule to the office suite's staging (entry 69).
- **Decision**:
  - **An HTML table is as wide as its content, or as wide as it states, and never wider than its text column.** A table without a width takes its widest lines when they fit and the whole column when they do not; a `width` attribute (pixels or a percentage, zero ignored, as the HTML rules for dimension values read it) or an inline `width` in `px`, `pt` or `%` is the table's width, but not narrower than its minimum (its widest words). The columns share that width by content (CSS 2.1, 17.5.2.2), for every HTML table, with or without a table inside. Tables of the other in-process writers (Markdown through HTML is HTML; Word, HWP and text are not) keep the whole column and their equal columns.
  - **A table sits where its `align` attribute, or an aligning ancestor, puts it.** `align="center"` centres it, `left` and `right` put it on that side (a float is drawn without text beside it). A `center` element, and a `div` whose `align` is `center`, `middle`, `left` or `right`, aligns the tables inside it, in lists and quotes too; the innermost aligning element wins, and a table's own `align` wins over its ancestors. A table inside a table cell is not aligned by the elements around the outer table.
  - **A page whose table needs more than its text column is shrunk, as a print engine shrinks a page that overflows.** The page is laid out that many times wider and taller, margins included, and every page is drawn scaled down onto A4 (or the page the document states): the text of the whole document gets smaller by the same factor, and nothing is cut. A table needs its least width (24 pt per column, and the least of the tables inside it) or the length it states, when that is more; the widest table decides. The factor is at most 1.5. A page that would need more is refused with the limit named: `a table with 4 columns does not fit the page width: it needs 768pt of 495pt, and a page is shrunk at most 1.5 times; ...`. A table of too many columns is refused before it is measured.
  - **Links and destinations follow the shrink.** A link's box goes through pdfkit's transformation matrix; a named destination is put through the same matrix before pdfkit records it.
  - **MathML is drawn as the text it shows, not refused.** `<math>` is in line, or on a line of its own with `display="block"`. What MathML Core's style sheet hides is left out: every child element of `semantics` and of `maction` after the first, and the content of `mphantom`. White space between the elements of a formula is not drawn; the text of token elements (`mi`, `mn`, `mo`, `ms`, `mtext`) is.
  - **A line that a newline ends is measured with the newline.** pdfkit's line breaker measures a hard break with the word before it, so a column as wide as its longest line wrapped each line in two once columns were as narrow as their content (a 150-line cell took 6 pages, 3 of them empty). The writer's width of a line now holds the newline's advance, which is the width at which it draws the line unwrapped.
- **Why**:
  - **What the references do with the width of a table.**

    | Source | What it says or does | Use here |
    |---|---|---|
    | CSS 2.1, section 17.5.2.2 (https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS21/tables.html#auto-table-layout) | The used width of a table with `width: auto` is the greater of its minimum and the containing block, but its maximum when that is narrower; a stated width is used unless the minimum is greater | The table width rule |
    | WeasyPrint `layout/table.py`, `auto_table_layout`, lines 736 to 745 (commit 7e2dda0d of 2026-10-22, BSD) | `auto`: the minimum when the room is less, the room when it lies between, else the maximum; a stated width is raised to the minimum | Ported as `usedTableWidth` |
    | WeasyPrint `layout/preferred.py`, `table_and_columns_preferred_widths`, lines 684 to 691 | A pixel width is the table's minimum and maximum when measured inside another box, unless its content asks for more; a percentage counts as `auto` | How a table with a width counts in the cell that holds it (`statedPoints`) |
    | Blink `core/layout/length_utils.cc`, `ComputeUsedInlineSizeForTableFragment`, lines 618 to 648 (chromium main bd5372b1 of 2026-10-24, BSD) | A table's inline size is resolved from the min and max of its grid, as a fit-content box | Browsers shrink an automatic table to its content |
    | HTML Standard, rendering (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/rendering.html) | `table[align=center]` is `margin-inline: auto`, `left` and `right` float; `center` and `div[align=center|middle|left|right]` align descendants, the most deeply nested one winning, a descendant with its own `align` excepted; in quirks mode a table resets `text-align` | The alignment rules, and why tables in cells are not aligned from outside |

  - **What the references do with content wider than the paper.**

    | Source | What it does | Use here |
    |---|---|---|
    | Blink `core/frame/local_frame_view.cc`, `ForceLayoutForPagination`, lines 3817 to 3835; `core/layout/pagination_utils.cc`, `CalculateOverflowShrinkForPrinting`, lines 456 to 486; `core/frame/settings.json5`, `printingMaximumShrinkFactor` 1.5, lines 1306 to 1314 (chromium main of 2026-10-24) | Lays the document out again with every page scaled by its largest inline overflow, at most 1.5; past that it clips | The shrink and its limit of 1.5 |
    | Gecko `layout/printing/nsPrintJob.cpp`, shrink-to-fit, lines 1169 to 1184 (gecko-dev 5836a062, MPL, behaviour only) | Shrinks the whole document to its widest frame, for text documents to 20% at the least | A second engine that shrinks the whole page |
    | WeasyPrint `auto_table_layout` (above) | A table is never narrower than its minimum; what lies past the page is not drawn | The engine that does not shrink, and loses the words |
    | Chrome 155, headless print to PDF on this Mac, A4 portrait against A4 landscape (word heights from `pdftotext -bbox`) | `govdocs1-000063` is shrunk 1.25 times in portrait, `-000458` 1.11, `-001143` 1.08, `-001702` 1.05, with no word past the page edge; in landscape `-001143` is not shrunk | Measured behaviour of the engine most users print with |

  - **Why the least width and not the widest words.** This renderer's cells have 4 pt of padding on each side and a column floor of 24 pt, so its tables are wider than a browser's for the same content. Shrinking to the widest words (Blink's measure) would shrink 24 of the 450 pages in landscape, 6 of them by the full 1.5, among them `govdocs1-001143`, which Chrome prints unscaled in landscape. With the least width, 2 pages are shrunk in landscape (`-001143` 1.035 times, `-001543` 1.039 times, the second for a stated width of 1,028 px), and words wider than their column are broken as before.
  - **MathML.** Blink's MathML style sheet (`core/css/mathml.css`, lines 67 to 79, chromium main of 2026-10-24) hides `semantics > :not(:first-child)` and `maction > :not(:first-child)` and makes `mphantom` invisible; the renderer has no formula layout, so it keeps what that sheet shows, as text, which is what a reader without MathML layout shows and what search and copy need. The refusal cost the whole page for one formula.
  - **The 450 saved pages of the public government corpus, in-process route** (worker route with `orientation`, landscape, and the in-process renderer alone, portrait; macOS and the Linux VM give the same counts). Landscape: 449 converted before and 450 after (`govdocs1-001143`, 768 pt of 741 pt, now shrunk 1.035 times), 0 refused after that converted before, 0 pages with a word past the page edge before and after, and the letters and digits of the page that the PDF lacks are the same on every page (36,423 on 20 pages, all content the renderer leaves out on purpose). Portrait: 429 before and 449 after; the 20 pages that were refused for nested tables convert, each shrunk at most 1.5 times, with none of their letters or digits missing; `govdocs1-001143` needs 1.55 times and is still refused. The page counts of 78 pages (landscape, macOS) change, because tables are as narrow as their content.
  - **Why macOS refused 21 pages that the Linux VM converted (row "Found by #845").** Fonts are not the cause: the least width of a table is 24 pt per column plus padding, which no font changes, and the same 21 pages are refused with the same messages on macOS and on the VM in portrait (495 pt of text width). #840 counted 447 of 450 in landscape (741 pt), and #845 counted in portrait. The worker's in-process route is portrait when no orientation is asked for and the office suite fails, so those pages were refused in production too; 20 of them convert now.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Tables look different.** Every HTML table on this route is laid out by content, so tables that filled the column are narrower, and columns that were equal are not; 78 of 450 pages change their page count (none loses text). Tables of other writers are unchanged.
  - **A shrunk page has smaller text.** At the limit of 1.5, 11 pt body text is drawn at 7.3 pt, as a browser draws it.
  - **Past 1.5 the page is refused, where Blink clips.** Clipping loses the words past the edge; a refusal names the cause, and the office suite route is tried first when it is installed and no orientation is asked for. One corpus page in portrait (`govdocs1-001143`) is refused.
  - **A float is not wrapped.** `align="left"` and `"right"` put the table on that side; text does not flow beside it.
  - **MathML is flat text.** `x²` reads `x2`, a fraction reads numerator then denominator, as the elements stand in the source.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keeping tables at the width of the column** (entry 51): the browsers and WeasyPrint make an automatic table as wide as its content.
  - **Shrinking only the table that is too wide**: no reference does it; a print engine scales the whole page, so text keeps one size across the document.
  - **Shrinking to the widest words** (Blink's overflow measure): over-shrinks this renderer's wider tables, see above.
  - **Clipping past the limit, or a landscape page for the table**: clipping loses words; a page turned for one table changes the document's page format, which no reference does on its own.
  - **Refusing MathML** (entry 51): costs the page for a formula.
- **Verified by**: `tests/html-pdf-nested-tables.test.ts` (red before the change: a table as wide as its content and as wide as `100%` and `200` px; alignment by `align`, `center` and `div align`, with a table's own `align` winning; a page of 25 columns shrunk 600 / 495.28 times with every word on A4; a table of 900 px shrinking the page and an internal link still landing on its heading; 40 columns refused with the limit named; `govdocs1-001143` in landscape with no word past the edge and no letter or digit missing; a column as narrow as its 150 lines cutting the row over 3 pages with no empty page) and the guards there for 5,000 cells (refused in under 2 s), widths of 99999999 px and 100000 % (converted, no word past the edge), tables nested 33 and 400 deep and a colspan of 1,000; `tests/html-pdf-inprocess-omissions.test.ts` and `tests/pdf-unicode-text-writers.test.ts` (red before: MathML drawn as `Before x+1 after.`, `y=2` on its own line without the annotation, `shown` without the second `maction` child and without `mphantom`; MathML nested 150 deep answered in under 5 s). The corpus runs above were made with a harness that converts each page and reads it with `pdfinfo`, `pdftotext -bbox` and `pdftotext -raw` against parse5's words of the page.
- **Revisit when**: a page that callers need is refused past the limit of 1.5, the renderer takes cell padding and spacing from the page (its tables would then be as narrow as a browser's, and the widest words could decide the shrink), or text flows beside a floating table.

## 90. HTML to PDF: the in-process PDF when the office suite's PDF has words past the page edge

- **Status**: Implemented (HTML to PDF row "Found by #844" of issue #783, epic #760), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request). It follows entry 69 (the office suite's staging rules) and entry 89 (the in-process renderer that now draws the pages those rules cannot fix).
- **Decision**:
  - **The office suite's PDF of an HTML page is read once before it is handed out.** The PDF text reader (pdf.js, on its worker thread) gives the box of every word in the page as displayed (rotation applied, the CropBox inside the MediaBox). A word counts as past the edge when its box reaches more than 0.01 pt beyond the left, right, top or bottom edge of its page. 0.01 pt is ten times the 0.001 pt to which the office suite writes coordinates, so it absorbs rounding and nothing else.
  - **When any word is past an edge, the in-process renderer's PDF is handed out instead**, and the answer names the words and the pages (`fallbackReason`, `native-soffice: 38 words past the page edge on pages 1, 3`). The office suite's file is deleted only after the other PDF exists.
  - **The office suite's PDF stays** when no word is past an edge, when the check cannot be made (the PDF is over the in-memory limit, cannot be read, or the read passes its 10 s budget or a limit of the PDF text reader: failing toward the earlier behaviour, never a refusal), when the in-process renderer refuses the page (a table it cannot fit even shrunk 1.5 times, for example), and when the request needs the office suite (`pdfStandard`) or forbids the in-process engine (`inProcessFallback: false`).
  - **Only HTML sources are checked.** Markdown, text and HWP take the office suite only for CJK or complex-script text and are not part of this row.
- **Why**:
  - **What a word past the edge is, in the PDF.** pdf.js leaves out every glyph whose origin is past the edge of the view box when it reads a page (`getTextContent` in `src/core/evaluator.js`, `compareWithLastPosition`, which tests the glyph origin against the view box; read in pdfjs-dist 6.3.289, `legacy/build/pdf.worker.mjs` lines 42034 to 42042), and Poppler's `pdftotext -bbox` shows the same boxes (a crafted page with `stra|ddle` cut by the edge gives the box `xMin 577.436 xMax 597.440` from both; a word wholly past the edge is in neither). So the check sees every word that stands across an edge, and a word the layout put wholly past it is not in the PDF text at all. A page whose overflow cut every word cleanly is not seen, and the page stays as it was.
  - **The reader agrees with Poppler on the whole corpus.** On the 448 PDFs the office suite wrote for the 450 govdocs pages (VM, LibreOffice 24.2.7, Poppler 24.02), pdf.js finds 6,868 words past an edge on 38 pages with a tolerance of 0, and `pdftotext -bbox` finds the same 6,868 words on the same 38 pages. The 410 other PDFs have no word past an edge at all (the check flags nothing there), so no tolerance is needed for noise.
  - **Why the tolerance is not the glyph bearing.** A box is the glyph advances, which include the side bearings of the first and last letters, so a bearing allowance of 0.5 to 2 pt is the obvious choice. It hides real cuts: the cut word is a glyph that starts before the edge and ends after it, and the glyphs after it are gone.

    | Tolerance (pt) | Words past an edge | Pages |
    |---|---|---|
    | 0 | 6,868 | 38 |
    | 0.1 | 6,783 | 38 |
    | 0.25 | 6,765 | 37 |
    | 0.5 | 6,724 | 35 |
    | 1 | 6,661 | 35 |
    | 2 | 6,194 | 35 |

    The three pages that 0.5 pt would keep each have one word that ends 0.2 to 0.4 pt past the right edge and is cut: `govdocs1-000877` (`Environmen` of `Environment`, 0.23 pt), `-001523` (`Confere` of `Conference`, 0.34 pt) and `-000063` (`abatement`, 0.38 pt, the last word of a line).
  - **What the standards and the engines say** (read for this change, no code copied):

    | Source | What it says | Use here |
    |---|---|---|
    | pdf.js `src/core/evaluator.js`, `getTextContent` and `compareWithLastPosition` (pdfjs-dist 6.3.289, Apache 2.0) | A glyph whose origin is past the view box is not in the text content; the view box is the page's CropBox inside its MediaBox | What the word boxes mean, and why a cut word is seen by its last glyph that starts on the page |
    | Entry 89: Blink `ForceLayoutForPagination` and `CalculateOverflowShrinkForPrinting`, Gecko `nsPrintJob` shrink-to-fit | A print engine lays the page out again smaller (at most 1.5 times in Blink) instead of cutting what lies past the edge | The decision itself: the pages the office suite cuts are drawn by the renderer that shrinks them |
    | Entry 89: WeasyPrint `auto_table_layout` | An engine that does not shrink loses the words past the edge, as the office suite does | The behaviour this entry stops handing out |

  - **The 450 saved pages of the public government corpus, through the worker route on the VM** (`executeWorkerConversion`, no options; origin/main at 14525c1f against this change; the same two pages are refused before and after for `&` in a style sheet, entry 51):

    | | Before | After |
    |---|---|---|
    | Pages converted | 448 | 448 |
    | Pages refused that converted before | | 0 |
    | Pages with a word past an edge (`pdftotext -bbox`, tolerance 0) | 38 | 1 |
    | Words past an edge | 6,868 | 18 |
    | Pages handed out as the in-process PDF because of this check | 0 | 37 |
    | Letters and digits of the page that the PDF text lacks (parse5 against `pdftotext -raw`), all pages | 288,581 | 56,424 |
    | The same on the 37 pages | 232,551 | 394 |
    | The same on the 411 other converted pages (unchanged) | 56,030 | 56,030 |
    | Pages with another page count (22 more pages, 7 fewer) | | 29 |

    The page that keeps its word past the edge is `govdocs1-001143` (18 words): the in-process renderer needs the page 1.55 times smaller in portrait (limit 1.5, entry 89) and refuses it, so the office suite's PDF stays. The 37 are the 38 pages with words past an edge less that one. Three other pages (`-000071`, `-001120`, `-001575`) already reach the in-process renderer through the 45 s stage timeout (entry 69), before and after. The largest changes: `govdocs1-001428` was 6 pages with 90,605 letters missing and is 62 pages with none missing; `-001429` was 284 pages with 80,080 missing (its layout is not deterministic, entry 69) and is 576 pages with none missing.
  - **The one page that has more letters missing, and why.** `govdocs1-000877` lacks 1 letter in the office suite's PDF (the cut `Environmen`) and 384 in the in-process one. The 384 are the text of seven tables with `style="display: none;"` (the drop-down menus, 391 letters in all). The office suite draws them; a browser, and the in-process renderer, do not print what the page hides. The two other pages with letters left in the in-process PDF (`-001703` and `-001718`, 5 each, 40 and 41 before) are content the renderer leaves out on purpose (entry 51).
  - **What the check costs** (VM, 4 cores, idle, Node 24, the 448 PDFs of the office suite, read one after the other on a warm thread, median of 5 runs per PDF, runs of 19.8 to 20.1 s in all): a median of 13.9 ms and a 95th percentile of 149 ms per PDF, 4.2 ms and 8.4 ms per page, 3.1 s for the largest (882 pages), and 0.29 s for the first PDF of a process (the thread starts). Through the worker route, a page that stays with the office suite takes a median of 26 ms and a 95th percentile of 264 ms longer than before (408 pages, one run each, which includes the run-to-run noise of the office suite), against a median of 0.35 s for the office suite alone. The read is one pdf.js thread going page after page (user time is 1.3 times real time), and the budget of 10 s covers about 2,400 pages at the median rate, 2.7 times the largest document of the corpus.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A page that overflows looks different.** It is laid out by the in-process renderer: tables as wide as their content, the page shrunk up to 1.5 times (entry 89), the fonts of that renderer. 29 of the 37 pages have another page count (some more pages because nothing is cut, some fewer because the tables are narrower). Their text is the page's text.
  - **The in-process renderer leaves out what the office suite draws.** Form controls, frames and SVG are left out with a warning (entry 51), and so is anything the page hides (`display: none`), which is why `govdocs1-000877` has 383 letters fewer.
  - **A page cut at its edge by a layout the check cannot see stays.** A word that the layout put wholly past an edge is not in the PDF, and a page whose only lost words are such words has no word the check can see.
  - **Every HTML conversion reads its PDF once more.** 14 ms at the median, 0.1 s at the 95th percentile of the corpus, and the read stops at 10 s.
  - **The check fails toward the earlier behaviour.** A PDF the reader refuses or a read that passes its budget keeps the office suite's output, so a hostile PDF cannot make the conversion fail, only skip the check.
  - **One page of the corpus keeps its words past the edge** (`govdocs1-001143`, portrait), until the in-process renderer can shrink it by 1.55 times or the office suite draws it.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A tolerance for the side bearings of the glyphs** (0.5 to 2 pt): hides cut words on 3 of 38 pages, see above.
  - **Counting the words of the HTML against the words of the PDF**: it needs a guess at what the page shows (hidden elements, form controls, generated text). The letters of the page that the PDF text lacks are 56,030 on the 411 pages this change leaves alone, so that count also holds hidden text, content left out on purpose and other losses, and cannot tell a page cut at an edge from a page that is whole.
  - **Handing out the in-process PDF for every HTML page**: it leaves out form controls, frames and SVG and lays tables out differently on the 411 pages the office suite draws whole, where the office suite keeps the page's structure.
  - **More staging rules for the layouts left** (data tables whose least width is more than the text area, centered tables of fixed cells, floating tables): entry 69 and the measurements of the change before this one found no attribute the suite's HTML import honours for them.
  - **Reading the in-process PDF with the same check**: its 450 pages had no word past an edge (entry 89) and the check would double the cost of the pages that fall back.
- **Verified by**: `tests/pdf-page-edge.test.ts` (words across the right, left, top and bottom edges of crafted PDFs counted with their pages, the rounding tolerance, a rotated page, a CropBox narrower than the MediaBox, the 1 ms deadline over 300 pages, bytes that are not a PDF), `tests/pdf-text-host.test.ts` (a job's deadline is shorter than the host's but never longer), and `tests/html-pdf-page-edge-fallback.test.ts` (red before the change: an office suite PDF with a word 27 pt past the edge is replaced by a PDF in which `pdftotext -bbox` finds no word outside its page and no letter is missing; kept when no word is past an edge, when the in-process renderer refuses the page (a table of 40 columns), when the read passes its deadline, when the PDF cannot be read, with `pdfStandard`, and with `inProcessFallback: false`; and two real pages of the corpus, `govdocs1-001794` and `-000640`, converted by the office suite with a word past the edge and handed out as the in-process PDF with none). The corpus run above, the cost and the tolerance table were made on the VM (Ubuntu 24.04, LibreOffice 24.2.7, Poppler 24.02, Node 24) with a harness that converts each page and reads it with `pdfinfo`, `pdftotext -bbox` and `pdftotext -raw` against parse5's words of the page.
- **Revisit when**: the worker image's LibreOffice (25.2) is measured and draws fewer pages past the edge, the nightly run shows a page whose in-process PDF is worse than the office suite's cut one, the in-process renderer can draw `govdocs1-001143`, or pages with only words wholly past an edge (not seen by the check) show up in real use.

## 91. Nightly rows of 2026-10-24: the AVIF encoder starts from the launcher helper, the floor of the demosaic thread test, a dated copy of one EPUB, and speed rows of public samples as known gaps

- **Status**: Implemented (rows "Found by #867" of issue #759, epic #759, and the failed jobs of nightly run 40074698318 on commit 4c4b1dc3), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request). QA decided that a speed row of a public sample may be a known gap (the second to last bullet of the Decision). The thread count of photograph AVIF is an open finding that waits for a measurement (the last bullet of the Decision, and Why), and this change leaves the environment of the quality jobs as it was. Entry 93 measured it, encodes photographs in one tile and gives the quality jobs the worker's heap bound.
- **Decision**:
  - **The AVIF command-line encoder is started through `launchSandboxedBinary`** (`src/lib/conversions/avif-cli.ts`), the launcher helper of entry 31, as `qpdf`, `gs`, `rsvg-convert` and Poppler are (entries 31, 34 and 75). The helper runs the same `executeSandboxedBinary` with the same options, so the sanitized environment, the network namespace where the host allows one, the address-space limit (5,120 MB), the file-size limit, the resident-memory poll, the 180 s time limit, the 1 MiB diagnostics limit, the typed errors and the stop of the process group on an abort are those of a direct start. The helper is used only where `launchPays` says the fork it saves costs more than its round trip (a process of more than 112 MiB, with the 4 KiB the encoder prints counted as the output to copy back); a direct start is the fallback until the helper is ready, with the helper off (`SANDBOX_LAUNCHER=off`) and in a small process.
  - **22 rows leave `bench/parity-gaps.json`**, the ones the gate named as "now at parity" in nightly run 40074698318: `video/clip.mp4->h264`, `audio/music.wav->opus`, `document/pdf-text->txt`, the nine `compression/mixed.*` rows, the eight `pdf-ops` rows (`protect`, `decrypt`, `unlock`, `split`, `extract`, `delete`, `reorder`, `rotate`) and `vector/shapes.svg->pdf` and `vector/shapes.eps->png`. The ratios of that run were 0.98 to 20 over 6 to 30 pairs.
  - **The floor of `tests/raw-demosaic-threads.perf.test.ts` is 1.6** (four threads over one), from 2.2, and the test prints the speed-up it measured, so a pass leaves a number in the log. 1.6 is what two whole cores give less a tenth.
  - **`book-pg84.epub` is fetched from a dated capture** (`https://web.archive.org/web/20261007052056id_/https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/84/pg84-images.epub`), whose bytes are the ones the manifest pinned (474,012 bytes, SHA-256 `7ae81b2a5cdb7ac08f39429784874157accb749dfd303e384f983ef31226d8f4`), not the file of the Gutenberg host, which is rebuilt in place (439,444 bytes, `last-modified` 2026-10-23, since the nightly run of 2026-10-24 failed on its digest). No baseline entry changes: the bytes are the same.
  - **The quality jobs keep their environment.** No `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` is set in the nightly quality shards or the `parity quality` job of a pull request (QA 2026-10-24: the thread count of photograph AVIF is decided after the measurement below, not before it), so photograph AVIF is encoded on 2 threads there (`imageThreadsFor`, heap not bounded) as it was when the baseline was recorded, and the speed jobs keep the `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX: "2"` they have.
  - **A speed row of a public sample can be a known gap, under the rules of a generated row.** `bench/parity-gaps.json` may hold an entry for such a row (the issue, the ratio, the `history` of CI-measured medians with the commit of each run). The nightly run, which times the samples of `PUBLIC_SPEED_SAMPLES`, judges the row as it judges any tracked row: it passes while its median is not below the 99 % one-sided prediction bound of the history or 65 % of the history's median (`SPEED_GAP_FLOOR`), and it fails below them (`judgeAbsolute`, unchanged). What changed is the check on an entry that a pull request adds or edits (`gapBackingFailure` in `bench/parity.ts`): the speed job of a pull request times the generated corpus only (`BENCH_CORPUS_TIER=pr`), so for a row it does not time (`timedByRun` in `bench/judge.ts`, from `rowInScope`) only the form of the entry is checked, as for a row measured against the base: the ratio is a number, and every history point the change adds carries a commit, which only `bench:refresh-speed` writes, from the `bench-speed-results` artifact of a nightly run. A row the run does time is still backed by its interval, as before. `tests/bench-public-unified.test.ts` now refuses an entry for a public sample that the nightly run does not time (a sample outside `PUBLIC_SPEED_SAMPLES`), where it refused every entry for a public sample.
  - **Two such rows are tracked.** `image/wm-deep-dart.png->avif/throughput` (issue 641, ratio 0.94, ten runs from 2026-10-18 to 2026-10-24: 0.8697, 0.8654, 0.8923, 0.8489, 0.8604, 0.8705, 0.8527, 0.8743, 0.9043, 0.9418; prediction bound 0.7999, geometric mean 0.8776) and `compression/silesia-xml.xz->tar/throughput` (issue 685, ratio 0.93, seven runs since the step of 2026-10-19: 1.0051, 0.9348, 0.9970, 0.9503, 0.7280, 1.0075, 0.9347; prediction bound 0.6358, geometric mean 0.9319). Both histories were written by `bench:refresh-speed --write` from the twelve `bench-speed-results` artifacts of the nightly runs of the default branch (2026-10-16 to 2026-10-24, oldest first, one report per call), with the baseline written to a scratch copy so that only the two entries enter the gap file. The tool keeps the latest 10 points per row, restarts a history at a step up, and adds no point for a run in which the row passed (2026-10-21 at 1.0366 and 2026-10-22 at 1.0079 for the xz row), so those two runs are not in its history. Judged against the report of 2026-10-24 (`--compare-report`), both rows are listed as tracked and the run passes.
  - **Open finding: the thread count of photograph AVIF.** The encoder's thread count changes the bytes of the file, and the reference's do not change with `-j` (Why, below). Nothing is decided and no entry tracks a photograph AVIF quality row for it: the `photo-b.png` entry and the `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` lines of the quality jobs that an earlier version of this change held are out. The cause is libvips' automatic tiling (`libvips/foreign/heifsave.c` lines 649 to 655 switch the encoder's `auto-tiles` on; libheif `libheif/plugins/encoder_aom.cc` line 1055 passes it to libaom as `AV1E_SET_AUTO_TILES`; libaom `set_auto_tiles` in `av1/av1_cx_iface.c` v3.13.1 lines 1019 to 1054 takes the tile count from the thread count). Next step: measure the pinned libvips build with auto-tiles off on x86-64 and arm64 (bytes against the reference, BD-rate by thread count, speed by thread count), then decide the thread count of the quality jobs and of the service from that measurement.
