That measurement is not part of this change.
- **Why**:
  - **The encoder row, `wm-deep-dart.png` to AVIF (reference 31 ms).** The reference's `avifenc` and ours are the same binary with the same arguments on the same file; `avifenc` takes 29.2 ms from the return of the start to its exit when started alone from this process and 29.5 ms in the conversion. Profile of the conversion on the arm64 VM (4 vCPU, medians of 30): 0.42 ms from the call to the start of the run (dispatch and header reads), 0.26 ms to create the directory and write the picture, 0.9 to 1.5 ms in the call that starts the process (a fork of the 210 to 270 MB process, against 0.3 ms from a process of 50 MB, entry 36), 29.5 ms of the encoder, 0.2 ms to read the output and remove the directory. The resource-limit wrapper adds 0.25 ms (head against base 1.006 to 1.010 with it left out, which the sandbox does not allow). Interleaved against the reference in the parity bench (24 pairs, six runs): base 0.924 to 0.935 of the reference, head against base 1.009 to 1.022 (median 1.014) with the encoder started from the helper. The helper takes the fork out of the main thread and costs a round trip of two pipes. Entry 36 measured the two equal at 206 MB (1.84 ms each) when it only timed the start; the interleaved pairs of the whole conversion put the helper 1.4 % ahead at the 210 to 270 MB this process holds, and what changed between the two measurements was not traced.
  - **What the picture cannot skip.** The encoder reads its input by file name and opens it twice, once to guess the format and once to read it (libavif 1.0.4, the version of the CI runner and of the VM, `apps/shared/avifutil.c` lines 165 to 172, `avifGuessFileFormat`, then `apps/shared/avifpng.c` line 246, `avifPNGRead`), so a pipe loses the bytes of the first open, and `--stdin` reads Y4M only (`apps/avifenc.c` lines 106 and 1175; 1.2.1, which the worker image installs, says the same at line 225), which would move the conversion to YUV into this process and change the bytes (entry 36). The file is therefore written, and that write, the start and the read-back are the cost of a conversion this short.
  - **Measured and left out, each on the same pairs.** A directory made once and never removed, to take the create and remove off the path: head against base 0.996 to 0.999 (nothing). The sanitized environment replaced by the full one: 0.992 to 1.002 (nothing). Starting the encoder from the PNG header, before the image library has read it: 1.004 to 1.012 alone and about 0.9 % on top of the helper, for a second entry point that repeats the checks of `isPlainPng` and has to stop the run when one fails. What remains against a reference that has none of it is the dispatch and header reads (0.4 ms), the write of the picture (0.3 ms), the round trip of the helper and the wrapper (about 0.5 ms) and the read-back (0.2 ms). It would close only with the picture reaching the encoder without a file, or with an encoder that starts faster (a build of `avifenc` that links its libraries in, installed as `AVIFENC_PATH`, which is a change of the worker image and the CI setup that this entry does not make and did not measure). The row read 0.85 to 0.94 on the CI runner in the nine runs and 0.94 in the last, after #867; with the helper it should read about 0.955, which is still under the line.
  - **The xz row, `silesia-xml.xz->tar`.** 7-Zip 26.01 (the pinned build, entry 50) runs the decode as one process (`x -so -y -txz -si`), which takes 17 to 19 ms for the 5.3 MB tar on the VM against 26.1 ms for `xz -dc` (entry 50). Over the nine runs the median of the row is 1.005, 0.935, 0.997, 0.950, 0.728, 1.037, 1.008, 1.008 and 0.935 on the CI runner; the interval at 50 pairs was [0.88, 1.01] in the last, so it cannot clear 0.97 whatever the median is, because the run-to-run spread of the runner is 11 % (`SPEED_HISTORY_MIN_LOG_SPREAD`). The same 7-Zip build reads 1.37 to 1.52 on `silesia-ooffice.xz->tar` and 1.05 to 1.18 on `silesia-xml.7z->tar` in the same runs, and 1.05 to 1.09 on this row on the VM (23 pairs), so the code is not slower than the reference. This tar is the most compressible source of the set (the .xz holds 5.3 MB in 453 KB), so the decode is mostly match copies, where the assembler decoder gains little over `xz -d`, and what ours adds shows (the start of 7-Zip, the 5.3 MB tar through a pipe and one copy). No decoder change was made: entry 50 measured the pieces (each under 1 ms) and found no variant faster.
  - **The demosaic floor.** The tile rows are independent, so the serial part is small (4 threads over 1 read 3.78 for AMaZE and 3.78 for AHD on the four cores of the VM, 3.67 and 3.70 on a 12-core laptop: a serial share of 1 to 3 %). Pinned to two cores of the VM (`taskset -c 0,1`) the same code reads 1.75 and 1.93, and to three cores 2.58 and 2.60. The 4 vCPUs of a hosted runner are hardware threads of fewer cores (an inference from how the VM size is defined; the runner does not report its topology), and nine nightly runs from 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-23 stayed over 2.2 while the run of 2026-10-24 read 2.18 for AMaZE (193.58 ms against 422.73 ms) after 8.9 s in the test, against 2.0 to 4.4 s on the other nights: all the extra passes the helper takes while the ratio is over the bound (up to 12) stayed over it, so that runner gave this process fewer than three cores' worth for the whole test. A floor of 2.2 is more than two cores give. 1.6 still fails threads that do not run side by side (1.01 and 1.00 with the candidate on one thread) and does not fail two cores' worth.
  - **The photograph AVIF rows by encoder thread count.** `VIPS_CONCURRENCY` 1, 2 to 3, 4 to 7 and 8 give `photo-b.png` BD-rate in SSIM of -0.47, +0.71, +1.99 and +3.49 % and in PSNR of -2.41, -1.24, +0.09 and +1.68 %, against a reference that does not change with `-j` from 2 to 8 (the same file for `-j 2, 3, 4, 6, 8`, libaom 3.8.2). The steps are libaom's automatic tiling: libvips 8.18 `libvips/foreign/heifsave.c` lines 649 to 655 switch the encoder's `auto-tiles` on, libheif `libheif/plugins/encoder_aom.cc` (read at v1.20.2, line 1055; sharp ships 1.23.5) hands it to libaom as `AV1E_SET_AUTO_TILES`, and libaom's `set_auto_tiles` (`av1/av1_cx_iface.c` lines 1019 to 1054, read at v3.13.1; sharp ships 3.15.1) takes the number of tiles as the smaller of the frame area over 128 x 128, 32 and the thread count, rounded down to a power of two: 1 tile for one thread, 2 for 2 or 3, 4 for 4 to 7, 8 for 8, exactly the steps above. Tiles cost compression, and they are why 4 threads are 1.4 to 1.9 times faster than the reference (photo-b 1.38, kodim23 1.89, clic-paul-itkin-46101 1.46 at 4 threads; 1.10, 1.30 and 0.93 at 3; 0.93, 1.20 and 0.86 at 2). The reference tool (`avifenc`) has its auto-tiling off (entry 36). On the 13 photographs of the quick image set that the thread count changes, 4 threads add 0.014 to 0.95 points of BD-rate (median 0.25, 25 rows, none lower) over 2 or 3, and two photographs pass the allowance of 1.5 only at 3 threads or fewer (`photo-b.png` +1.99 % in SSIM, and in the full family `clic-schicka-307.png` +1.67 % in PSNR and +1.95 % in SSIM with 410 bytes over its 3 % allowance; its baseline, recorded at 2 threads on the CI runner, is 0.22 and 0.28 %); the `clic-sergey-zolkin-21232.png` rows that entry 1 tracks read +1.09 and +1.34 %, inside the allowance, at 4 threads on arm64. The CPU matters as well: the reference's own bytes for `clic-mullermarc-184.png` differ by 2.9 % between the CI runner (x86-64) and the VM, so these values are the VM's and the CI run decides.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - The helper is one more process of the worker, already started for `qpdf` and the renderers; a conversion that arrives before it is ready starts the encoder directly. An encoder that is killed with the helper (a helper that dies) fails the runs it held, as for the other programs.
  - A floor of 1.6 lets a four-core machine lose more than half of its speed-up (3.7 to 1.7) without failing; with the candidate on two threads the speed-up reads 1.76 and 1.96, over the floor, and it is the test's check of the thread count the result reports (4) that catches it.
  - The dated capture depends on a public web archive being reachable when the corpus is fetched; the digest check refuses any other bytes, the corpus cache keeps the file between runs, and a failed fetch is a skipped row, not a wrong one. Six other Gutenberg files are pinned to the host the same way: their digests match today, and captures with the pinned bytes exist for four of them (`pg11` EPUB, `pg345` EPUB and MOBI, `pg1661` EPUB and MOBI, `pg2701` EPUB) but not for the `pg11` MOBI, so they are not moved here.
  - An entry for a public row is not backed by the pull request that adds it: its speed job does not time the row, so a ratio or a history that was written by hand is caught by the commit it must carry (the form check) and by review of the `bench:refresh-speed` output, which anyone can rerun on the same artifacts, and then by the nightly run, which judges the row against the entry with no further excuse. The artifacts are kept 30 days, so an entry is written within that time of the runs it holds. The decision whether a row is timed comes from `bench/scope.ts` and the corpus manifest, which are the change's own files and not gate files.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Handing the picture through a pipe, the standard input or a named pipe**: the reader opens it twice and `--stdin` is Y4M (above).
  - **A directory pool, a single reused directory, or removing it after the answer**: head against base 0.996 to 0.999 with the directory made once and never removed.
  - **Starting the encoder before the image library has read the header**: 0.9 % for a second path that repeats `isPlainPng`.
  - **Dropping the resource-limit wrapper**: 0.8 % and a weaker sandbox; the limits stay.
  - **Another speed floor for the demosaic test from one night's number**: 2.0 would have passed that night and failed the next noisy one; the floor is set from the two-core figure, not from the night.
  - **Stretching the gate for the xz row** (more pairs, a wider interval, a lower line): the gate is not loosened for one row; the row is tracked instead, under the line and the floor of every tracked row.
  - **Timing the public samples in the speed job of a pull request to back their entries**: it adds the public speed rows to every pull request's speed job, which the gate files of the base fix (`scripts/ci-parity-base-gate.mjs`) and which costs many pairs per row; not measured, and the nightly run already judges them.
  - **Capping photograph AVIF at 3 threads** to keep tile columns down: `photo-b.png` returns to +0.71 % in SSIM, and the speed of `clic-paul-itkin-46101.png` falls to 0.93 of the reference, past the speed allowance (decision for QA).
  - **Switching libvips' auto-tiles off in the worker's libvips build** (a one-line patch of `heifsave.c`, to be recorded with the pinned libvips version and re-applied on each upgrade): not measured yet, it is the next step of the open finding; it gives the reference's tile layout and loses the tile parallelism that gives the speed (decision for QA).
  - **Raising the allowance of the AVIF rows for photographs**: a gate change that this entry does not make.
- **Verified by**: `tests/image-avif-launcher.test.ts` (the encoder's parent process is the helper, the file equals the one written with the helper off, the working directory is the run's own and is removed, a failing encoder is the typed error; red with the call back on `executeSandboxedBinary`, 2 of 3), `tests/image-avif-direct-handoff.test.ts`, `tests/bench-parity.test.ts` (the gap file after the 22 removals and the two public rows; a tracked public row passes inside the bound of its history and fails below it in the nightly run, a new entry for a row the pull request does not time is checked for its form, and a row the run times is still backed; red without the `timedByRun` wiring in `bench/judge.ts`), `tests/bench-public-unified.test.ts` (an entry names a row some run times), `tests/raw-demosaic-threads.perf.test.ts` (red with the candidate on one thread, 1.01 and 1.00 against 1.6), and the fetch of the pinned EPUB through `httpBytes` with the digest of the manifest. Measured on the 4-core arm64 VM with the head against the base interleaved in the parity bench (`--parity --speed-only --quick --base-root`) and, for the thread counts, `--quality-only --quick` and the full image family; the x86-64 numbers come from the nightly run.
- **Revisit when**: the measurement of the pinned libvips build with auto-tiles off is made (decide the thread count of photograph AVIF in the quality jobs and the service, then record the baseline and the entries), the worker image gets an `avifenc` of its own build, one of the two public rows reaches parity (`bench:refresh-speed` lists it; remove its entry), the artifacts of a pull request's speed job can carry the public samples, or the Gutenberg host stops rebuilding its files.

## 92. Acknowledging an intended speed slowdown against the base, row by row, single-use

- **Status**: Implemented (speed gate, epic #759), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request). It adds the mechanism only; the first change to use it is the photograph AVIF tiles change, which matches the reference encoder's single-tile AV1 encode and is 18 to 41 % slower than its base on four photograph rows while it stays at or above the reference (0.98 to 1.15).
- **Decision**:
  - **A section of `bench/parity-gaps.json`, `acceptedSlowdowns`, holds the acknowledgements.** Each entry is `{ id, issue, pr, reason }`: one speed row id, the issue that records the trade-off, the pull request the entry was written for, and a one-line reason. `validateGaps` (`bench/parity-gaps.ts`) refuses a quality row id, a missing or non-integer issue or pull request, an empty or multi-line reason, a field it does not know, a row listed twice, a row that is also a tracked gap (a gap is a row below the reference, an acknowledged slowdown stays at it), and more than 16 entries (`MAX_ACCEPTED_SLOWDOWNS`; the cap is ours, since an entry is removed in the next bench change and a handful are open at a time).
  - **The rule.** In a run that measures the row against the base, when `speed-slower-than-base` would fail the row (the one-sided upper bound of base time / head time under the row's line, confirmed by fresh pairs) and an acknowledgement names the row, the row passes as `speed-slowdown-acknowledged` if the head is not credibly below the reference: the existing reference bound of the row (`abHeadVsReferenceUpper` under the pass line, 0.90 (entry 114), with its confirmation `abLostConfirmed`, the test `speed-lost-parity` applies, without that rule's condition that the base was at the reference). A head credibly below the reference fails as `speed-slower-than-base`, as before, and the message says the acknowledgement does not apply. A row with no entry takes the old path: the verdicts of all the rows the gate judged before are unchanged.
  - **Single-use, enforced by the gate.** An entry applies only if the gap file of the base (`--base-gaps`, which the speed job already passes) does not hold an entry for the same row and the same `pr`. Once the change has merged, the base holds it, so it excuses nothing, not even a later change that slows the same row; rewording the reason does not make an entry new, a new `pr` does. With no gap file of the base no entry applies.
  - **Stale entries are reported.** A row with an entry whose slowdown the run does not show (the entry is in the base, or it is new and the head is not credibly slower than the base) passes as `acknowledgement-unused`, listed under ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS NOT NEEDED with `remove <row> from acceptedSlowdowns in bench/parity-gaps.json`, the way `tracked-now-at-parity` lists a gap entry that is no longer needed (`bench/parity.ts`). It is a pass, not a failure: on its own change a noisy run may miss a real slowdown, and a failure there would make the change flaky.
  - **A new entry is backed by the run.** A new entry for a row of the shard that the run did not measure against the base (a typo, a row the run does not run, a row it could only time against the reference) fails as `acknowledgement-not-backed`; a row the run does not time at all (a public sample in a pull request) is checked for its form only, as a gap entry is. A shard checks the entries of its own family.
  - **`bench:refresh-speed` keeps the section** when it rewrites the file (`planSpeedRefresh`, `reseedGapHistories`).
- **Why**:
  - **A trade the gate cannot tell from a defect needs a recorded decision.** The gate fails any row that is credibly more than its line slower than the base. A change that gives up speed for the output the reference gives has nothing to do but lower the line for the row in `AB_ROW_REGRESSION` (which is for noise and is capped) or leave the row failing. Performance triage in browser projects handles the same case with a status on the alert: a regression is "acknowledged" when it is accepted as a trade-off and tied to a bug, and it still counts as a regression against the next change. The entry here is that status: an issue number, the change, the reason.
  - **The reference comparison is the floor.** A row the change slows may not go below the tool it is measured against; that is what the parity gate is for. Reusing the row's own bound and confirmation means the acknowledgement adds no new statistic and no new threshold.
  - **Single-use by comparison with the base, not by a date.** An expiry date would need the gate to read the clock, and a merge would not end it. The base already carries the change after the merge, so the gate can tell from the base's own gap file; no extra bookkeeping is kept.
  - **A section of the gap file rather than a file of its own.** The gate reads the gap file and the gap file of the base in every run (`--base-gaps`), `bench/parity-gaps.ts` is among the files the job takes from the base (`scripts/ci-parity-base-gate.mjs`), so a pull request cannot loosen the validation or the rule that judges it; a file of its own would need a flag in `bench/run.ts` and in `JudgeOptions`, a new argument in the workflow, an entry in the gate files, and a rule in `bench/family-map.json`. The cost is that `bench:refresh-speed` rewrote the file from the gap list alone (two lines changed to keep the section) and that the family-map code reads `gaps` only (below).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A label or a PR-body marker that excuses the row**: invisible in the diff, no issue, not kept with the code.
  - **An entry that outlives its change** (excusing any later slowdown of the row): it would turn one decision into a standing licence.
  - **A failure for a stale entry**: it would fail a change for the merge of another; the report and the next bench change handle it, as for a gap entry at parity.
  - **A row below the reference**: that is a tracked gap (entry 17), which has its own history rule; the two are exclusive.
- **Verified by**: `tests/bench-parity.test.ts` (through `main`, the gate command, on saved reports: an acknowledged row slower than its base and at the reference passes; the same row credibly below the reference fails; a row without an entry fails; an entry the base holds excuses nothing; an entry not needed is reported; a new entry for a row the run did not measure fails; the form of the section, one case per refusal) and `tests/bench-speed-gap-floor.test.ts` (the section survives `bench:refresh-speed`). The tests were red before the change (24 failing). The existing bench suites pass unchanged.
- **Known limits**: `scripts/ci-parity-families.mjs` and `scripts/ci-parity-shards.mjs` compare the `gaps` list of the file only, so a change that edits `acceptedSlowdowns` alone does not name the row's family as changed; the family of the conversion code the change touches runs its speed shard, which is where the entry applies. An entry whose row no run produces any more is not reported.
- **Revisit when**: a stale entry survives more than one bench change on the default branch, the cap of 16 is reached, or an acknowledgement is needed for a row below the reference.

## 93. Photograph AVIF in one tile: the libvips of the worker image leaves the encoder's auto-tiles off

- **Status**: Implemented (row "Found by the nightly of 2026-10-24: photo AVIF quality depends on the thread count" of epic #759, the open finding of entry 91; issue #641), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request). The speed rows of photographs are a trade-off that waits for QA (Trade-offs, first bullet). Amended 2026-10-25 (QA request, row "with one tile and row-mt, AVIF bytes no longer depend on the thread count" of epic #759): a graphic that the image library encodes takes the thread lease too (Decision, "Nothing else changes", and the bullets "Graphics take the lease" in Why and Trade-offs).
- **Decision**:
  - **The libvips of the worker image sets libheif's `auto-tiles` parameter to false.** `docker/sharp-libvips/libvips-heif-auto-tiles.patch` changes one argument in `vips_foreign_save_heif_build` of `libvips/foreign/heifsave.c` (libvips 8.18.7, line 653: `"auto-tiles", TRUE` becomes `FALSE`) and the comment above it. An AVIF is then one tile whatever the thread count, as libheif's own default gives. The threads still split the work: libheif turns libaom's row multithreading on when it has more than one thread.
  - **The build applies it with one more line in `posix.sh`.** `docker/sharp-libvips/heif-auto-tiles.patch` adds `patch -p1 < "$SHARP_LIBVIPS_HEIF_TILES_PATCH"` directly after the line of entry 86, `build.sh` applies it after `webp-thread-level.patch` and exports the path, and `Dockerfile.worker` copies both files into the `sharplibvips-build` stage, so the cache key of `cache-key.sh` moves with them and a hunk that stops applying fails the build. There is no new download.
  - **The quality jobs run with the worker's heap bound.** `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX: "2"` is set in the env of the `parity-quality` job of `ci.yml` and of the quality step of the nightly `bench-parity-quality` shards, as the speed jobs already have it, so a photograph is encoded on the threads the worker leases (`imageThreadsFor`, 4 to 8 against 2). With one tile the file is the same on 2 threads and on 8, so the setting no longer changes a quality row; it keeps the gate on the configuration that is deployed.
  - **The two acknowledgements of this entry's change leave the gap file** (entry 92: single-use, and the base holds them now). The speed run of the 2026-10-25 amendment lists both as `acknowledgement-unused`, `photo-a.jpg->avif` at 0.99955 and `photo-b.png->avif` at 0.99302 head against base over 24 pairs each, so `acceptedSlowdowns` of `bench/parity-gaps.json` is empty.
  - **Nothing else changes.** The lease (`imageThreadsFor`), the effort, the quality and the chroma of the AVIF encode stay as they were; a picture that the image library encodes takes the lease whatever its content (`encodeAvifFromPipeline`; a graphic was kept on one thread while threads made tiles), and the AVIF command-line encoder path is not touched. With the command-line encoder installed, as in the worker image, the library encodes a graphic only above `AVIF_CLI_MAX_PIXELS` (48 megapixels) or when no supported command-line encoder is found. The two gap entries of `clic-sergey-zolkin-21232.png->avif` stay until the x86-64 run of the pull request names them at parity.
- **Why**:
  - **What the reference engine sets.** The reference service converts PNG and JPEG to AVIF with ImageMagick. Its writer (`coders/heic.c` at tag 7.1.2-34, `WriteHEICImage` from line 2477) takes the AV1 encoder of libheif (line 2578), sets the lossy quality only when one is given (2643 to 2647), `speed` only with `heic:speed` (2651 to 2657), `chroma` only with `heic:chroma` or an identity matrix (2659 to 2672), the chroma downsampling only with its option (2693 to 2722), and encodes (2726). It sets no thread count and no tile parameter anywhere in the file. libheif's AV1 encoder (`libheif/plugins/encoder_aom.cc` at v1.23.5, the version sharp-libvips pins; priority 60 against 40 for SVT and 20 for rav1e, line 250) then uses its defaults: speed 6 (line 297), threads from `std::thread::hardware_concurrency()` up to 64 (313 to 325), quality 50 (334), chroma 4:2:0 (355), `auto-tiles` false (441 to 443) and `enable-intrabc` true (449 to 451). At the encode it sets `g_threads` (1155), turns `AV1E_SET_ROW_MT` on when there is more than one thread (1189 to 1193), passes `auto-tiles` (1198) and sets no tile rows or columns (1201). The reference's AVIF is therefore one tile coded with row multithreading on all cores.
  - **What libvips set.** `heifsave.c` of 8.18.7 sets the quality (588), lossless (594), `speed` as 9 minus the effort (600 to 601), `chroma` (613 to 614), `threads` from `vips_concurrency_get()` (629 to 640), `auto-tiles` true (649 to 657), `enable-intrabc` false (659 to 667) and `tune` (671 to 673). The saver has no argument for the tiles, and sharp 0.35.5 has no option for them, so no setting of ours reaches the parameter.
  - **Why the thread count changed the file.** libaom's `set_auto_tiles` (`av1/av1_cx_iface.c` of 3.15.1, the pinned version, lines 1086 to 1119, called at 1493 to 1497) makes no tiles below two threads and otherwise the smaller of the frame area over 128 x 128, 32 and the thread count, rounded down to a power of two. One tile also explains why 2 threads and 8 now give the same file: libaom takes the row-multithreaded path when `row_mt` is on and it has more than one worker (`av1/encoder/encodeframe.c`, lines 2445 to 2451), and on that path each superblock row starts from the entropy context saved at the superblock above and to the right (lines 1270 to 1275), whatever the number of workers. One worker adapts the context in sequence instead, so a one-thread encode is a different file (a container whose memory limit pays for one thread).
  - **Bytes** (`photo-b.png` to AVIF through `convertImage`, arm64 VM, `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`, the thread count set with `VIPS_CONCURRENCY`):

    | Threads | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 8 |
    |---|---|---|---|---|---|
    | Base (auto-tiles on) | 8,912 | 8,930 | 8,930 | 9,033 | 9,155 |
    | Head (one tile) | 8,912 | 8,869 | 8,869 | 8,869 | 8,869 |

    The digests of the head's four files from 2 threads up are equal. A graphic, which takes no lease, writes the same file on base and head (`screenshot.png` 6,614 bytes on one thread).
  - **Quality** (the full image family, `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity --quality-only --family image`, 823 rows, arm64 VM): base without the heap bound (2 threads, what CI measured) passes with 0 failing and 119 within the allowance; base with it (4 threads, what the worker runs) fails 6 rows (`photo-b.png->avif` SSIM BD-rate +1.99 %, `clic-schicka-307.png->avif` +1.67 % in PSNR and +1.95 % in SSIM, and its bytes, SSIM and PSNR rows); the head passes with 0 failing and 90 within the allowance, and its 829 rows are the same with and without the heap bound. On the 120 AVIF BD-rate rows the head is at or below the base of 2 threads on every row (mean -0.30 points, -1.55 to 0; the unchanged rows are the graphics and deep pictures, which take other paths). The photographs of the open finding:

    | Row (BD-rate, %) | Base, 2 threads | Base, 4 threads | Head, 2 or 4 threads |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | `photo-b.png` SSIM | +0.71 | +1.99 | -0.84 |
    | `photo-b.png` PSNR | -1.24 | +0.09 | -2.68 |
    | `clic-schicka-307.png` SSIM | +0.28 | +1.95 | -0.95 |
    | `clic-schicka-307.png` PSNR | +0.22 | +1.67 | -1.03 |
    | `clic-sergey-zolkin-21232.png` SSIM | +1.37 | +1.34 | +0.13 |
    | `clic-sergey-zolkin-21232.png` PSNR | +0.78 | +1.09 | -0.50 |
    | `kodim23.png` SSIM | +0.07 | +0.91 | -0.42 |
    | `clic-paul-itkin-46101.png` SSIM | -0.09 | +0.15 | -0.34 |

  - **Speed** (`--parity --speed-only --family image --base-root`, head and base each on its own build, `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`, two runs of 24 to 30 interleaved pairs a row; the host was loaded by other work, which both sides of a pair share). Head against base: `photo-a.jpg->avif` 0.640 and 0.642, `photo-b.png->avif` 0.822 and 0.805, `kodim23.png->avif` 0.588 and 0.587, `clic-paul-itkin-46101.png->avif` 0.699 and 0.726; against the reference tool the head reads 1.13 and 1.15, 1.11 and 1.10, 1.08 and 1.08, 1.015 and 0.976. Every other AVIF row reads 0.98 to 1.01 against the base. The tiles were the parallel work: on 4 threads an encode of `photo-b.png` used 1.40 cores on the head against 1.78 and 2.19 on the base (two rounds of 15 encodes), and in a profile of 60 encodes the calling thread's share of the samples rose from 23.0 % to 27.1 % while the total stayed at 64 to 65 %. With one tile libaom packs the bitstream on one thread (`pack_bs_mt_enabled` is set only for more than one tile, `encodeframe.c` lines 2446 and 2447) and the rows of the wavefront wait on the row above. Entry 91 measured the base on 4 threads at 1.38 to 1.89 times the reference; the head is where the reference is, because it does the same work.
  - **Graphics take the lease** (row of 2026-10-25). The reference engine gives every picture libaom's row multithreading on all cores: libheif's AV1 encoder defaults `threads` to `hardware_concurrency()` for any picture (`encoder_aom.cc` v1.23.5 line 319), passes it as `g_threads` (1155) and sets `AV1E_SET_ROW_MT` when it is above one (1189 to 1193), and ImageMagick's writer sets no thread count for a graphic either (`coders/heic.c` 2477 to 2726). The image library's graphic path stayed on one thread because the tiles that threads made had moved an interface from -14.4 % to +1.6 % BD-rate; with one tile that reason is gone, so `encodeAvifFromPipeline` leases for every picture it encodes.
    - **What was measured.** The arm64 build of the worker's libvips was not rebuilt. The library of the npm package (the same sharp-libvips 1.3.4 and libvips 8.18.7) was changed by one instruction, the argument of the `auto-tiles` call in `vips_foreign_save_heif_build` (`mov w2, #1` to `mov w2, #0` at file offset 0x16a7e8, SHA-256 `97c2ae9a...bc8f` to `c7794aeb...7c63`), which is what the patch of this entry does in the source. It behaves as the entry measured for photographs: the 1024 x 640 interface is 8,972 bytes on 1 thread and 8,925 bytes on 2, 3, 4 and 8, and the stock library writes 8,972, 9,053, 9,053, 9,090 and 9,407 bytes on 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8. The build of the worker image (the -O3 libwebp, libpng and mozjpeg of entry 84, nothing in AVIF) is the one the x86-64 run of the pull request uses.
    - **Speed** (`convertImage` in one process with the command-line encoder hidden by an `AVIFENC_PATH` that names no file, 8-bit graphics, 4 cores, `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`, 5 pairs of processes that alternate base and head, the median of 6 to 60 conversions in each; the 51 MP picture 3 pairs of 2 conversions):

      | Picture | Base, one thread | Head, lease of 4 | Head against base |
      |---|---|---|---|
      | 32 x 32 | 3.3 ms | 3.6 ms | +9 % |
      | 128 x 80 | 16.2 ms | 16.8 ms | +4 % |
      | 320 x 200 | 59.0 ms | 44.2 ms | -25 % |
      | 640 x 400 | 175.0 ms | 97.4 ms | -44 % |
      | 1024 x 640 | 398.7 ms | 249.7 ms | -37 % |
      | 2048 x 1920 | 1,469 ms | 636 ms | -57 % |
      | 7168 x 7168 (51 MP, the command-line encoder installed: above its 48 MP bound the library encodes) | 3,367 ms | 1,360 ms | -60 % |

      Why not 4 times: the 51 MP conversion used 4.26 s of CPU time in 1.79 s of process time on the head (2.6 of the 4 cores, startup included) against 4.02 s in 4.10 s on the base, so the extra work of the threads is 6 % and the rest is waiting. By the entry's own mechanism the waiting is the wavefront of one tile (a superblock row starts after the row above, `encodeframe.c` 1270 to 1275 of libaom 3.15.1) and the bitstream packing on one thread (2446 and 2447), and the PNG decode before the encode is one thread as well (inferred from those lines and the core count, not profiled per phase). The gain is 1.6 times on the interface with 4 threads (1.5 times with 2), 2.3 times on 4 megapixels and 2.5 times on 51. Peak resident memory is within 4 % at 51 MP (1,111 to 1,155 MB) and 9 % at 640 x 400 (184 to 200 MB).
    - **Concurrent jobs** (three conversions at once in one process, as the worker runs `WORKER_CONCURRENCY=3`, `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`; the lease is process-wide and is the cores up to 8). 51 MP graphic: on 4 cores the batch takes 4.16 and 3.96 s on the base and 3.49 and 3.39 s on the head (-16 %), on 2 cores 5.93 and 5.56 s against 5.65 and 5.47 s (-5 % and -2 %); resident peak 2.8 to 2.97 GB on both. 4 MP graphic: on 4 cores 1.55, 1.53 and 1.53 s against 1.31, 1.29 and 1.29 s (-16 %); on 2 cores 2.25, 2.36 and 2.24 s against 2.39, 2.40 and 2.40 s (+7 %, +2 % and +7 %, and the mean latency of a job 2.0 s against 2.4 s), where the cores are the limit and the lease only adds workers to wait for them.
    - **Bytes.** The file is the same on any lease from two threads up (screenshot above; `tests/image-threads.test.ts`). It is not the file of one thread: 8,972 against 8,925 bytes for the interface (-0.5 %), 659,161 against 656,731 for the 51 MP graphic (-0.4 %). Of 90 outputs (10 pictures, AVIF, JPEG and WebP, quality 30, 70 and 90) the head writes the same bytes as the base in the default configuration, where the command-line encoder writes every graphic; with that encoder hidden 21 differ, all AVIF files of graphics at 320 x 200 and larger; the photographs, the 32 x 32 and 128 x 80 graphics, JPEG and WebP are identical.
    - **Quality of the library's graphics** (`--parity --quality-only --family image`, 823 rows, `AVIFENC_PATH` naming no file, the library of this entry's patch): the base fails 27 rows against the command-line reference (the library encoder is 4 to 38 % behind it in BD-rate on screenshots and charts, which is why the command-line encoder writes graphics), the head 28. Over the 120 AVIF BD-rate rows 82 are equal and 38 differ; over the 55 of single pictures PSNR changes by +0.05 points on average (median 0; 8 up, 8 down, -1.07 to +4.77) and SSIM by -0.28 (4 up, 12 down, -7.94 to +4.21). The added failing row is `wm-screen-fountain.png->avif/bd_rate_ssim` (0.63 to 1.88 %, allowance 1.5), on a picture that fails four other rows of this path in both runs. The same run with the command-line encoder installed, the configuration of the gate, passes: 823 rows, 0 failing, 90 within the allowance, as the head of this entry measured.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The photograph AVIF rows lose the tile parallelism.** The head is 18 to 41 % slower than the base on 4 threads, still at or above the reference tool on three of the four photographs and at it within the spread on the fourth (0.976 and 1.015). The speed job of a pull request fails a row that is more than 10 % slower than its base whatever the reference reads, so `photo-a.jpg->avif` and `photo-b.png->avif` (the generated photographs it times) are expected to fail it on the x86-64 runner too (a prediction from the mechanism, not measured there). Whether that loss is accepted for the reference's layout and quality, and how the gate records it, is for QA.
  - **Graphics pay the thread pool when they are tiny, and a saturated machine does not gain.** A 32 x 32 picture takes 0.3 ms longer on 4 threads and a 128 x 80 one 0.6 ms (the pool is started for each encode); three 4 MP conversions on 2 cores take 2 to 7 % longer. The lease reaches a graphic only above 48 MP or without the command-line encoder, so the worker's graphics under that bound are not affected; the worker's own saturated case measured (three 51 MP conversions on 2 cores) is 2 to 5 % faster. The one-line way back is `content === 'photo' ? await withImageThreads(encode) : await encode()` in `encodeAvifFromPipeline`.
  - **A graphic that the library writes is a different file from the one it wrote on one thread** (-0.4 to -0.5 % in bytes, BD-rate moved both ways), and one row of the path that is not gated moves past its allowance (Why, "Quality of the library's graphics").
  - **One more libvips patch to carry.** A sharp release with another libvips moves the hunk or makes it unnecessary, and the build fails until it is looked at. Upstream, the change would be a saver argument for the tiles.
  - **A one-thread encode is a different file** from a multi-thread one (8,912 against 8,869 bytes for `photo-b.png`), still one tile; it happens only where the memory limit pays for one thread or the machine has one core.
  - **The arm64 rebuild is not byte for byte the one entry 86 recorded.** The base rebuilt here (Rocky Linux 8 root in a temporary VM, gcc-toolset-15 15.2.1-7.1, binutils 2.44-3) has SHA-256 `714926cf43b17232aa8cdba71bada7667b9fc5240fb9655730c551fdfbeef4b3`, not entry 86's `38449af5ce94...ecb`, with the same size (18,848,888 bytes); the head is `55e3b31bdeca6406db4825599544666c36f57d8962dc9d92c9fee58819084bea`. Base and head were built in the same root one after the other, so the comparison holds; the cause of the drift was not traced.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Capping the photograph lease at 1 or 3 threads**: 1 thread reads 0.56 to 0.60 of the reference's speed, 3 threads keeps two tiles (`photo-b.png` +0.71 % in SSIM) and still makes the file depend on the count (entry 91).
  - **A fixed tile layout that does not follow the thread count** (two tile columns always): it keeps part of the speed and gives the files of the base on 2 threads (+0.71 % for `photo-b.png` in SSIM), but libheif has no tile parameter for libaom (`encoder_aom.cc` line 1201), so it needs a libheif patch too, and it is not the reference's layout; not built or measured.
  - **Raising the allowance of the AVIF rows**: a gate change that hides the cause.
  - **Leaving the quality jobs on 2 threads**: the gate would keep measuring a configuration the worker does not run.
  - **`enable-intrabc` back to libheif's default (on)**: libaom uses intra block copy only with screen-content tools, which it does not choose for photographs; not measured, and not part of the finding.
- **Verified by**: `tests/sharp-libvips-build.test.ts` (the libvips patch turns the parameter off and changes no other code line, it fails on a `heifsave.c` it was not written for, the line it adds to `posix.sh` applies it after the WebP line and fails when the file is missing, `build.sh` applies and exports it and `Dockerfile.worker` copies both files; red with the files absent, 3 of 4), `tests/image-threads.test.ts` (a 512 x 256 photograph and a 512 x 256 graphic are each the same AVIF on 2 threads and on 8, and a graphic is encoded on the leased count and the previous count put back; the first runs where the worker's libvips is installed, on Linux: red on the base build, green on the head build in the arm64 VM; the graphic cases are red on the base source and green on the head source), `tests/ci-parity-workflow.test.ts` (both quality jobs set the heap bound; red before the workflow change), the byte, quality and speed runs above, and the x86-64 quality and speed rows of the pull request.
- **Revisit when**: QA decides the speed trade-off, the x86-64 run reads a graphic encoded by the library slower with the lease than without it (the cost of tiny pictures and of saturated cores above), the command-line encoder bound moves, libvips gets a saver argument for the tiles or sharp is upgraded (the hunk and the byte comparison are measured again), libheif gains tile parameters for libaom, or the x86-64 run reads a photograph AVIF row below the reference.

, libvips gets a saver argument for the tiles or sharp is upgraded (the hunk and the byte comparison are measured again), libheif gains tile parameters for libaom, or the x86-64 run reads a photograph AVIF row below the reference.

## 94. PDF text: annotation text on a page left out for glyphs without a mapping, the text and form matrices of an appearance, and the composite-font glyphs Poppler prints as control codes

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783 rows "`cc-0400651.pdf` is refused", "composite fonts without a ToUnicode map" and "legacy Arial/Times glyphs at GID 172 and up"; epic #760), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request in issue #783: follow what Poppler prints). It narrows the page rule of entry 49 and corrects the walk of entry 80; entry 70 is unchanged.
- **Decision**:
  - **A page left out for glyphs without a mapping keeps the text of its annotations when OCR is off.** Entry 49 leaves out a page whose glyphs without text outnumber the others. Such a page now loses only the text its own content draws; the text its annotation appearances draw (entry 80) stays, and the warning says so: `Left out the page text of page N and kept the text of its annotations: more of its glyphs have no Unicode mapping than have one.` A page without annotation text gets the warning of entry 49 as before. A document is refused with `PdfTextUnmappedError` only when no page has text left, which now counts the annotation text a left-out page keeps.
  - **With OCR on, the page goes to OCR whole**, as before: the page is drawn with its annotations before it is recognized, so keeping their text as well would read it twice.
  - **The verdict is unchanged.** A page is left out when its glyphs without text outnumber its visible glyphs, annotation glyphs included, so no page that read before is left out now and no page goes to OCR that did not.
  - **The walk reads the text matrix and a form's matrix in the shapes pdf.js gives them.** pdf.js 6.3.289 puts `Tm` in the operator list as one Float32Array operand (`pdf.worker.mjs`, `getOperatorList`, lines 41744-41745: `operatorList.addOp(fn, [new Float32Array(args)])`) and a form XObject's /Matrix as a Float32Array (`buildFormXObject`, lines 40465-40466 and 40499); its canvas reads them so (`pdf.mjs` 18556 `setTextMatrix(opIdx, matrix)`, 18989 `paintFormXObjectBegin(opIdx, matrix, bbox)`). The walk tested each operand with `Array.isArray`, so it ignored both: text after `Tm` sat at the origin of the appearance and text of a nested form ignored the form's matrix. Annotation text now lies where the page shows it, which is what entry 80 decided.
  - **Glyphs of composite fonts without a ToUnicode map that are control codes stay left out.** Poppler prints them as the control codes themselves, so there is no character to follow (below).
- **Why**:
  - **`cc-0400651.pdf` was refused for want of a reading rule, not of a CMap.** Its one page draws 22 glyphs of an `MS PMincho` subset whose ToUnicode map gives U+F0AC to U+F0F2 (private use; entry 49 leaves them out), and three FreeText notes whose appearances set `中止` and `別途変更あり` (twice) in the non-embedded `JSGothic-Md` with the predefined CMap `90ms-RKSJ-H` and Adobe-Japan1. The reader already loads that CMap and the collection's `-UCS2` map (entry 70) and read the three notes right; but 22 glyphs without text against 14 that read made the page a left-out page, and with no other page the document was refused. Poppler prints the notes and the 22 private-use characters: `Page::displaySlice` draws every annotation after the page content into the same text output (`poppler/Page.cc` lines 626-637, Poppler 26.09; GPL, read for behaviour only) and `TextPage::addChar` drops no character but U+0000 (`poppler/TextOutputDev.cc` lines 2684-2688). pdf.js gives a FreeText note's text through `getTextContent` as well (`hasTextContent`, entry 80). The notes are set in fonts of their own, so the left-out page fonts say nothing about them.
  - **The notes lay at the page's lower-left corner.** Their appearance boxes are in page space and place the text with `1 0 0 1 x y Tm`; with the matrix ignored, the reader put all three at the origin. With the matrix read they lie at y = 731, 693 and 639, where the drawn page shows them.
  - **What Poppler prints for the composite fonts without a ToUnicode map.** For a font of the Adobe-Identity collection with no ToUnicode map Poppler uses the identity mapping, so the text of a glyph is its CID (`poppler/GfxFont.cc` lines 1752-1759, `GfxCIDFont::GfxCIDFont`, and 1939-1948, `getNextChar`: `ctu->mapToUnicode(cid, u)`). It reads the embedded program's `cmap` only to draw a font that is not embedded (`getCodeToGIDMap`, lines 2081-2094, which returns nothing for an embedded Adobe-Identity font), and its built-in ZapfDingbats encoding belongs to simple fonts (`Gfx8BitFont`, from line 947; lines 1084-1087). The programs of the fonts in question keep only outlines and metrics (`glyf`, `loca`, `hmtx`, no `cmap`, no `post`, no glyph names), and their CIDs are the subset's glyph ids from 1 upwards. So Poppler prints a C0 control code for every glyph the reader leaves out: in `govdocs1-002701.pdf` 1,018 control codes (Symbol 826, MonotypeSorts 94, Wingdings 55, MT-Extra 43; U+0001 alone 390 times) where the reader leaves out 1,018 glyphs, and in `govdocs1-003638.pdf` 246 times U+0010 (an AGaramond hyphen, CID 16) for 246; in the regression sample `gd-064375.pdf` 86 for 86, `gd-444996.pdf` 102 for 102, `gd-364361.pdf` 37 for 37 and `cc-7000461.pdf` 4 for 4. Nothing in the file names these glyphs; the AGaramond hyphen sits at the glyph id the Macintosh order gives a hyphen, but no width reference for AGaramond exists, which entry 70 requires.
  - **What Poppler prints for the legacy Arial and Times New Roman glyphs past glyph id 171.** The same identity mapping: the CID read as a code point, a Latin-1 letter or sign for ids 172 to 255. The reader prints the same characters (pdfjs gives the CID too), so the 341 real-world and 229 regression glyphs of entry 70 read as Poppler prints them, and no source gives these fonts' order past 171.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A document whose every page is in fonts without a mapping, with an annotation that draws text (a stamp, a note), now gives that text and a warning** where it was refused with the advice to turn OCR on. The warning names the pages, and OCR still reads them when asked. Poppler prints the stamp and the unmapped glyphs.
  - **Annotation text placed by `Tm` now joins the lines it lies on.** In `govdocs1-001134.pdf` the text of an annotation on the date line now follows the underline and reads `DATE:______________________________June 20, 2006`, where Poppler prints the date on the line before; in `pdfjs-issue17069.pdf` the `SANDBOX` stamp has its drawn size (73 pt, it was 1 pt), so the Markdown no longer marks three short lines of the page as headings against that 1-pt run.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Judging the page by its own glyphs alone**: a page that reads today because its annotation text outweighs a few unmapped glyphs would become a left-out page and go to OCR.
  - **Keeping the glyphs that map on every left-out page**: it changes entry 49 for every such page and hands out fragments of text set mostly in fonts without a mapping.
  - **Reading the 22 private-use characters of `cc-0400651.pdf` through the symbol tables**: the font is `MS PMincho`, not a symbol font, and its own ToUnicode map gives the private-use values; no reader gives them other characters.
  - **Giving the control codes of the composite fonts a character**: no reference does, and entry 49 never replaces a glyph by a guess.
- **Measured**: text, Markdown and HTML of the 1,261 real-world PDFs and of every tenth PDF of the regression corpus by id (950), origin/main against the change (6,633 conversions each). 42 conversions differ, in 15 files:
  - `cc-0400651.pdf` converts on all three routes where it was refused: `中止`, `別途変更あり`, `別途変更あり`, the words Poppler prints, with the warning above.
  - 13 files with annotation text placed by `Tm` or a form's matrix read it where it lies: `cc-1000637.pdf`, `cc-2400347.pdf` and `gd-578967.pdf` (signature fields and link captions; word recall against `pdftotext` 0.966 to 0.973, 0.940 to 0.947 and 0.936 to 0.966), `govdocs1-000826.pdf`, `-001564.pdf`, `-001565.pdf`, `-002203.pdf`, `-002997.pdf`, `-003896.pdf`, `-004323.pdf` and `-004329.pdf` (the same words in another order; their order against `pdftotext`, by the matching ratio of the word sequences, rose on two and stayed on the rest), `govdocs1-001134.pdf` (recall 0.996 to 0.995, the joined word above) and `pdfjs-issue17069.pdf` (Markdown and HTML only, the headings above).
  - `gd-026598.pdf` to Markdown hit the 60 s limit on origin/main and converted on the change, but it hits the limit on both on a second run and its text and HTML do not change: it varies from run to run and the change does not reach it.
  - Glyphs left out, summed from the warnings of the Markdown route: 50,944 before and after on the real-world corpus and 108,082 before and after on the regression sample; no file's count changed. Of the real-world count, 1,275 are glyphs of composite fonts without a ToUnicode map (1,018 in `govdocs1-002701.pdf`, 246 in `govdocs1-003638.pdf`, 11 in five others), the same as #868 measured. Refused: 9 real-world files before and after, 7 regression files before and 5 after (`cc-0400651.pdf` and the run-to-run `gd-026598.pdf`).
- **Verified by**: `tests/pdf-annotation-text.test.ts` (red on origin/main, 5 of its 7 new tests, the two controls held before: notes placed by `Tm` above and below the body text and a note whose form lifts its word above the body, in Poppler's word order; a page of 12 glyphs without a mapping with an 8-letter note converts to the note's words with the warning, where it was refused; the same page with OCR allowed goes to OCR whole; the same page without a note is still refused; 10,000 notes on a page of 50,000 such glyphs keep every note once, within 30 s; `cc-0400651.pdf` gives the words `pdftotext` prints) and `tests/pdf-annotation-text-walk.test.ts` (the operator shapes of pdf.js 6.3.289: `Tm` as one Float32Array and a form's /Matrix as a Float32Array, both red before).
- **Revisit when**: pdf.js changes the operands of `setTextMatrix` or `paintFormXObjectBegin`; a corpus file has a left-out page whose annotation text Poppler does not print; or a source gives the characters of a composite font whose program names no glyph.

## 95. XPS and OpenXPS pages: GhostXPS as a separate program, on a package the worker has read and rewritten first

- **Status**: Implemented (XPS and OpenXPS rows of issue #783), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request: approve an XPS renderer for the worker, and keep the limits the renderer lacks). It replaces the withdrawal of `xps` and `oxps` to PDF in entry 40 and opens the page-image and vector targets of both sources. Amended 2026-10-25 (QA request, rows "Found by #879" of issue #783): the image budget also counts pixels, and the PostScript route has the same 128 MiB read limit for image targets. Amended again 2026-10-25 (review of #886, rows of issue #783): the pixel budget is the job's own run limit at the fastest measured rate, every brush is charged, a part is read only when a brush names it, and a name is read as GhostXPS reads it.
- **Decision**:
  - **GhostXPS (`gxps`, part of GhostPDL 10.08.0) draws the pages.** An XPS or OpenXPS source goes to PDF through `gxps -sDEVICE=pdfwrite`, and every other page target (PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, GIF, BMP, TIFF, ICO, PSD, SVG, PostScript, EPS) is made from that PDF by the native PDF tools every PDF source already uses (entry 34). The text targets (`txt`, `html`, `zip`) keep the in-process reader of entry 40. The program is built by `scripts/install-ghostxps.sh` from the unmodified release archive pinned by SHA-256 (`94943e3c4adb7115d132b3c28b913672f2e62e6a9d802f7e754e716b1634174a`), with the copies of its libraries that ship in the archive, so it needs only the C library; the worker image carries it in the `ghostxps` stage and CI installs the same script (cached by its hash, with the SHA-256 of the program written beside the build: a restored program is used only when it still has that digest, and is built again otherwise). A worker without it answers an unavailable engine (HTTP 503) for these pairs and does not fall back to a text-only PDF. The path is `GXPS_PATH`. The program decodes attacker-controlled images and fonts with the libraries built into it, so it is built as a position independent executable with the stack protector and stack clash probes (`-fstack-protector-strong -fstack-clash-protection -fPIE`) and linked with a read-only relocation table and immediate binding (`-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -pie`); the script reads the program's ELF header and dynamic section with `readelf` and fails the build if it is not type DYN, has no `GNU_RELRO` segment or does not bind at load time. The archive and its source digest do not change.
  - **It runs as an unmodified separate program** in the process sandbox (entry 11): no network, an address space of 2 GiB, an output file of at most 512 MiB, the job's time limit, and GhostPDL's default safe mode, in which the input may be read only while it is drawn and only the output file may be written (`pcl/pl/plmain.c`, `minst->safer`).
  - **The worker reads the package first and hands the program a package it wrote itself.** GhostXPS inflates every part into a buffer of the size the central directory states, with no limit on the parts, their total or the compression ratio, and it reads no ZIP64 record (`xps/xpszip.c`, `xps_read_zip_dir`: a ZIP64 size is a negative number to it, and the Word print in the real samples uses ZIP64 records). So the package is opened under the limits of the conversion's other archive readers: 50,000 entries and a compression ratio of 100 to 1 (`ARCHIVE_SECURITY_LIMITS`, with the 32 MiB floor below which the ratio is not applied), one inflate budget of 256 MiB for all parts together (the same budget as the XPS text reader), every entry checked against its CRC, a part named twice (XPS part names ignore case) refused, and the entries are written again as a stored ZIP in the job directory. The program sees only that file.
  - **The pages are counted the way GhostXPS finds them before it starts** (`xps/xpszip.c` `xps_process_file`, `xps/xpsdoc.c` `xps_parse_metadata_imp`): every `DocumentReference` and `PageContent` at any depth of the fixed document sequence and then of each fixed document in turn. The limits of the text reader hold (1,000 documents, 10,000 pages, every part named once, so a cycle of documents ends at once), and a package that names more than one fixed document sequence is refused, because GhostXPS draws the last one and the count would be of another. A request for the images of every page of a document longer than 500 pages is refused before it is drawn (the limit of the other document page chains), unless it selects pages or asks for the first page. Every page the documents list must then be in the package (a part name is compared without regard to case, as the entries are), or the document is refused as corrupt before the program starts.
  - **A document the program could not draw is a failure.** GhostXPS prints "Warning interpreter exited with error code" on its error output and still exits with success, after writing a PDF of the pages it reached or an empty file (`pcl/pl/plmain.c`, `pl_main_run_file_utf8`). That line, an exit with an error, and an empty or missing output all end in a typed `ConversionFailedError` that carries the first 300 characters of what the program printed. The output is also counted: the PDF must hold as many pages as the documents list, counted by the PDF tools from the file (`pdfinfo`, without reading the file into memory), whatever the program printed, or the conversion fails with the two numbers. So a partial PDF is never handed out, also by a program version that skips a page without the warning. On the pinned 10.08.0 build every page failure tried (a missing page part, a page that is not XML, a foreign namespace, an unreadable glyph run or image list, a negative page size) prints the warning and stops at that page, and none was found that is skipped silently; the count is the guard for the case that changes.
  - **The pages are read for what they make the program decode again.** GhostXPS keeps a font after the first page that loads it but decodes an image for every page that draws it, so the inflate budget, which counts a part once, does not bound the work: ten thousand small pages that name one large image pass every size and ratio check and hold a worker slot until the run limit. Each page part is read (64 MiB at most, the XML tree limits of the reader, the job signal checked between pages) and charged the size of every image and colour profile it names, **once for every brush that names it** (GhostXPS decodes the part for each `ImageBrush` with no cache, `xps/xpsimage.c` `xps_parse_image_brush`, lines 469 to 483), through `ImageSource` (also the parts of a `ColorConvertedBitmap` markup) and a `ContextColor` profile. A brush in a resource dictionary, in a part or inline in the page, is charged once for each `{StaticResource key}` of the page that names its key (`xps/xpsresource.c` `xps_parse_resource_reference`), and an entry nothing on the page uses is neither charged nor read; each dictionary is read once, and a dictionary that names a dictionary is charged by its size and not followed, so a chain or a cycle costs one read each. The sum is limited to 512 MiB, twice the inflate budget, and a part is charged at least 1 KiB per naming, which bounds the number of namings the budget can hold. **Each image is also charged by the pixels its header declares, for every brush that names it, against the pixels the job's run limit can decode** (`maxRepeatedPixels`, `src/lib/conversions/office/xps-resources.ts`; the next point). The kind of image is told as GhostXPS tells it by its first bytes (`xps/xpsimage.c` `xps_decode_image`, lines 144 to 176): JPEG, PNG and TIFF are read by the image library under the input pixel limit of every still image (100 megapixels by default, a larger declared picture is refused with the 413 of that limit), and a JPEG XR (`.wdp`) header, which the image library cannot read, is read in process from the bitstream header, the size the renderer takes (`xps/xpsjxr.c`, `jpegxr/flags.c` line 80, `jpegxr/cr_parse.c` `jxr_read_image_container` and `jpegxr/r_parse.c` `r_image_header`), not from the container. A part that is no image (a colour profile) costs no pixels, and the header of a part is read once however many brushes name it, and only when a brush names it: an unreadable header of an image that nothing draws is not a refusal, as GhostXPS reads a part only for a brush; a brush that names an image whose header cannot be read is refused (it fails closed). The byte budget stays: bytes bound dense images, pixels bound smooth ones. Fonts and dictionaries are charged the first time a page names them. A package over the budget is refused with a `PayloadLimitError` that states the number, before the program starts. A page that is not well-formed XML is refused at the same point (a typed `DataParseError`) because its references cannot be read.
  - **An image target reads the drawn PDF into memory only up to 128 MiB, on both Ghostscript-family routes.** The PDF tools behind page images take a buffer, and the package's parts (up to 256 MiB) are alive while it is read, so the output limit of 512 MiB would hold up to 768 MiB for one request. The PDF is measured first and refused above 128 MiB (half the inflate budget) with a `PayloadLimitError` that states both sizes. A PDF target hands the file on by its path and keeps the 512 MiB output limit. The PostScript route (EPS, PS) read the whole file for its image targets with no limit under its 512 MiB output limit, so a program that wrote 500 MiB of PDF was read whole into the worker; it now takes the limit from the same constant and the same refusal (`MAX_DRAWN_PDF_BYTES_FOR_IMAGES`, `readDrawnPdfForImages` in `src/worker/worker-output.ts`), which both routes of the table above use. The EPS to PNG route that draws pixels in one run reads no PDF and is not affected.
  - **PostScript and XPS share one route table in the worker.** Both are a Ghostscript-family program that writes a PDF and hands it to the page tools, so `engines.ts` holds one table (sources, program, engine label) and one runner instead of a copy of the PostScript route for XPS.
- **Why**:
  - **A maintained engine draws the pages, and the output is held to the package.** GhostXPS is the XPS interpreter of the GhostPDL family that Ghostscript, already in the worker, belongs to. What the PDF must show is fixed by the package: the pages it lists, each page's size and the characters of its glyph runs in drawing order. A text-only PDF (entry 40) dropped every picture, drawing and font without saying so, and writing an XPS renderer is a project of its own (paths, obfuscated fonts, brushes, images).
  - **The unlimited places of the engine are closed in front of it, not inside it.** The reference engine has no bound on the parts, their total or the ratio, so a small package could make it allocate without limit; the reader that already protects the text route and the archive routes decides first. The same reading gives GhostXPS a package it can read when the original uses ZIP64.
  - **A separate, unmodified program keeps the AGPL with the program** (entry 11, `docs/licensing.md`). The image carries the licence text and a note that names the archive and its SHA-256.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A package is inflated and written twice** (once to check it, once as the stored ZIP): each test of a real sample (105 KB, 75 KB and 561 KB), page images included, ends in under 0.6 s on the Linux arm64 test run. A large document costs memory up to the 256 MiB budget.
  - **A build step and an image layer**: GhostPDL is built from source (the CI step has a 300-second limit and is cached by the script's hash) because Debian ships no package of GhostXPS; its own libraries are built in, which adds the CVE tracking of those copies to the pin. The version moves only by changing the three lines of the script and running `tests/xps-render.test.ts`.
  - **Every page is parsed in the worker before the program starts.** The XML parse of the pages costs little (on the Linux arm64 test machine listing the 10,000 pages of the hostile package takes 90 ms, scanning 500 small pages 6 ms, and refusing that package after its 513th page 13 ms), and it adds a way to refuse: a page that Node's strict XML parser rejects and the program's parser would accept is refused. The byte budget bounds the repeated decoding of dense images: a noisy JPEG of 4 megapixels (2.85 MB) costs 0.58 s a page in the program, which is 5 MB a second, so 512 MiB is about 100 s. It did not bound images that are small in bytes and large in pixels: a smooth JPEG of the same 4 megapixels (39 KB) costs 0.16 s a page, 0.25 MB a second, so 10,000 pages that name it stay under the budget (390 MB) and were bounded by the run limit only; the pixel budget (below) closes that. A page of text in a shared font costs milliseconds, and a scan with one unique image on each of 1,000 pages is far inside the budget; a logo of 100 KB on every page of a document over 5,000 pages is refused.
  - **The hardened build is not a measurable change on the build machine.** The Ubuntu compiler of the testbed and CI already defaults to PIE, immediate binding, a read-only relocation table and stack clash probes, so the program is the same size (9,458,816 bytes on arm64) with and without the flags there; the flags matter for the Debian compiler of the worker image, which defaults to PIE only, and the `readelf` check is what proves the property on each build. The program still runs in the 2 GiB sandbox: a resource dictionary that names itself, which makes it recurse until the address space is gone, ends in the memory-limit refusal.
  - **Some XPS features stay GhostXPS's**: the initial and medial forms of the Farsi and Arabic yeh share one glyph, so the PDF names one of the two letters; the real-sample test reads both as the same letter.
  - **The pixel budget is the job's run limit times 23.4 million pixels a second** (2026-10-25). Measured with GhostXPS 10.08.0 built by `scripts/install-ghostxps.sh` on the 4 vCPU Linux arm64 test VM, `pdfwrite`, one image named by every page, the page time being the slope between packages of 10 and 40 pages: a smooth 4 megapixel JPEG (60 KB) 0.264 s a page, 15.2 million pixels a second; a smooth 4 megapixel PNG (223 KB) 0.171 s, 23.4; a 4 megapixel TIFF with LZW 0.210 s, 19.0, and uncompressed (12 MB) 0.171 s, 23.4; a smooth 36 megapixel JPEG (347 KB) 1.56 s, 23.1; and, which the byte budget already counts, a noisy 4 megapixel JPEG (3.3 MB) 0.73 s, 5.5, and a noisy 1 megapixel PNG (3.0 MB) 0.118 s, 8.5. A page also costs a fixed part: the two JPEGs fit 0.10 s a page plus 40 ns a pixel. The budget refuses only a package that cannot finish: its pixels are the job's own run limit (the stage limit of the job, 120 seconds by default and 600 at most, `runTimeoutMs` in `src/worker/xps-render.ts`, held to the time the job has left) times the fastest measured rate of an image, 23.4 million pixels a second (the smooth PNG and the uncompressed TIFF), so no package under it is refused for being too slow to decode at that rate, and a package over it could not finish whatever its images are. At the default limit that is 2,808 million pixels: 702 brushes of one 4 megapixel image, 2,808 of a megapixel and 78 of 36 megapixels; at 600 seconds 14,040 million. A document of 10,000 pages that names one 4 megapixel image is refused in 40 ms, before the program starts. **What the earlier budget did to a real document**: it was set at the slowest smooth rate (15 million pixels a second) and 100 seconds, 1,500 million pixels, and refused a scan of more than 172 pages at 300 dpi A4 (8.7 megapixels each) that the 120 second limit lets finish at 23 million pixels a second; the same scan is now refused above 322 pages. **The cost of the choice**: an image slower to decode than the fastest rate (a smooth JPEG at 15 million pixels a second) can use the whole limit before the program is stopped by it, as it could for any package under the byte budget; the run limit still ends the job.
  - **A name is read as GhostXPS reads it** (2026-10-25). An `ImageSource` is split only when it starts with `{ColorConvertedBitmap`, on literal spaces, into the image, the profile and the closing brace; any other value is one part name, spaces and braces in it (`xps/xpsimage.c` `xps_find_image_brush_source_part`, lines 413 to 450). The name is resolved by `xps_absolute_path` and `xps_clean_path` (`xps/xpsmem.c`, lines 60 to 132) without decoding it: `a%20b.png` names a part with a percent sign, a name with `..` above the root stays at the root, and the buffer for a name holds 1,023 bytes. A part is the entry of that name or, when there is none, its pieces `name/[0].piece` to `name/[n].last.piece` joined in order (`xps/xpszip.c` `xps_read_zip_part`, lines 346 to 441), so the pieces are charged as the one part they make and their header is read from the joined bytes; a series without its last piece is no part. Checked on GhostXPS 10.08.0 (the pinned build, Linux arm64) and 10.07.1 (macOS distribution), with the same result, with a package of one image brush: a part named with a space, with braces and with a literal `%20` is drawn, `%20` over a part named with a space is not, a part held in two pieces is drawn, a `{ColorConvertedBitmap ...}` is drawn and a `..` above the root is drawn.
  - **The pixel check reads one header per image part, about 0.1 ms each.** The image library reads a JPEG, PNG or TIFF header in 66 to 98 microseconds (5,000 calls each, measured on the development machine under load), so a package that names the most distinct images it can hold (50,000 parts) costs about 6 seconds of header reads before it is refused or drawn (measured: 6.2 s for one page naming 50,000 distinct 1 x 1 PNG parts, 4.2 s for 500 pages naming 100 each); the job signal is checked before each read, and a document of a page count the budget allows reads each part once, not once per page.
  - **A JPEG XR image is read by a reader written here, because the image library has none.** It follows the container and bitstream header code of the library GhostXPS builds in (`jpegxr/cr_parse.c`, `jpegxr/r_parse.c`), reads the bitstream size and not the container's (a picture cut from a window states 40 x 30 in its container and 37 x 22 in the bitstream, and GhostXPS draws 37 x 22), and refuses the ISO box container, which the XPS specification does not use for `.wdp` parts, as an unreadable header. The test files are real encoder output (tests/helpers/jpegxr-samples.ts); there was no `.wdp` among the real samples to read.
  - **A package that names an image whose header cannot be read is refused**, also when no page draws it, where GhostXPS would not decode it. The byte budget already treats a named part as drawn.
  - **The page count is the text reader's, not the program's**: it follows the program's rules for finding pages and agrees with it on the samples; a package the two would read differently is refused (more than one sequence) or drawn as the program reads it.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **MuPDF**: AGPL as well, and its XPS reader is the oracle the text reader was built against, but it would add a second drawing engine to the image and a library whose limits we would still have to put in front of it. GhostXPS is already the engine of the PostScript route's family and ships from the same archive as Ghostscript.
  - **A text-only PDF of the XPS text**: it drops pictures and drawings (entry 40).
  - **An in-process XPS renderer**: a project of its own, and the PDF it produced would be ours to prove against an engine that already does it.
  - **Handing GhostXPS the original package**: it reads no ZIP64 package (the Word print of the real samples) and trusts every size in the central directory.
  - **`-dNOSAFER` or a wider output path**: safe mode is the default of GhostPDL and costs nothing here.
  - **Linking `libgxps` or GhostPDL as a library**: not allowed for AGPL code by entry 11.
- **Verified by**: `tests/xps-render.test.ts` (the three XPS files of the Apache Tika test documents, a Word print with ZIP64 records, a PowerPoint print and a page with right-to-left text and hyperlinks: the PDF has the pages the package lists, read by a reader written here from ECMA-388 that shares no code with the product, and `pdftotext -raw` gives the same letters and digits page by page; for PNG and JPEG one image for every page with the page's aspect ratio and not one flat colour; ten other page targets by their signatures; a package written from the specification and an OpenXPS (ECMA-388) package; and the refusals: a part past the 100 to 1 ratio, a chain of 1,001 fixed documents, a document that names the sequence it belongs to, 10,001 pages, 501 pages of images, a page that is not XML, a page in a foreign namespace that GhostXPS reports and still exits with success, a resource dictionary that names itself, a listed page that is not in the package, a PDF with fewer pages than listed and a PDF above the image-target read limit (each with a stand-in program that writes the PDF, so the checks hold whatever the real program prints), and 10,000 pages that share one image against the 512 MiB budget with its exact boundary at 512 pages of 1 MiB, a font shared by 1,536 pages that is not charged again, and a shared resource dictionary that a brush of the page uses, with a typed error and its message in each case), `tests/xps-image-header.test.ts` (the kind of image by its first bytes as `xps_decode_image` tells it; the size of three real JPEG XR files, one with a long header and one cut from a window, and of JPEG, PNG and TIFF from their headers; nine damaged JPEG XR containers refused; a PNG of 60,000 x 60,000 pixels in under 100 bytes and a JPEG XR file of 4 billion pixels refused with the 413 of the input pixel limit before any pixel is decoded) and the pixel budget of `tests/xps-render.test.ts` (702 pages of a 4 megapixel picture at the budget and one more over it; 702 brushes of one picture on one page and 703; the same for a dictionary brush used 702 and 703 times, in a part and inline; ten thousand pages that share one smooth 4 megapixel JPEG, which the byte budget lets through; one page that names 3,000 parts of a megapixel; a colour profile named by 2,000 pages charged by bytes only; an entry that nothing uses left unread although its image is corrupt, and the same image refused when a brush or a used key names it; part names with a space, braces, a literal percent sign, `..` above the root, a colour converted bitmap, and pieces, against those that GhostXPS does not find; the default run limit, 300 seconds, 30 seconds and the 600 second ceiling at and one brush over their budgets; each red before its change), `tests/postscript-native-route.test.ts` (a PDF of 128 MiB handed to the page tools whole, one of 129 MiB refused with both sizes before it is read, and a PDF target handing the larger file on by its path; red before the PostScript route had the limit), `tests/worker-ghostxps-packaging.test.ts` (the image stage, the pinned digest, the build and hardening flags and the order of the `readelf` checks, the licence and source notes), `tests/ci-setup-tasks.test.ts` (the setup task builds and records the digest, uses a cached program whose digest matches, builds again when the digest differs or is missing), the CI and registry tests that list the program, and `tests/registry-engine-conformance.test.ts` for every advertised XPS and OpenXPS pair. The pinned 10.08.0 program, rebuilt with the hardening flags, passes `tests/xps-render.test.ts` on Linux arm64 (28 of 28, with the pages and letters of the three real files equal to the package's); the macOS developer run uses the distribution's build.
- **Revisit when**: GhostPDL publishes a release with a ZIP64 reader or a bound on the parts (the rewrite step may then go, the limits stay), a CVE is published for GhostXPS or one of the libraries built into it, a real XPS file is found whose words or pictures the PDF loses, or the registry gets a target that is not made from the PDF.

## 96. RocketBook (.rb) e-books: an in-process reader of the container, written from the format's behaviour

- **Status**: Implemented (row "RocketBook (rb)" of the follow-ups from #788 in issue #783), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request). It replaces the RocketBook parts of entry 40: `.rb` is no longer a format only the office suite imports, and the typed refusal that named a missing import filter is gone with the one format that needed it.
- **Decision**:
  - **A reader of the container, `src/lib/conversions/office/rocketbook-reader.ts`, with a document model on top (`rocketbook-model.ts`) and a converter (`rocketbook-source.ts`).** The container is read as the format's reader of the reference service reads it, and is not copied from it (that reader is GPL-3.0, so only its behaviour is followed): bytes 0 to 13 are the signature `B0 0C B0 0C 02 00 "NUVO" 00 00 00 00` (calibre `src/calibre/ebooks/rb/__init__.py` line 5, `reader.py` lines 38 to 41); the 32-bit little-endian offset of the table of contents is at byte 24 and the size of the whole file at byte 28, and a file of another size is corrupt (`reader.py` lines 43 to 48, 50 to 52); the table is a 32-bit page count and then one 44-byte entry per page: a 32-byte name padded with NULs and percent-escaped, the stored size, the offset and the flags (`reader.py` lines 54 to 61, `rb/writer.py` lines 62 to 69); the page with flag 2 is the info page of `KEY=value` lines, of which `TITLE` and `AUTHOR` are read (`metadata/rb.py` lines 14 to 49), the author string being split at `&`, ` and ` and ` with ` (`metadata/__init__.py` lines 27 to 33); a page whose name ends in `html` is text, a page flagged 8 is a chunk count, the size of the text, the size of every chunk and then one zlib stream per chunk, any other page that is not flagged 1 or 2 is stored as it is, and the text is Windows-1252 (`reader.py` lines 74 to 96, 116 to 118); a page whose name ends in `png` and whose flags are 0 is a picture (`reader.py` lines 98 to 103, 120 to 123); the HTML pages are the spine in table order (`reader.py` lines 109 to 127, 138). The same layout is on the MobileRead page for RB, which names the container (an HTML file, its images and a `.info` file of metadata) and the readers and writers, and has no byte layout; the layout above was checked against the two real files of the corpus read with a hex dump and Python's zlib, and against a file that calibre 9.17.0 wrote with a picture, 5 chunks and two heading levels. Flag 1 is skipped as the reference skips it; no source consulted says what it means (it may mark a protected page), so a book whose only text pages carry it is refused as having no text.
  - **The book goes through the shared e-book pipeline.** The pages are read by the HTML reader into the document model (`htmlToDocumentModel`, with the pictures the pages name, links kept as bookmarks, and the title and authors of the info page) like the chapters of an EPUB (`source-model.ts`, whose link mapping `mapBookLink` is now shared). EPUB, PDF, TXT and HTML (and Markdown, DOCX and ODT, which the registry does not list) are written from that model, so headings, emphasis, lists, links and pictures survive; the Palm family, Sony, Open eBook and RTF targets and page images are written from its text by the writers the PML, HTMLZ and OEB sources use. The ZIP target keeps the source in an archive, as for every format.
  - **The registry lists the targets the reference lists for `.rb` (PDF, RTF, TXT, AZW3, EPUB, LRF, MOBI, OEB, PDB, and ZIP) and HTML.** HTML is not in the reference's list; the model writes it with no extra code and it is the one extra target the task asked for.
  - **Bounds, none of which the reference has.** calibre trusts every offset and size and inflates every chunk without a limit (`reader.py` lines 79 to 92). Here every limit is a constant of `ROCKETBOOK_LIMITS` that a test can lower: at most 65,535 pages (the limit of this project's other e-book container, `mobi-reader.ts`; a table of N pages needs 44 N bytes, which is checked first, so a count larger than the file is a format error and not an allocation); every page, chunk table and chunk must lie inside the file, and the pages, the header and the table of contents must not overlap (a page stored twice would otherwise be inflated once per entry); at most 256 MiB of text for the whole book (`MAX_DOCUMENT_INFLATE_BYTES` of `bounded-inflate.ts`, `MOBI_MAX_TEXT_BYTES`), charged to one `InflateBudget` by the inflate of each chunk and by each stored page, and a page that states more text than that is refused before any of it is inflated; at most 1 MiB for one chunk (the writer cuts text in 4096-byte chunks, `rb/writer.py` line 13, so this is 256 times as much); at most 256 MiB of pictures (`HTML_MODEL_MAX_IMAGE_BYTES`) and 2,000 embedded pictures and 256 levels of nesting (the HTML model's); and 64 KiB of the info page. The overlap rule, the page limit, the chunk limit and the 64 KiB are this project's; the text and picture limits are those of the readers it already has.
  - **The chunk table is checked whole before any chunk is read, and each page must inflate to the text it states.** The writer stores the chunk count, the size of the text and one size per chunk, cuts the text in 4096-byte chunks and so writes `ceil(size / 4096)` chunks, and gives the page the size `8 + 4 count + sum of the chunk sizes` (`rb/writer.py` lines 45 to 47, 75 to 78, 93 to 103).
