On the Linux VM (4 cores; five passes that alternate base and change, each pass a fresh process per side and file that converts once to warm up and then three timed times, so 15 timed conversions per side and file) the Markdown of seven scanned documents costs, per page, 47 ms (`govdocs1-002608.pdf`, 132 pages: 0.38 s to 6.6 s), 48 ms (`govdocs1-003685.pdf`, 70 pages: 0.38 s to 3.8 s), 60 ms (`govdocs1-004513.pdf`, 135 pages: 1.1 s to 9.3 s), 117 ms (`govdocs1-000157.pdf`, 22 pages of fax tiles, 727 pictures: 0.20 s to 2.8 s) and 218 ms (`govdocs1-003440.pdf`, 12 JBIG2 pages: 0.08 s to 2.7 s) more; the two files with few or small pictures cost 25 ms a page (`govdocs1-000142.pdf`) and 18 ms (`govdocs1-003071.pdf`, 1,286 pictures that were already decoded). The results are larger in step: `govdocs1-004513.pdf` goes from 2 MB to 33.6 MB of Markdown.
  - **A scan of several hundred pages can reach a limit it did not reach**: at 47 to 218 ms a page the 60 s deadline of the text thread is about 270 pages of the slowest kind and 1,300 of the fastest, and the 128 MiB of picture bytes is about 800 pages at the 0.16 MiB a page of `govdocs1-003685.pdf` and `govdocs1-004513.pdf`. A document past either is refused with the typed error of entry 81 where before it converted without its pictures. No file of the two corpora moved from a result to an error: the refusals (10 for text, 12 for Markdown and HTML) are the same files before and after.
  - **Text results get faster where the pictures were decoded for nothing**: `govdocs1-002608.pdf` 261 ms to 148 ms and `govdocs1-003071.pdf` 372 ms to 207 ms (medians of 15, same bytes); the other five files are within the run-to-run range.
  - **A decoder's worst case is 256 MiB per module and thread**: two modules in each of the 4 threads of the pool hold at most 2 GiB beside the 4 GiB of thread heaps, inside the 10 GiB of the default worker and the 14 GiB of the memory worker (`docker-compose.yml`). A real picture took at most 43 MiB of the JPEG 2000 module and 16 MiB (its initial size) of the JBIG2 module in the 251 files below, and large pictures made for the test 76 to 87 MiB (a lossy 8000 x 8000 RGB reduced by pdf.js to 2000 x 2000, a lossless 2048 x 2048 RGB, a 2048 x 2048 RGBA).
  - **The estimates are of the large allocations, not of every byte**, and they count a picture the decoder would refuse anyway (a reduction past the codestream's levels, a region PDFium will not allocate) as if it decoded it; such a picture is left out instead of failing, with the same result. A dropped picture leaves no placement (a picture whose decoder fails leaves a placement without data), so on that page the JPEG pictures go the PNG route of entry 81.
  - **After a JBIG2 decode aborts, the module keeps the memory it leaked for the rest of the document** (the C++ stack does not unwind in WebAssembly); later pictures of that document decode in what is left, and the next document gets a new module (`WasmImage.cleanup`). Forty aborts in one document left the pictures after them decoded, at 314 MiB of resident growth.
  - **The check costs little**: over the 251 files with such a picture, the bytes handed to pdf.js take 162 ms longer to prepare in all (1,841 ms to 2,003 ms, best of three per file, in process on the Mac at a load average of 3.4), at most 68 ms for one file (`govdocs1-002489.pdf`); a job that writes no pictures does not run it.
  - **A document with more than 64 MiB of decoded wrapper bytes ahead of its picture codecs is refused** (413), where before it converted; none of the 1,261 real-world PDFs reaches it: each reads within one 64 MiB budget even when the stored bytes of every picture are counted as well.
  - **The licence texts of the decoders have to ship** (`docs/licensing.md`, section on the WebAssembly decoders): `Dockerfile.worker` copies the six `LICENSE_*` files of the `wasm` folder into `/licenses/pdfjs-dist-wasm/`, because `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` embeds only the licence files at the root of a package (section 6.2).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **`useWasm: false`**: the same pictures, 1.1 to 2.7 times the time (above).
  - **A `wasmUrl` for picture jobs only**: the decoder keeps its bytes for the whole thread (above), so the saving would depend on the order of the jobs.
  - **Decoding the three formats outside pdf.js** (OpenJPEG and a fax decoder from the worker image): a second colour path that differs from pdf.js's for the same picture, and the pictures of a page come from its operator list already.
  - **Leaving the pictures out and recording a warning**: the pictures are the content of the document (entry 81).
  - **Refusing the job (413) for a picture past a limit, as `pdf-jbig2-guard.ts` does for Poppler**: one oversized picture would cost the text and every other picture, where PDFium and pdf.js leave out only that picture. Inline pictures, which cannot be left out, are refused.
  - **Deleting the `*_nowasm_fallback.js` files from the worker image to close the JavaScript fallback**: the tests and a development run read the package's own folder, and a new pdfjs-dist would bring the files back; the `wasmUrl` below the folder depends on neither.
  - **Lowering the maximum in the worker image (`Dockerfile.worker`) with a pinned digest**: the tests and a development run would read the unpatched files, and a new pdfjs-dist would need a new digest; the factory reads the module's sections and fails closed when it cannot lower the maximum.
  - **A count of 256 decoded pictures a page**: pages of real documents decode up to 446 (`govdocs1-003690.pdf`), whose pictures past the 256th are not recorded but would be refused.
  - **A document budget of decode time from pixels**: the decoders' speed depends on the content by three orders of magnitude (a white CCITT row of 65,535 columns decodes at 38,000 pixels a millisecond, the CCITT scans of `govdocs1-002608.pdf` at 186 and a JBIG2 scan at 25 with the rest of the conversion), so a budget either refuses documents that finish or does not bound the slow ones; the 60 s deadline stays the bound on time.
- **Measured**: text, Markdown and HTML of the 1,261 real-world PDFs and of every tenth PDF of the regression corpus by id (950), origin/main (`d6605e4c`) against the change, 6,633 conversions each, three processes per side; Word of the 251 of those files that have such a picture.
  - **Text**: 2,211 conversions, one differs: `cc-2800979.pdf`, a scan without fonts whose OCR text differs with the load of the machine (1,984 and 1,986 bytes in the loaded run; 1,982 bytes in all three runs of each side when run alone, Markdown included).
  - **Markdown and HTML**: 238 files change, and no output changes otherwise (the OCR file above is the 239th). Pictures in the Markdown: 96,639 to 108,509 (11,870 more); the same 12 refusals before and after.
  - **Word**: 250 of 251 documents change, drawings 14,020 to 17,819 and media files 12,554 to 15,963; the 251st (`govdocs1-000282.pdf`) is refused by the 5,000-picture limit of the Word writer before and after.
  - **Oracle** (`pdfimages -list`, 120 files with a CCITT, JBIG2 or JPEG 2000 image row): the Markdown holds those pictures at those sizes in 104. The 16 others: 12 files have no text layer (`pdftotext` finds no character), their Markdown is the same bytes as their text and holds no picture before and after (the pages are recognized, as for the scans of entry 98); `govdocs1-001659.pdf` holds all 19 pictures, but 11 of them are JPEG 2000 pictures under a larger CCITT /Mask and the reader writes them at the size of the mask (`182x78` for the listed `121x52`); `govdocs1-004121.pdf`, `govdocs1-003071.pdf` and `govdocs1-004389.pdf` have pages with 642, 2,505 and 3,150 image rows and stop at the 256 pictures a page.
  - **Times of the corpus runs are not compared**: both sides ran with other work on the machine (load average 7 to 10).
  - **Decoder memory and the check (review of #887)**: the Markdown and Word outputs of the 251 files with such a picture, before the check (`9b0801c9`) and after it, hold the same pictures: 23,688 in the Markdown, every Markdown file the same bytes, 17,819 drawings and 15,963 media files in the Word files, and the same one refusal; the check leaves out no picture of them. Over the 1,261 real-world PDFs the largest estimate is 34.2 MiB (`govdocs1-001307.pdf`, which took 43 MiB of module memory), the longest walk 69 million pixels (`govdocs1-003399.pdf`), the most decoded pictures 496 a document and 446 a page, and no JBIG2 picture has more region pixels than its page. Read in the reader's thread (Mac, Node 24), each hostile picture of the tests is left out with no resident growth to speak of (0 to 1 MiB after a warm-up job), where without the check a 4096 x 4096 RGB JPEG 2000 behind FlateDecode grew the process by 197 MiB and was decoded, and stacked JBIG2 regions grew it by 174 MiB before the abort; a JPEG 2000 of 8000 x 8000 behind LZW, which the check cannot read, ends at the maximum with a null picture and 52 MiB of growth, and without the maximum it was decoded in 1.4 s with 963 MiB of growth. After the fixes of the second review round the 251 files give the same result again: 23,688 pictures in the Markdown, every file the same bytes as before the round (`db2f2a45`), no error, and no document given more than the budget.
- **Verified by**: `tests/pdf-picture-decoders.test.ts` (the decoding and the text-job tests were red before the change: a CCITT Group 4, a JBIG2 and a JPEG 2000 picture made by other tools, read as the pixels they code and written into Markdown through the text thread; a text job decodes none of them; hostile pictures, each within 15 s and 512 MiB of resident set: a JBIG2 page declaring 100,000 x 100,000 pixels, a CCITT picture of a billion columns, a JPEG 2000 size marker of 60,000 x 60,000, a 12,000 x 12,000 picture in 1,178 bytes decoded within the pixel limit, 600 distinct JPEG 2000 pictures on one page kept to 256; the 4 pictures of `govdocs1-000142.pdf` and the 70 of `govdocs1-003685.pdf` at the sizes `pdfimages` lists), `tests/third-party-notices.test.ts` (the licence texts are copied into `/licenses`), `tests/pdf-picture-decoders-limits.test.ts` (all in the reader's thread with the resident memory of the process sampled: a module lowered to 256 MiB grows to it and no further, and a module without a memory maximum, or with one that cannot hold the new one, is refused; a 4-component 2048 x 2048 and a 3-component 3584 x 3584 JPEG 2000 behind FlateDecode decoded at full size, an 8000 x 8000 decoded at the 2000 x 2000 pdf.js reduces it to; left out within 96 MiB of growth: a 3-component 4096 x 4096 JPEG 2000 behind FlateDecode, a JP2 whose decoy size marker would have it decoded at 8000 x 8000, a JBIG2 generic region of 65,535 x 65,535 on a 64 x 32 page, eight intermediate JBIG2 regions of 16,384 x 16,384, a CCITT picture of 8 x 65,535 decoded at 65,535 columns; an inline CCITT picture of that size refused and a small one read; 32,769 CCITT pictures on a page refused before decoding; 100 pictures that share a JBIG2Globals stream of 1 MiB converted, which reading it once per picture would refuse; 65 JPEG 2000 streams of 1 MiB stored without a wrapper converted, which charging them to the 64 MiB wrapper budget would refuse; under the maximum, within 416 MiB of growth: an 8000 x 8000 JPEG 2000 behind LZW and three JBIG2 pictures whose regions stack past it give null pictures and the picture after them is decoded, and 4 threads of the pool doing so at once. Each test of the check fails with the check taken out by hand, each test of the maximum with the maximum taken out, the shared-globals test with the globals read again for each picture, and the 65 MiB test with stored bytes charged), `tests/pdf-picture-guard.test.ts` (red before the review fixes except the `CCF` spelling, which was already read: /F, /DP and /H before /Filter, /DecodeParms and /Height, `JPX` decoded at full size where `JPXDecode` is reduced, an indirect /Subtype, an /SMask with a codec filter and no /Subtype, the file header of a JBIG2 stream and of its JBIG2Globals with and without a page count, a content stream whose filter is written /F inflated within the byte budgets, 16,384 against 16,385 components and 32 against 33 levels, a COC marker that runs out of bytes neither throwing nor refusing the document for an object or an inline picture, 200,000 objects named in one update, 1,000 pictures that share 8 MiB of zero bytes as JBIG2Globals, 4,000 inline images with an array that is never closed, and 100 pictures whose /Length runs to the end of a 16 MiB stream, of which the first three are read), `tests/pdf-picture-header-errors.test.ts` (a header reader made to throw a RangeError: the image object is left out, an inline picture is not refused, another error is not hidden), `tests/pdf-wasm-fallback.test.ts` (the pinned pdfjs-dist version, both modules taking the maximum, no fallback file below the `wasmUrl` while the folder has them, and a module that cannot take the maximum giving a null picture where the same folder given to pdf.js as `wasmUrl` decodes it in the JavaScript fallback), the corpus comparisons above, and the Linux VM timings above.
- **Revisit when**: pdf.js stops keeping the fetched decoder bytes, or changes the size limits of its decoders, its reduction of JPEG 2000 pictures or how it reads their size; pdf.js.jbig2 or pdf.js.openjpeg change the codecs they build (the estimates follow PDFium bb1f9f71 and OpenJPEG 8314119b); a real picture needs more than the 192 MiB check or the 256 MiB maximum; a real document reaches the 60 s deadline or the 128 MiB of picture bytes only because of these pictures; pdfjs-dist is upgraded (`tests/pdf-wasm-fallback.test.ts` pins 6.3.289), or pdf.js gives a way to turn the JavaScript fallback off or reads `wasmUrl` for something else in Node; the scan follows the cross-reference as pdf.js does (the #783 row); or the worker image gets a decoder that is faster than the pdf.js modules.

## 102. IGES: the Global and Terminate sections are checked before the kernel reads a file, a mesh is written to IGES by the kernel, and OBJ carries the colours in an MTL file

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, the four rows "Follow-ups from #792 (STEP and IGES)"; epic #760), decided 2026-10-25 (QA request in issue #783). It changes three statements of entry 43 (the Hollerith follow-up, "OBJ carries no materials" and "no mesh to IGES through the kernel"); entry 43 points here.
- **Decision**:
  - **An IGES file is checked before the kernel reads it** (`src/lib/conversions/cad-iges-preflight.ts`), by the records the kernel's own reader sees (80 columns, the section letter in column 73, the Global section as the first 72 columns of its records joined: OCCT 7.9 `src/IGESFile/liriges.c` lines 53 to 57 and 105 to 113, `igesread.c` lines 107 to 108).
  - **The Terminate line must count the records the file holds.** One Terminate record, `S`, `G`, `D` and `P` each followed by seven digits (IGES 5.3 section 2.2.6; the layout is read off the five real files, `S      1G      4D   1302P  11517`). A file with no Terminate line, two of them, a malformed count, or a count that differs from the records is refused with HTTP 422 before the program starts, and the answer names the section and both numbers ("its Terminate line counts 11,518 Parameter Data records, but the file holds 11,517"). The kernel only warns about a missing line (`igesread.c` lines 125 to 128) and reads whatever records are there: a copy of `occt-hammer.iges` cut after 50 percent converted to a part of the model without any error, and `pyocc-testfile.igs` cut after 75 percent made the reader fault (exit 139).
  - **A Hollerith count of the Global section that the file itself shows to be too large is rewritten; any other count that no delimiter follows is refused.** IGES 5.3 gives a string as `nHtext`, n characters, then the parameter delimiter (sections 2.2.2 and 2.2.3). The kernel honours n literally (`analiges.c` lines 220 to 243), so a count that is too large swallows the delimiter and the blanks to the end of the record, the next parameter is dropped (`analiges.c` line 259, `reste = -1`), and every later parameter moves one place: `testfile.igs` counts 38 for the 32 characters of its file name, the unit flag (2, millimetre) is read as the scale and the model is 25.4 times too large. No reader recovers: the kernel does not, and the other open reader refuses such a record (libIGES `iges_io.cpp` lines 231 to 330, behaviour only). The rule is therefore the narrowest that the file proves: the text of the declared n characters ends in a delimiter that only blanks follow up to the declared end, and the delimiter does not follow the declared end (blanks before a delimiter are accepted as the kernel accepts them). The count becomes the text before that delimiter, written in the width it had (`032H`), so no record changes length. A count whose text is longer than declared, or that runs past the Global section, is refused with the count and the parameter named, because converting it would read the length unit from the wrong place. The count digits are read up to 9; a longer count is refused as larger than any section.
  - **Mesh to IGES is written by the kernel** (`cad-convert --from mesh`, `native/cad-convert/cad-convert.cpp`). The worker parses the STL or OBJ as before and hands the program the indexed triangle list; the program builds the compound of planar faces as FreeCAD's `makeShapeFromMesh` does (`src/Mod/Part/App/TopoShapePyImp.cpp` line 1710 calling `TopoShape::setFaces`, `TopoShape.cpp` lines 3341 to 3460: one vertex per mesh vertex, one edge per pair of neighbouring triangles with the second taking it reversed, a wire of three edges, a face of the wire, triangles with two coincident corners left out, line 3419) and the kernel's IGES writer writes it. The in-repo IGES encoder (`encodeIges`, 330 lines) is deleted: the kernel's reader faulted on its output (exit 139 on a 10 mm cube), and its Global section counted `1H` for `m.igs` of five characters, the very fault of the first row.
  - **A mesh takes at most 50,000 triangles to IGES.** Every triangle is a trimmed surface (about 1.8 KB of text, 89 MB for 49,928 triangles). 50,000 is the most whose file the kernel's reader reads back inside the worker's 2 GiB (1.62 GB, 10.3 s; 99,458 triangles take 3.19 GB to read back although the write needs only 702 MB and 8.7 s). The worker applies the limit before the program starts, with the count and the limit in the answer, and the program applies it again (exit 5, `too-large`), with the size of the file checked against its header before anything is allocated.
  - **A mesh lists at most 150,000 vertices and no coordinate beyond 2e100, and every face index names a listed vertex.** 150,000 is three corners for each of the 50,000 triangles, so a vertex that no triangle uses cannot size the arrays past what the triangles could. 2e100 is `Precision::Infinite()` (`Precision.hxx`), the kernel's own "no bound"; a finite 1e300 overflows the collinearity test to NaN and reaches the edge and face builders. The worker refuses each case with HTTP 422 before the program starts (an index outside the list used to throw an untyped range error, and a NaN index was written as vertex 0); the program applies the same limits with exit status 5. The OBJ writer fails with exit status 5 when a material name holds a character outside letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, so a name can never add lines to the OBJ or MTL file; the kernel's material map names them `mat_N` today.
  - **OBJ carries the colours of the document model in an MTL file.** The faces are visited as the kernel's OBJ writer visits them and the materials are named and defined by its material map (`RWObj_CafWriter.cxx` lines 133 to 152 and 301 to 310 in OCCT 7.6.3, `RWObj_ObjMaterialMap`, `RWMesh_FaceIterator`; the MTL is created when a face has a colour, lines 160 to 170 and 255 to 258). The OBJ names its material file in an `mtllib` line. A model with colours comes as a ZIP of `<name>.obj` and `<name>.mtl` (the declared archive of several files that a workbook with several sheets already uses, `output-check.ts`), named like the request with every character outside `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -` replaced by `_`; a model with no colour is the OBJ alone, with no `mtllib` and no `usemtl`, as before. Colours are the `COLOUR_RGB` of a STEP file and the colour entities of an IGES file as the document model holds them (the red cube and blue cylinder: `Kd 0.866667 0.321569 0.156863` and `Kd 0.231373 0.380392 0.705882`, the numbers of the STEP text).
- **Why**:
  - A repair the file proves is safe where a guess is not. The count is wrong only when the declared end is not followed by a delimiter; the repair applies only when the text itself ends in the delimiter the count swallowed. Every other count is left to the kernel or refused, so no valid file changes: the five real IGES files (all four others unchanged byte for byte, the Hollerith text across records of `pyocc-sunglasses_lens.igs` included) and thousands of generated ones are checked.
  - The Terminate line is the format's own cut-off marker. Without it the kernel turns half a file into half a model or faults, and a customer gets a part with missing surfaces.
  - The kernel is the only reader of IGES here, so the only IGES writer that can be trusted to be read by it is the kernel's. FreeCAD builds the mesh B-rep with the same calls and exports it with the same writer.
  - Writing the faces one at a time: `IGESControl_Writer::AddShape` runs the shape-healing sequence over the whole shape and that run is quadratic in the number of faces (the profile is in `ShapeProcess_ShapeContext::RecordModification`): 9,800 triangles took 18.7 s as one compound and 0.9 s to 1.1 s one by one, to a file within 0.7 percent in size (17.5 MB and 17.4 MB); 99,458 triangles take 9.5 s. The same time on STEP and IGES B-reps does not occur, because their writer works from the document model.
  - Reusing the kernel's material map and not its whole OBJ body keeps the OBJ the way entry 43 wrote it: the kernel's OBJ writer repeats the vertices of every face and writes normals and texture coordinates, which makes the corners of neighbouring faces unequal for a reader (a closed solid read back as open by the independent mesh reader, 23,602 bytes for the red cube against 4,564).
- **Results** (macOS host with Open CASCADE 7.9, and Ubuntu 24.04 arm64 with 7.6.3, the oldest version the program builds against; both pass every test named below):
  - `testfile.igs` converted to STL: the extent of the model is that of the control points in the file (39.74 mm by 40.53 mm), where the kernel wrote 25.4 times that; the unit read from the file is flag 2 (millimetre), where it was flag 1.
  - The four other real IGES files and the eight STEP files convert as before: the area and the box of every STL and OBJ agree with the independent mesher, to the tolerances of the existing tests.
  - Truncation: the real files cut at every tenth of their length, and a generated file cut every 37 bytes, are refused; the Terminate line of a complete file is accepted with LF, CR LF, CR or no line ends. A hundred thousand wrong Hollerith counts are repaired in 20 ms.
  - Mesh to IGES: a 10 mm cube from an OBJ and from a binary STL, an open sheet and a torus of 288 triangles are written, read back by the program (closed solid, 12 faces, volume 1000.00 mm^3, 600 mm^2) and by a separate build of the kernel (600 mm^2).
  - Write and read-back cost on Ubuntu 24.04 arm64 (Open CASCADE 7.6.3): 25,088 triangles 2.2 s and 202 MB to write, 5.1 s and 832 MB to read; 49,928 triangles 4.3 s and 367 MB, 10.3 s and 1.62 GB; 99,458 triangles 8.7 s and 702 MB, 21.0 s and 3.19 GB. macOS arm64 with 7.9: 9,800 triangles 1.2 s and 89 MB; 99,458 triangles 9.5 s and 702 MB. No x86-64 machine was available; CI runs the tests there.
  - Colours: the red cube and the blue cylinder come out with the `Kd` of the STEP text on exactly the faces of their part (cube 600 mm^2, cylinder 471.2 mm^2); through IGES the cube keeps its colour and the end faces of the cylinder keep theirs, the side does not (a property of the IGES that the kernel writes from this STEP file or reads from it, found while testing and not changed here).
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A STEP or IGES file with colours converts to OBJ as a ZIP.** The result type depends on the content, as it does for a workbook with several sheets. A client that wants the plain OBJ takes the member of the archive. The alternative of colours in the vertex lines (`v x y z r g b`) keeps one file but is read by fewer programs than the MTL file of the format.
  - **A file refused by the Terminate line may be one the kernel would read.** An exporter that writes wrong counts but a complete file is refused. The five real files and the Terminate lines of the kernel's own writer pass; the refusal names the section and both counts so the file can be repaired.
  - **The written IGES is a set of trimmed surfaces, not a shell or a solid** (entities 186 and 514 are not written; the faces are not sewn, which dominates the run time of a large mesh: FreeCAD's own comment puts the saving at 90 percent, `TopoShape.cpp` lines 3437 to 3441). The kernel reads each triangle back as a face, and a CAD program that wants a solid sews the faces.
  - **50,000 triangles is a cut**: a mesh of 1,000,000 triangles (the limit of the STL reader) can be written to STEP, STL and OBJ and not to IGES. IGES carries a surface per triangle at 1.8 KB, which is why a larger mesh is better delivered as STEP.
  - A triangle whose corners lie on a line is left out of the IGES (FreeCAD's check is for coincident corners only; the kernel would write a face of no area for it). A mesh with no triangle that is a face is refused.
  - The OBJ writer's empty `Ka`/`Kd` material, which the kernel defines for a face style without colour in some files (`pyocc-io1-ug-214.stp`, `mat_1`), is kept as the kernel defines it.
  - The faces of an OBJ are ordered by material, the faces with none first, because OBJ cannot end a material (the kernel's writer writes a bare `usemtl` line, which strict readers refuse).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Reading the Hollerith string to the next delimiter whatever the count**: one extra rule over the kernel for every file, and wrong for a text that holds the delimiter; the narrow rule changes only a file that proves its fault.
  - **Refusing `testfile.igs` for its count**: it is a real file of a mainstream exporter, and the repair gives its true size.
  - **Fixing `encodeIges`**: it is 330 lines of our own entity writing (502, 504, 508, 510, 190, 514, 186) with no reference, and the kernel reading it is the only test; the kernel's writer is what every other converter's IGES comes from.
  - **The kernel's whole OBJ writer** (`RWObj_CafWriter`): see Why.
  - **One `AddShape` for the whole mesh**: quadratic, see Why.
- **Verified by**: `tests/cad-iges-preflight.test.ts` (the real `testfile.igs` repaired in one byte with the file name of 32 characters and the unit flag and name at parameters 14 and 15; the other four real files unchanged; counts that shrink in digits, that lie across records, that are followed by blanks, with the default delimiters, too short, past the section and of any size up to 20 digits; a hundred thousand counts in 20 ms; each of the four Terminate counts wrong, 9,999,999, a cut at every 37th byte and at every tenth of the real files, records removed, a second Terminate line, a malformed one, and text that is no IGES file; with mutation checks that fail the repair and the Terminate tests), `tests/cad-occt-real-samples.test.ts` (the extent of `testfile.igs` equal to its control points; a cut-off real file and a Terminate count one too high refused before the kernel; the colours of the red cube and blue cylinder on the faces of their part, through IGES, the OBJ alone for a model with no colour, the names of the ZIP members, every material an OBJ uses defined in its MTL file for all ten samples; the program on empty, short, long, out-of-range, NaN, infinite, 0xffffffff and 50,001-triangle inputs, and a mesh of 49,928 triangles written and read back), `tests/cad-step-iges-encoders.test.ts` (mesh to IGES for a cube from an OBJ and a binary STL, an open sheet, a torus, a coincident corner, a line of collinear corners and an empty mesh), `tests/cad-occt-wrapper.test.ts` (the Terminate refusal and the 50,001-triangle refusal never start the program; 50,000 triangles are handed to it in the input form; the ZIP of an OBJ and its MTL, a hostile file name kept inside the scratch directory).
- **Revisit when**: a real IGES file with a wrong Terminate line is found that the kernel reads correctly (then the counts that may differ are named); the worker's memory limit changes (the 50,000 follows it); IGES solids from meshes are wanted (sewing, `BRepBuilderAPI_Sewing`, as `TopoShape::sewShape` does); the kernel's OBJ writer shares vertices; or QA decides the OBJ should always be a plain file.

## 103. Compound-file sources (.sdw, .sdc, .sda, .shw, .qpw): the class ID of the root storage and the names under the root say which kind a file is

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, the row "Compound-file sources are told apart by extension only"), decided 2026-10-25 (QA request). It replaces the container-signature-only rule of the compound-file bullet in entry 38, which now points here.
- **Decision**:
  - **The spoof check reads the root of the compound file** (`compound-file-kind.ts`) for these five names. It follows the directory chain from the first directory sector of the header through the FAT sectors that the header and the DIFAT chain list (a sector of either kind read once, the list ending at the count the header gives, as `parseCfbf` does; the chain is followed only as far as the sector looked up needs), reads only whole sectors that lie inside the bytes it is given, and takes the class ID of the first entry (which must be the root storage, as libmagic requires, `ole2compounddocs` line 95) and the names of the entries under the root, in upper case, following the child link and the sibling links.
  - **Sources.** libmagic `Magdir/ole2compounddocs` (commit 41b1123): the class IDs of StarWriter, StarCalc and StarDraw 3 to 5 (lines 642 to 713) and of Corel Presentations (lines 612 to 617). LibreOffice `include/comphelper/classids.hxx` (commit 9cb04a8): the same IDs by their `SO3_*` names (lines 28 to 212), and `sot/source/sdstor/stg.cxx` lines 853 to 862 for reading the class ID of a storage. Apache Tika `POIFSContainerDetector.detect` (commit eb8d704, lines 290 to 316): `StarCalcDocument`, `StarWriterDocument` and `StarDrawDocument3` under the root, a `Workbook` stream deciding first, and no class ID read. The names are compared in upper case for the letters a to z only, as the office suite compares them, so `ſtarcalcdocument` (long s) is not `StarCalcDocument`. libwps `WPSHeader::constructHeader` (lines 220 to 228): a `NativeContent_MAIN` stream for Quattro Pro 9. The behaviour is followed; no code of those projects is copied.
  - **The verdict.** A class ID that belongs to another kind, or names of another kind, refuses the file, and so does the root class ID of a Word, Excel or PowerPoint file (Word 6-95 and 97-2003, Excel 5-95 and 97-2003, PowerPoint 4, 95 and 97-2003, as libmagic `ole2compounddocs` lists them, lines 295, 300, 322, 329, 357, 408 and 415 of release 5.41), whatever streams the file holds: a Word file with an added `StarWriterDocument` stream is a Word file. The names then accept only a file whose class ID is all zero or is listed nowhere. A class ID of the kind, or a name of the kind, accepts it. A root that names no kind is refused. The kinds a class ID can name are the five and their neighbours (StarImpress, StarMath, StarChart, StarOffice master documents, WordPerfect documents and graphics), so that their files are not taken for a neighbour. A class ID that no database lists says nothing: the Quattro Pro 9 sample carries `EB626F5C-12A9-4F24-A0FC-01B5C2534C35` and is accepted by its stream. A class ID of all zeros, with the stream names of the kind, is accepted, as Tika never reads the class ID of these files.
  - **Corel Presentations is accepted by its class ID only** (`402EFE62-1999-101B-99AE-04021C007002`). No engine names it by a stream (`PerfectOffice_MAIN` is also the stream of WordPerfect documents and Quattro Pro 7 and 8 files), so a `.shw` file with a zero or another class ID is refused.
  - **StarOffice 3 gives StarDraw and StarImpress one class ID** (`AF10AAE0-B36D-101B-9961-04021C007002`, `SO3_SIMPRESS_CLASSID_30`, which libmagic line 652 names StarDraw): `Draw_3.1.sda` of the corpus carries it, so `.sda` accepts it. The StarImpress 4 and 5 class IDs are refused under `.sda` (Impress is `.sdd`). The stream `StarDrawDocument3` is in both applications' files; Tika reads `CompObj` to tell them apart, and this check does not, so a StarImpress file with no class ID is taken for either.
  - **The limits of the parser that reads the file in full apply** and are the same constants (`CFBF_MAX_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES` 65,536, the two sector shifts 9 and 12, the reserved sector numbers; `hwp.ts` now imports them from `compound-file-kind.ts`). A directory chain or tree that returns to a sector or an entry it has read, a FAT or DIFAT sector listed twice, and a first directory sector that is a marker (free, end of chain, FAT or DIFAT, from `0xfffffffa` up) are malformed, as in `parseCfbf`. The directory is read from the bytes given, never from beyond them, so the work is at most 65,536 entries of 128 bytes whatever the declared sizes.
  - **A directory past the bytes given is read where it lies when the file is whole.** The check is handed the first 64 KiB of an upload on the storage paths (`HEADER_WINDOW_BYTES`), and the directory of a larger file lies past them. For the five names, the callers that hold the file on disk (`assertNotSpoofedFilePath`: the resumable upload, the worker) or in a store (`assertCompoundFileKindInObject`, called by the job route for a storage key) therefore read the directory sectors and the FAT, DIFAT and directory sectors they lead to at their offsets, through one walk of the root that asks for byte ranges (`readCompoundFileRootFrom` over a file, `readCompoundFileRootFromAsync` over range requests to the store). The ranges are served from blocks of 64 KiB, each fetched once, and a read fetches at most 256 blocks, twice the 128 that the largest directory accepted (65,536 entries of 128 bytes, 8 MiB) fills when it lies in one run; a directory that needs more is malformed. No reference parser bounds the blocks, because they read a file in memory: the bound is ours and follows from the entry maximum. Every backend answers `openReadStream` with a range and the remote client refuses a store that does not honour one (the header read already needs it), so no backend keeps the window rule. For a file that is whole, a root the source ends before is refused like any other that names no kind.
  - **The window rule remains for a buffer of exactly 64 KiB.** A caller that holds only the start of a file and gives it as a buffer (the registry in the browser, the first chunk of a streamed upload before it is stored) cannot see past it: a buffer of exactly that length whose directory (or a sector of it) lies past it is accepted on the container signature, as Visio files are, and a shorter or longer buffer is the whole file and is refused. The object is then checked again where it is stored, by the job route, and a header whose first directory sector is a marker is refused at any length.
  - **A refusal is the existing typed refusal** (`FileExtensionSpoofError`, HTTP 400), whether the file is of another kind, has no readable root, or is malformed.
- **Why**:
  - **The extension alone let any compound file in under these names.** A Word, Excel or PowerPoint file named `.sdw` reached the StarOffice filters of the office suite, which failed with an error that did not name the cause. The row of #783 asked for the class ID or the stream names to be read.
  - **Entry 38 said the class IDs of the real files differ from the databases; that was true of shared-mime-info only.** shared-mime-info lists StarWriter 3 and 4 and no StarCalc or StarDraw. libmagic and LibreOffice list the StarOffice 3 to 5 IDs of all three, and the four StarOffice files of the corpus carry exactly those: StarWriter 3 `DC5C7E40`, StarCalc 3 `3F543FA0`, StarDraw 3 (the shared ID) `AF10AAE0`, StarWriter 5 `C20CF9D1`, StarCalc 5 `C6A5B861`, StarDraw 5 `2E8905A0`. Only Quattro Pro 9 has an ID no database lists, which is why its stream decides.
  - **Class ID and names are both read** because each is what a different engine uses, and a file in which they disagree is not one of these kinds for any of them.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A Word, Excel or PowerPoint file with a StarOffice stream added, or a compound file whose names fold into a StarOffice name only by Unicode case rules, is refused.** No real file of the five kinds is such a file.
  - **A large file costs range requests.** A compound-only file of 64 KiB or more reads its directory beyond the header: one block for a directory in a run (two for a FAT sector and a directory sector in different blocks), at most 256 for a scattered one. Smaller files cost none.
  - **A truncated or damaged compound file under these names is now refused as a spoof (400) where it was refused later as corrupt.** The refusal is typed and arrives earlier and cheaper; the message names the declared format and the container type of the bytes.
  - **A StarImpress file named `.sda`, a Quattro Pro 7 or 8 file named `.qpw`, and a Corel Presentations show with another class ID named `.shw` are refused.** They are other kinds under a wrong name (Quattro Pro 7 and 8 files are `.wb3`).
  - **The Quattro Pro 9 content field (`QPW9`) and `CompObj` are not read.** libwps reads the first field of `NativeContent_MAIN`, and the office suite reads it when it converts; reading a stream here needs the mini FAT and costs more than a name does, for the same kind of answer.
  - **The check is a few microseconds**: 4.2 to 8.2 us per call on the five kinds of the corpus cut to the 64 KiB window (median of 7 runs of 20,000 calls, Mac, tsx, load average 6 to 7 from other work, so the figures are for comparison only), against 2.0 to 3.8 us for the first version, which read the buffer directly. The walk that asks for byte ranges, so that one reader serves a buffer, a file and a store, costs about twice that; the verdicts are the same on every file. A check that runs once per upload is not on a path where 4 us matters.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Parsing the whole file with `parseCfbf` in the spoof check**: it copies every stream, and the storage paths hold only the first 64 KiB.
  - **Reading only the class ID**: Quattro Pro 9 is unlisted, and Tika accepts the Star formats by name with any class ID.
  - **Reading only the names**: no engine names Corel Presentations by a stream, and a class ID of another kind is the cheapest sign that a file is not the claimed one.
  - **Following libmagic's offset rule (the directory at the first directory sector times the sector size, one sector)**: files with more than four entries keep the rest of the directory in other sectors, so the FAT is followed.
- **Measured**: the five checks over the ten real files of the corpus (three StarWriter, two StarCalc, two StarDraw, two Corel Presentations, one Quattro Pro 9): each is accepted under its own name and refused under the other four, and the root names of each equal the names that `parseCfbf` reads.
- **Verified by**: `tests/compound-file-kind.test.ts` (the ten real files, the class ID of each, the names against the full parser, every table row in both directions, a wrong class ID, names of another kind, a missing root, a bad sector shift, a chain and a tree that return to themselves, 65,568 directory entries within two seconds, a directory past the bytes given, the root class ID of each Word, Excel and PowerPoint kind refused under all five names, `ſtarcalcdocument` and a dotless `nativecontent_maın` not taken for the names, the six marker values of the first directory sector malformed, a Word file whose directory lies past 64 KiB refused and a StarWriter file accepted through a byte source and an asynchronous one, a directory sector past FAT index 108 and in the second DIFAT sector read, a DIFAT chain that returns to itself malformed, and a directory spread over 300 blocks malformed after at most 256 fetches while 200 are read; each fails with its fix taken out by hand), `tests/spoof-check-variants.test.ts` (the registry and the server gate with the same cases; a Word file named `.sdw` with its directory past 64 KiB refused by path, as a whole buffer and in a store by range requests that stay inside the object, a StarWriter file accepted the same ways, and a header whose first directory sector is a marker refused at 64 KiB less one, 64 KiB and 64 KiB plus one) and `tests/remote-storage-wiring.test.ts` (the job route refuses that Word file in the object store by at most three range reads, none past the end of the object).
- **Revisit when**: a real StarOffice, Corel Presentations or Quattro Pro file is refused here (the nightly run lists it); an engine names Corel Presentations by a stream; the office suite reads StarImpress 3 to 5 files under `.sda`.

## 104. PDF text: a composite font whose ToUnicode map lacks a code reads it from the font program and prints nothing where the program has none, never the code itself

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, the row "composite fonts with a partial ToUnicode print the missing codes as the codes themselves"; epic #760), decided 2026-10-25 (QA request). It extends entry 70 to fonts that have a map, and settles the alternative that entry 98 rejected for the same reason ("the font-program maps of entry 70 rely on pdf.js printing the code").
- **Decision**:
  - **The reference.** Poppler reads a composite font that has a /ToUnicode map through the map alone: `GfxCIDFont::GfxCIDFont` takes the map first and uses the Adobe-Identity mapping only when there is none (`poppler/GfxFont.cc` 26.09, lines 1753 to 1759), `getNextChar` maps the code through it (lines 1939 to 1948), and a code the map does not list maps to nothing (`CharCodeToUnicode::mapToUnicode`, `poppler/CharCodeToUnicode.cc` lines 499 to 519). GPL, followed for its behaviour only. pdf.js writes the code itself as the character for such a code (`_charToGlyph`, `pdf.worker.mjs` of pdfjs-dist 6.3.289, line 34836: `toUnicode.get(charcode) || charcode`), and for a font whose codes are glyph ids that is a wrong letter: the `e` and `6` of `cmex10` and `cmmi10` in `govdocs1-002384.pdf`.
  - **For an Identity-H or Identity-V composite font of TrueType outlines (CIDFontType2) whose /ToUnicode stream lists codes, the text thread's copy of the file gets an entry for every code the font can select that the map lacks.** The codes are the glyphs of the program (`maxp`), or the entries of its /CIDToGIDMap stream, at most 65,536. A code's text is, in the order of ISO 32000-1 section 9.10.2: the font's own map (it follows the added entries in the new stream and wins, because the later entry of a code wins in pdf.js's CMap reader and the stream ends at the first `endcmap`), then the program's Unicode cmap through the CID-to-glyph map, then, for a program that names no glyph, the glyph order of Arial and Times New Roman of entry 70, and otherwise none. A code with none is written as a `bfrange` of private-use characters from U+E000, cut every 4,096 codes so that the characters stay below the U+F000 to U+F0FF where the symbol-font tables keep theirs; the reader leaves them out and counts them as glyphs no encoding maps, as it does for control codes (entry 49).
  - **The CIDs that already are the code point their glyph maps to now get an entry.** Entry 70 leaves them out of the maps it writes for fonts without a map, because pdf.js and Poppler both give the CID itself for such a font (Poppler's Adobe-Identity mapping, lines 1752 to 1759). A font that has a map no longer falls back to the CID, so these are explicit here: 72 of the 77 glyphs of `BMPJCL+TimesNewRoman` in `govdocs1-000272.pdf` have ASCII letters and digits as codes and read as before.
  - **A map that lists no code is no map.** pdf.js reads a font whose map ends up with no code as a font without one (`buildToUnicode`, line 42874), and Poppler's `parseCMap1` reports failure when it mapped nothing (`CharCodeToUnicode.cc` lines 167 to 175), so the font is read by entry 70. What the map lists is read as pdf.js reads it (`pdf-tounicode-coverage.ts`; `parseCMap`, lines 18465 to 18520): `bfchar`, `bfrange`, `cidchar` and `cidrange` entries, an entry that does not parse skipped, a range wider than 2^24 - 1 ignored (`MAX_MAP_RANGE`, line 18143), a range that ends before it starts empty, a code with an empty destination listed but without text, the scan ended by `endcmap`.
  - **Left as the file has them**: a map that names another CMap with `usecmap` (pdf.js adds that CMap's codes, `extendCMap` line 18521), a /ToUnicode that names a CMap instead of holding a stream, a font dictionary that does not end in `>>` (the new /ToUnicode goes last, since the later key wins), an encoding other than Identity-H and Identity-V, a CFF program (CIDFontType0: its glyph count is not read), a program without `maxp`, and a font with no embedded program. Their codes keep the reading they had.
  - **Bounds.** The 64 fonts, 64 MiB of decoded programs and 262,144 codes of entry 70 hold, and a gap counts every code it spans; a map that would pass them is not added (the font keeps its reading) and the later fonts are still tried, as before. The decoded ToUnicode streams are charged to the same 64 MiB. Ours: the fonts' own maps are copied into the update at most 8 MiB in all (a font's own map follows its entries in the new stream, once for each distinct body), and fonts written from the same program, CID-to-glyph map and own map share one body and one stream (a producer that writes a font again for every page: 12 fonts of `cc-6800070.pdf`, 64 sharing a map in the tests). Each ToUnicode stream is read once however many fonts name it. The coverage of a map is two marks per entry in a table of 65,536 codes, so a map of 100,000 ranges that each span all of them costs its tokens and 65,536 steps. A code past the glyphs of the font gets no entry (it is not a glyph, and entries for all 65,536 codes of each font would cost a document 4 fonts at the limit above and the time of cloning the maps to the main thread).
- **Why**:
  - **Where it happens.** In the 1,261 real-world PDFs, 258 files have a composite font with a ToUnicode map that lists codes, 709 such fonts are drawn on the pages read (505 TrueType, 204 CFF); in 17 files, 5,834 glyphs of 23 TrueType fonts (the largest code 243) and in 1 file 1 glyph of a CFF font are drawn with a code the map lacks, counted from the operator list with pdf.js's own glyph objects (5,834 of the 523,020 glyphs that the TrueType fonts draw, and 1 of the 511,760 of the CFF fonts). Most are Symbol, Wingdings and TeX symbol fonts from print drivers whose maps list the characters they have and not the bullets and operators, so Poppler's map gives those no text.
  - **Why the program's text is tried before nothing.** The Times New Roman fonts of Word-written files keep ASCII codes as CIDs and a ToUnicode map of five entries (`govdocs1-000272.pdf`, `govdocs1-000280.pdf`, `govdocs1-003704.pdf`): pdf.js read them right by the fallback, and the map lists none of the codes of 72 of the 77 glyphs of the first, so Poppler's rule gives them no text. Reading the program keeps those words; leaving the code out would lose them.
  - **Why entries and not a change to the reader.** The text of a page comes from pdf.js as strings in which a glyph that fell back to its code cannot be told from the same character mapped by the file (mapping text back was rejected in entry 70). The map is the one place where pdf.js decides.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A glyph with no text now takes no place in the line**: Poppler's word is split by the width it keeps (`di icult` for a ligature whose code is unmapped in `cc-3600799.pdf`), ours reads `diicult`. This is the cost of five word-level drops below.
  - **Glyphs now count as left out, with a warning**: `govdocs1-002384.pdf` 25 to 440 glyphs (pages 2 to 13 and more), `gd-070040.pdf` 12 to 1,246. They were control characters or code letters before and are reported as what they are. No page of the corpora was left out as a whole by the change (the largest shrink of a text result is 4.4 % of `cc-4000484.pdf`, 3.7 KB).
  - **A code past the glyphs of the font, and the codes of CFF fonts, keep the code as text.** One glyph in the real-world corpus (`govdocs1-004148.pdf`, a CFF font, code 12); none past the glyphs of a TrueType font there. The regression corpus was not counted from the operator list.
  - **The update is longer for the files it touches**: of 10,744 PDFs (1,261 real-world, 9,483 of the 9,500 regression PDFs that could be read), 232 and 1,933 get one, a median of 3.3 KB, 90th percentile 28.6 KB, 99th 439 KB, largest 2.3 MB (`cc-0000287.pdf`, a file of 6.1 MB) where before they got 117 KB in all. Preparing the bytes for pdf.js takes 29.5 to 30.3 s for the 2,165 files against 26.9 to 27.4 s (median of 3 per file, three alternating passes, Mac at a load average of 6.5, `uptime` 8:45); the slowest conversions of them, to text: `cc-6800070.pdf` 52 ms to 83 ms, `cc-6400146.pdf` 279 ms to 316 ms, `gd-328637.pdf` 115 ms to 145 ms (median of 7, alternating processes). Before the sharing of bodies, `cc-6800070.pdf` took 159 ms and the update of the 2,165 files was 386 MB.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Leaving the map's missing codes to pdf.js and removing the characters afterwards**: the string cannot tell a code from the same character mapped by the file.
  - **A NUL entry for every code with a `bfchar` each**: the same result at 2.8 MB for `cc-6800070.pdf` and 74 ms to prepare, against 0.56 MB and 15 ms with runs.
  - **Entries for all 65,536 codes of every font**: four fonts of a document at the limit above, and a map of 65,536 strings per font to clone to the main thread.
  - **The Poppler rule without the program** (nothing for every missing code): loses the words of the Word-written Times New Roman fonts above.
  - **Changing pdf.js**: a patch of its fonts file to every upgrade; the update keeps the standard's own mechanism (section 7.5.6) that entry 70 uses.
- **Measured**: text and Markdown of the PDFs whose update changed (2,165), origin/main against the change, 232 real-world and 1,933 regression files for text, all 232 and the 44 changed regression files plus a random 150 of the unchanged ones for Markdown, in-process, a fresh thread pool per side (the Markdown of the 150 unchanged ones did not change either).
  - 51 files change, the same 51 for text and Markdown: 7 of the real-world corpus and 44 of the regression corpus. Text: 952 characters removed and 1 added in the 7, 4,513 removed and 121 added in the 44. By the main thing removed: 20 files code letters of symbol and math fonts (`e`, `6`, `z`), 19 control characters (U+0089 and the like, printed before for Wingdings bullets), 4 punctuation and symbols, 1 layout only. The 121 characters added are in 5 regression files and 1 real-world file (`gd-523510.pdf` 84, `gd-064645.pdf` 24, `cc-6000800.pdf` 11): the letters the program gives where the code was another (`Futódomb` for `)utódomb`).
  - Word-level F1 against `pdftotext` 26.09 (words are runs of letters and digits, pictures of Markdown left out): real-world 4 files up, 3 equal, none down; regression text 19 up, 20 equal, 5 down by 0.0001 to 0.0017, Markdown the same. The largest rises are `govdocs1-002384.pdf` 0.9131 to 0.9354, `cc-4000484.pdf` 0.8008 to 0.8488, `gd-031192.pdf` 0.9836 to 0.9930, `govdocs1-001668.pdf` 0.9630 to 0.9718.
  - The five drops. `cc-3600799.pdf` 0.9939 to 0.9922: one ligature code, Poppler splits the word and we do not (above). `cc-6000800.pdf` 0.6346 to 0.6345: the change reads `Futódomb út`, `Kossuth Lajos út` and `Dr.Pécsi Gyula utca` that Poppler leaves out, so the words match no word of Poppler's. `gd-070040.pdf` 0.9411 to 0.9410, `gd-326174.pdf` 0.9692 to 0.9689 and `gd-499819.pdf` 0.9777 to 0.9775: Wingdings bullets that were control characters at the head of list lines; without them the lists lay out differently (`gd-499819.pdf` gets its paragraph back in order) and a running footer line appears 5 times fewer in `gd-070040.pdf`; the layout of those lines was read from the texts, not traced to the stage that changes it.
  - `govdocs1-002384.pdf`: `6\t=\tratio of feed to chip width` becomes `\t=\tratio of feed to chip width`, as Poppler prints it, and the paragraph around `The δ function is used to simulate a point force at the tool tip` is whole.
- **Verified by**: `tests/pdf-text-partial-tounicode.test.ts` (the codes a map lacks read from the program or left out, in text and Markdown; the update puts only the missing codes first and names its stream last; a map that lists no code, a range wider than pdf.js maps, a range that ends before it starts and an entry without a destination are no map; a CID that is its code point; a CID-to-glyph stream; `usecmap`, a named CMap, a font without `maxp`; a CID past the glyphs; 100,000 ranges that span the code space; 64 fonts that name a 65,535-glyph program get 4 maps; 32 fonts that each have a map of 1 MiB get 7 copies; 64 fonts that share a map get one stream; 4.8 MB of unterminated blocks scanned once; the real `govdocs1-002384.pdf`), `tests/pdf-tounicode-coverage.test.ts` (which codes a CMap lists), and the existing `tests/pdf-text-font-program-tounicode.test.ts`, `tests/pdf-text-standard-glyph-order.test.ts`, `tests/pdf-text-cid-widths-bounds.test.ts` and `tests/pdf-object-stream-leading-white.test.ts`, which hold the maps of entry 70.
- **Revisit when**: a CFF font with a partial map shows glyphs with a code in the corpora (the glyph count of a CFF program would have to be read), a file shows a CID past the glyphs of its TrueType font, a word-level comparison with Poppler on a real file loses words to the private-use run, or pdf.js stops falling back to the code (the entries of the CIDs that are their code point could then go).

## 105. FFmpeg 9.0.2 from its release archive in the worker image, built against the codec libraries of Debian, so that xHE-AAC decodes whole

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, row 129), decided 2026-10-25 (QA request). It reverses the decision of entry 97 ("no pinned FFmpeg") for the image. The refusal code of entry 46 stays; what changes is which FFmpeg the image runs.
- **Decision**:
  - **The image runs FFmpeg 9.0.2, built from the unmodified release archive.** `scripts/install-ffmpeg.sh` downloads `ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz` (published 2026-09-18) over HTTPS and checks its SHA-256 `8c3850283eb25fa026482078a04051e0be17347b09ef81a0849bec15a96e002e` before anything in it runs; the detached signature of the same archive was also checked against the FFmpeg release key `FCF986EA15E6E293A5644F10B4322F04D67658D8` when the pin was chosen. No patch is applied. The pin moves with `FFMPEG_VERSION` and `FFMPEG_SHA256` together. The reference service's formats API lists FFmpeg 6.1.4 and 7.1.3 (both deprecated), 8.1.2 and 9.0.1 (default, latest) for m4a to mp3 (queried 2026-10-25); 9.0.2 is the newest release of the same line.
  - **The Debian package is not installed.** The worker looks in `/usr/bin` before `/usr/local/bin`, so a package copy would shadow the build; the image build fails if `/usr/bin/ffmpeg` or `/usr/bin/ffprobe` exists. `/licenses/tool-versions.txt` ends with the line `ffmpeg 9.0.2 (source, sha256 <digest>)`, which the install script writes from its own version and digest variables, so a bump changes one place. The build is installed in `/opt/ffmpeg` (programs and shared libraries only: `make install-progs install-libs`, no headers, no pkg-config files) and linked as `/usr/local/bin/ffmpeg` and `ffprobe`. The `ffmpeg` stage of `Dockerfile.worker` builds on the same pinned Node.js image as the runner, so it links the same Debian libraries; the runner installs their runtime packages (`libx264-164`, `libx265-215`, `libvpx9`, `libsvtav1enc2`, `libdav1d7`, `libopus0`, `libmp3lame0`, `libvorbisenc2`, `libtheoraenc1`, `libtheoradec1`, `libwebp7`, `libwebpmux3`, `libsoxr0`, `libzimg2`, `libass9`, `libdrm2`, with `libva-drm2` it had).
  - **Configuration.** `--enable-gpl` (libx264 and libx265 are GPL-2.0-or-later, so the programs are GPL; they run as separate processes as before), never `--enable-nonfree`, `--enable-version3` or libfdk-aac (the script fails the build if `-buildconf` names `--enable-nonfree`). `--disable-autodetect` with each library named, so a missing development package fails the configure and nothing is linked by accident. Hardening is the toolchain upstream ships (`--toolchain=hardened`, `configure` lines 5006 to 5012 of the archive: position-independent executables, read-only relocations, immediate binding, the stack protector, fortified libc calls), checked after the build with `readelf` as for GhostXPS, on the two programs and on every `libav*.so` (the demuxers and decoders live in the libraries): read-only relocations, immediate binding, and a `RUNPATH` equal to the install lib directory with no `RPATH`; optimisation is FFmpeg's own default, `-O3`. `--enable-shared --enable-rpath`, so the two programs share one copy of the libav libraries.
  - **What is linked, and why.** The encoders the argument builders name: libx264, libx265, libvpx (VP9), libsvtav1 (AV1), libopus, libmp3lame, libvorbis; libtheora and libwebp for the targets that take FFmpeg's default encoder (`ogv`, animated `webp`); libdav1d (AV1 decode); libsoxr (the resampler the audio path asks for, found through `--enable-libsoxr` in `-buildconf`), libzimg (`zscale`, the HDR tone mapping), libass (`subtitles`); VAAPI and NVENC for the hardware paths (`h264_vaapi`, `hevc_vaapi`, `h264_nvenc`, `hevc_nvenc`; QSV was off in the Debian build too); zlib, bzip2, lzma and iconv for containers and subtitle character sets. The script fails the build when an encoder, decoder or filter of that list is missing from `ffmpeg -encoders`, `-decoders` or `-filters`.
  - **What is left out.** The network protocols and TLS (`--disable-network`: the worker reads a file in a sandbox without a network, so an HLS or DASH playlist that names a remote segment now fails with `Protocol not found` where it failed on the missing network before), the capture and playback devices (only `lavfi` stays, for generated sources and the hardware probe), ffplay, the documentation, DASH input (no `--enable-libxml2`: the DASH demuxer probes by content, so an upload holding an MPD would be demuxed and its local segment files read from the worker's disk, and neither we nor the reference service accept DASH input; `libxml2-dev` and the runtime `libxml2` package are no longer named for FFmpeg), and every codec and filter library the conversions never name (libaom, libopenjpeg, libgsm, libspeex, libshine, libtwolame, libxvid, libbluray, libcdio, OpenCL, Vulkan, frei0r, ladspa, rubberband, vidstab, libplacebo, flite, codec2, jxl, OpenAL, SDL...).
  - **xHE-AAC.** Nothing in the conversion code changes. The detection of a decode that skips packets (`partialDecodeIn`, `unsupportedCodecIn`) reads FFmpeg's log, so it never fires for a stream FFmpeg 9.0.2 decodes whole and still answers `UnsupportedMediaCodecError` for any older build (the CI runner's 6.1, a self-hosted worker on 7.1). Removing it would let those builds write a 0.256 s file for a 1.000 s clip again. The refusal is not a version table.
  - **The test helpers learned the behaviour of FFmpeg 8 and 9** where they had written down 7.1's: the pixel format of a half-float OpenEXR (`gbrpf16le`, decoded in its own format so no conversion stands between the file and the compared values), the movie timescale of an MP4 (the track's rate, not 1000), the full length of the last MP3 packet in MP4, and the start of an AAC track in Matroska (0, not the priming offset). Each change keeps the assertion and widens only the value that the FFmpeg version decides.
- **Why**:
  - Row 129 of issue #783 records that xHE-AAC m4a files convert only with FFmpeg 8 or newer, and our image refused them by name. Debian 13 ships 7.1.5 and trixie-backports holds no FFmpeg (entry 97), so the only way to the same decoder is a build of ours.
  - Following the maintainers' signed release and the distribution's libraries keeps the build checkable (one archive, one digest) and keeps the codec libraries under Debian's security updates. The rejected static builds carry no such trail (see below).
  - The Debian package pulls 61 packages the conversions never load (libflite1 27 MB, libcodec2 16.5 MB, libavcodec61, libavfilter10, libplacebo, libjxl, libopenmpt, OpenAL, libcaca, libsrt, libzmq...). Subtracting them and adding the build is 86.0 MiB smaller on arm64 (below).
- **Results** (Lima VM `default`, arm64, 4 cores, a Debian 13 chroot; "base" is the Debian package 7.1.5-0+deb13u1 of the current image and "head" this build, both in the same chroot with the same Debian codec libraries; the amd64 image is built by the CI run of the pull request and was not measured here):
  - **xHE-AAC.** `fate-xhe_target_level.m4a` (1.000 s) on base decodes 0.256 s and logs `Error submitting packet to decoder: Not yet implemented in FFmpeg`; on head it decodes 1.000 s, mean volume -15.3 dB, no decoder error. Through the worker's engine on head it converts to flac, wav, mp3, aac (ADTS), ogg, opus and m4a, each 1.000 s (ADTS 1.024 s and Opus 1.0065 s carry the encoders' priming), mean volume -15.2 to -15.6 dB.
  - **Wall time of the product's conversions** (`convertWithNativeFfmpeg`, the long-lived worker's steady state: each process converts four small files first, so the hardware probe and the other one-time answers are cached; 7 rounds, base and head alternating, the side that goes first flipped each round, 0 errors in 168 runs; median in ms, range in brackets): 60 s WAV to MP3 318 [317 to 321] to 288 [286 to 289]; to M4A 579 [576 to 585] to 433 [428 to 454]; to Opus 403 [399 to 413] to 372 [369 to 380]; to FLAC 95 [94 to 102] to 57 [54 to 59]; to OGG **420 [415 to 449] to 744 [732 to 785]**; 10 s 720p MP4 to H.264 1051 [1018 to 1054] to 993 [990 to 1005]; to VP9 3558 [3501 to 3688] to 3512 [3495 to 3546]; to HEVC 2974 [2956 to 3019] to 2903 [2884 to 2985]; to MP3 118 [116 to 133] to 56 [51 to 72]; 2 s 320x240 MP4 to H.264 105 [102 to 109] to 72 [71 to 81]; M4A to FLAC 150 [145 to 155] to 92 [83 to 99]; the 30 s 1080p HDR10 clip to H.264 (tone mapping) 28321 [27913 to 29096] to 28181 [27573 to 29159]. The run before the warm-up was added (7 rounds as well, one-time answers included) read 416 to 322 ms for the MP3 and 1620 [1592 to 1682] to 1012 [988 to 1091] ms for H.264.
  - **Why the numbers are what they are.** The encoders are the same libraries, so the long encodes move by 1 to 5 percent (the raw H.264 command is 1040 to 1120 ms on base and 1000 ms on head). `ffmpeg -version` takes 34.0 ms on base and 3.0 ms on head (100 starts, 5 alternating rounds, 33.8 to 34.1 against 3.0 to 3.2), and an `ffprobe` of the small clip 36.3 ms against 4.7 ms, because base opens 212 shared objects and head 88; a conversion starts three to six of these processes, which is the 30 to 60 ms saved on the small jobs. The first H.264 conversion of a process opens an NVENC and a VAAPI session to find out whether either works, and a failed open (`Cannot load libcuda.so.1`) takes 550 ms on base and 5 to 10 ms on head (`ffmpeg -encoders` 63 ms against 4 ms): the 600 ms between the two first runs. The one slower case is libvorbis: it forces a frame size of 64 samples (`libvorbisenc.c` line 43, set at line 330), so a minute of audio crosses the command line's threads as 41,000 frames, and FFmpeg 9's thread queue, which differs from 7.1's (a `choked` state and an `AVContainerFifo` in `fftools/thread_queue.c`; a patched build did not isolate the cause), costs two futex calls per frame where 7.1 costs one (strace: 111,437 against 48,721 for 60 s; 42,437 against 13,035 context switches; CPUs used 0.82 against 1.10). The raw command shows the same 0.70 s against 0.39 s with no product code; a 1 s clip is faster (27 against 52 ms), 10 s is 132 against 117 ms and 60 s is 728 against 422 ms, so the cost is 5.3 ms for each second of audio. No option changed it (`-filter_threads 1`, `-threads 1`, `-thread_queue_size`, `-frame_size`, `asetnsamples`).
  - **The output is the same, or better defined.** The video stream of H.264, HEVC and VP9 outputs has identical packets on both (MD5 of the copied stream); of the 12 conversions compared, MP3 (60 s WAV), Ogg Vorbis and Opus outputs have identical packets, the FLAC of a WAV decodes to the same samples (the file is 0.05 percent larger), and an H.264 output of the HDR10 clip has identical packets. The AAC encoder of FFmpeg 9 is not bit-exact with 7.1: the file is 2.2 percent smaller for the music clip at 64 kbit/s and its SNR at the true alignment of 1024 samples is 14.07 dB against 13.54 dB (the decoders of both builds give identical samples for the same stream). On the 36 AAC rows of the audio benchmark the median SNR difference is 0.0 dB (7 rows better by more than 0.05 dB, 2 worse), the median bit rate difference -0.015 kbit/s, and the true-peak shift moves by up to -1.4 and +0.7 dB. The decoder now trims the padding at the end of an AAC stream: M4A to FLAC is 60.000000 s where 7.1 wrote 60.000363 s, and an AAC track of an MP4 converted to MP3 is 10.000 s where 7.1 wrote 10.005 s. A FLAC encoded from the 1024-sample frames of an AAC decode has smaller blocks (2584 frames against 575, 0.65 percent larger).
  - **Benchmark** (`ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity`, same VM). Audio on head: 420 rows measured, 419 at or above the reference tool, one row below it (`pteraxys-part1.flac->flac` throughput, ratio 0.913 [0.828 to 0.964], 0.921 in a second run; base 0.972 [0.961 to 0.980] over 50 pairs, "unstable at the cap", so the row also fails on base). Our side of that row went from 53 to 118 MB/s and the reference's from 55 to 133 MB/s, so the ratio fell because the spawned reference got cheaper to start, not because ours got slower. Against our own baseline file the gate names 7 rows on head and 2 on base. `sqam-51-speech-fr-f.flac->opus` true peak is on both; the other 6 of head are AAC rows (see above): the SNR of `music.wav->aac` reads 2.96 dB because the benchmark's lag estimator (`estimateLagSamples`, a dot product over a window) picks 351 samples for the new encoder's stream where the true lag is 1024 (ours and the reference both read 2.96), and five rows (loudness, true peak and bit rate of `edge-studio-96k-24bit.wav->aac`, and the true peak of the harpsichord and Baird tracks) move by the encoder change alone. The benchmark's estimator is left as it is in this change. Video on head: 298 rows evaluated, 296 at or above the reference, one failing (`clip.mp4->h264` throughput, 0.977 [0.959 to 0.990] over 36 pairs and 0.969 [0.951 to 0.984] in a speed-only run, the interval straddling the 0.97 line; base passed both runs), and the same 2 regressions against the baseline file as base (`aom-scenecomposition-1080p.y4m->hevc` PSNR and bit rate). 268 of the 286 video quality and size rows are identical to base and 18 differ by at most 0.02 percent (the VP9 bit rate). In the speed-only runs our side is faster on head in 11 of 12 video rows and in all 21 audio rows (FLAC 1.8 to 4.1 times), and so is the reference.
  - **Image size** (arm64, Debian 13, `apt-get -s` on the package list of the `runner` stage with and without `ffmpeg`, sizes from `Installed-Size`): 1497.3 MiB with the package, 1385.6 MiB with the 17 runtime libraries instead (-111.7 MiB, -41.7 MiB to download, 61 packages fewer), plus 25.7 MiB for `/opt/ffmpeg`: **-86.0 MiB**. The build takes 2 min 17 s to 2 min 24 s on four cores (8 min of CPU).
  - **Compatibility of the arguments.** The FFmpeg Changelog from 8.0 to 9.0.2 (`Changelog` of the archive, lines 180 to 266) removes CELT decoding, the old NVENC options and SDK versions before 11.1 (9.0), and the old HLS protocol handler (8.1; the HLS muxer the packaging uses stays); the options removed earlier (`-psnr`, `-map_channel`, 7.0) are not passed. Every option that the argument builders and probes pass (81 for ffmpeg, 8 for ffprobe) is listed by `ffmpeg -h full` and `ffprobe -h` of 9.0.2 (the check ran on 7.1.5 too: only `-i`, which neither lists, is missing on both). The ffprobe JSON of an H.264 and AAC MP4 differs from 7.1.5's by `mime_codec_string` (added) and `closed_captions`, `film_grain`, `refs` and `tags.vendor_id` (gone), none of which the code reads (`git grep` finds none in `src`). The `-preset p4` and `-cq` the NVENC path passes are the current API.
  - **Tests.** The 70 media, edge, HDR, oracle and packaging test files fail the same 16 tests on base and on head (an ImageMagick tool missing in the chroot, colour fixtures, a thumbnail SSIM of 0.9786 under a 0.98 floor, none of them FFmpeg 9's doing); before the helper changes head failed 16 more (OpenEXR pixel format and a half-float conversion that is 3e-6 off in `swscale` of 9.0, the MP4 timescale, the last MP3 packet, the Matroska start).
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **FFmpeg is ours to update.** The point releases come about monthly (9.0.1 on 2026-08-12, 9.0.2 on 2026-09-18) and carry security fixes; Debian's security team no longer covers the programs, only the codec libraries. The pin has to be bumped by hand (the script's header says how), and the sandbox of every FFmpeg run is what stands between a hostile file and the host in between.
  - **OGG output is 1.77 times slower** on a one-minute track (5.3 ms for each second of audio) until FFmpeg's thread queue costs less per frame. No other target of the 12 measured is slower.
  - **The AAC encoder changed**, so AAC files are not byte-for-byte what 7.1 wrote, and the benchmark's baseline file (measured on the CI runner's FFmpeg 6.1) names five AAC rows. The runner is not moved by this change.
  - **Hardware paths are compiled in and not run**: the VM has no GPU, so `h264_vaapi`, `hevc_vaapi`, `h264_nvenc` and `hevc_nvenc` are checked as present in the encoder list only; the code probes a session before it uses one, as before.
  - **amd64 is not measured here.** The CI run of the pull request builds that image. x86 assembly needs `nasm`, which the stage installs.
  - **The CI runner still tests with the distribution's FFmpeg (6.1.1).** Moving it needs this build in the CI setup and a new baseline.
  - **The AMR target is unchanged**: `libopencore_amrnb` was not in the Debian build either, the target answers 503 as before, and it needs `--enable-version3` with that library (Apache-2.0) if QA wants it.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A static build pinned by SHA-256.** johnvansickle.com offers release 7.0.2 and a git build of 2024-06-29 (2026-10-25), no 9.x. BtbN/FFmpeg-Builds publishes a rolling `ffmpeg-n9.0-latest` asset and dated autobuilds of which 38 remain on GitHub, built with its own set of libraries and with no signature to check; a digest of one of those pins a third party's build, not the maintainers' release.
  - **The Debian forky or sid package of 9.0.2**: it would mix the libraries of another release into trixie, and it brings the long list of libraries again.
  - **Codec libraries built from source as well** (x264, x265, libvpx, SVT-AV1, dav1d, Opus, LAME): seven more pins with a security watch each, in place of Debian's updates.
  - **Removing the refusal of a partial decode**: see above.
  - **LTO and `-march` levels** (x86-64-v2 and v3): the rule is that an optimisation goes in only when x64 and arm64 both show a gain, and x64 cannot be measured here. FFmpeg's assembly is chosen by the CPU at run time, so the flags would only touch the C paths.
  - **A patch to FFmpeg's thread queue for the OGG cost**: it is upstream's code; it belongs in a report to FFmpeg with the strace figures above.
- **Verified by**: `tests/worker-ffmpeg-packaging.test.ts` (the stage and its development packages; the runtime package of every linked library; no distribution `ffmpeg`; the copy, the links and the checks of the runner; the script's pin, hashing before unpacking, hardening checks, required encoders, decoders and filters, no nonfree and no network flags, the licence and source note), `tests/runtime-baseline.test.ts` and `tests/phase-4-security-and-sandbox-hardening.test.ts` (the stage list), `tests/media-undecodable-streams.test.ts` (the xHE-AAC clip to flac, wav, mp3, aac, ogg and opus: converted whole, within 0.1 s of its length and not silent, when a separate ffmpeg decodes it whole, refused with the codec named otherwise; 6 targets now, 4 before), and the media, edge, HDR and oracle test files named under Results, run with `FFMPEG_PATH` and `FFPROBE_PATH` on the build in the chroot. The helpers changed for FFmpeg 8 and 9 are `tests/helpers/ffmpeg-exr.ts`, `tests/helpers/ffmpeg-media-fixtures.ts` (`ffmpegMajorVersion`), `tests/edge-media-demux.test.ts`, `tests/edge-media-mux.test.ts`, `tests/hdr-fixture-builders.test.ts`, `tests/hdr-source-conversion.test.ts` and `tests/media-dropped-streams.test.ts`.
- **Revisit when**: FFmpeg releases 9.0.3 or a later point release (move the pin and run the media tests with the new build), Debian stable ships FFmpeg 9 or newer (then the stage can go), FFmpeg's thread queue stops costing two futex calls per frame (the OGG row), QA wants AMR (`--enable-version3` and libopencore-amrnb), the CI runner moves to this build (a new baseline file for AAC), or an amd64 measurement shows an optimisation level worth the extra flag.

## 106. Local multipart uploads: the session id must be one the store generated, the session belongs to its owner and keeps its own key, parts are bounded by the declared size and the S3 part limits, and the assembled file passes the spoof check

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #761, the first row of "External review of `abcdf793`"), decided 2026-10-25 (QA request). It applies the rules the object-store branch of `/api/v1/uploads` and the TUS path already follow to the local-disk branch.
- **Decision**:
  - **The upload id is checked where it reaches the disk.** `LocalFsStorage` takes only the exact form `createMultipart` generates, `up_<epoch ms>_<24 hex digits>`, in every method that takes one (part, complete, abort, presign, signature check, session read), and resolves the session directory and requires its parent to be the parts directory. Any other id is the S3 error `NoSuchUpload`, which the API answers with 404.
  - **The owner and the declared size are recorded in `session.json` at initiate**, next to the key the server chose. Part, complete and abort look the session up first and answer 404 `Upload session not found or has expired.` when the id is unknown or the session is another user's, as the object-store branch does with `getUploadSession` and `getUploadOwner`.
  - **The client's `key` is not used for a local upload.** Complete and abort act on the session's key; the client may leave `key` out. A client `expectedSize` other than the declared size is a 400, as in the object-store branch.
  - **Bounds, from the S3 multipart upload limits** (Amazon S3 User Guide, "Amazon S3 multipart upload limits": part numbers 1 to 10,000, at most 10,000 parts, a part at most 5 GiB): a part number outside 1 to 10,000 is a 400 in the route and in the store, a complete that lists more than 10,000 parts is a 400, and the bytes of one part are counted while they stream and stopped at the smaller of 5 GiB and what the declared size leaves after the other stored parts (10 GiB for a session that declared none, the route's existing initiate limit). A part over that is the S3 error `EntityTooLarge` (400) and its partial file is removed. The assembled object must be exactly the declared size. Parts that streamed at the same time were each bounded by what was left when they started, so a part, once renamed into place, counts the other stored parts again and is deleted with `EntityTooLarge` when the sum is over the declared size; and complete reads the size of every listed part and refuses, before it opens an assembled file, a list whose sizes do not add up to the declared size.
  - **The assembled file is checked before it is published.** `completeMultipart` runs `assertNotSpoofedFilePath` on the assembled temporary file against the format the session's filename or content type declares (`resolveDeclaredFormat`), as the TUS engine does on its last chunk; a mismatch deletes the file and is a 400, an unknown format the existing Unknown Format 400. The parts stay so the client can abort.
  - **The parts of the in-process store** (`PUT /api/v1/uploads/direct/part`, the store that backs `STORAGE_DRIVER=local` jobs) get the same bounds: the route passes `uploadPartStream` the smaller of 5 GiB and what the declared size leaves after the other stored parts (`multipartPartByteLimit`, the function the local-disk store uses), a part over it is a 413 and is not kept, and `POST /api/v1/uploads/direct/complete` checks the assembled size against the declared size for every store, not only for an object store.
  - **Temp files are the writer's own.** The assembled file and each part are written to a temp name with 6 random bytes after the timestamp, as `putStream` already named its files, and opened with `wx`, so two completes of one upload, or two uploads of one part, cannot write into the same file. The parts are copied into the assembled file with one `stream/promises` `pipeline`, so a write error such as `ENOSPC` or `EIO` rejects the complete and removes the temp file instead of leaving the request open.
  - **An operating-system error is not an answer.** `/api/v1/uploads` action errors that carry an errno code and syscall are no longer returned with their message, which names server paths: `ENOENT`, which is what a part or complete sees when an abort removed the session under it, is the 404 `Upload session not found or has expired.`, and any other is a 500 `Upload storage error` whose detail goes to the server log.
  - **A resumable upload id is checked where it becomes a path.** `TusEngine` takes only the exact form `createSession` generates, `tus_<epoch ms>_<16 hex digits>`: `getSession` answers null and `terminateSession` false for any other id, and `getPaths` throws `TusNotFoundError`, so an id such as `../x` finds no `.info` file outside the TUS directory and deletes none.
  - **The signed multipart route** (`/api/storage/multipart?action=presign`) signs an upload part URL only for the session's own key and answers any other key with 400 `Key does not belong to this multipart upload session.`, which the object-store backend already returned, and a part number that is not a whole number from 1 to 10,000 with a 400. Its sessions live in memory and are looked up by id, so the id never reaches a path there.
- **Why**: the route passed the client's `uploadId` straight into `path.join` under `.parts/`, so an authenticated abort with `uploadId=..` removed the whole storage root, a part with `..` wrote into it, any signed-in user could write, complete or abort another user's session, and a part had no size limit.
- **Trade-offs**:
