  - **Raising the 1,000 ms, 1.5 s or 60 MiB bounds**: it hides a run that is slow for another reason and still fails when the host is busier than the sample.
  - **Retrying a failed case**: the failure is the information, and a retry of a wall-clock comparison passes whenever the host is quieter than the first time.
  - **A work counter inside the MOBI reader**: the reader is production code and the issue is limited to tests; the same-size comparison needs none.
  - **The median of alternating runs for the block sort**: it read as wide as the best pass (0.446 to 0.490 against 0.44 to 0.50).
  - **Calling the collector in the child of the peak-memory case**: one conversion runs in the child and the collector cannot be called inside it; the heap bound is what the service does.
- **Verified by**: `tests/rocketbook-reader.test.ts` (a reader that inflates one stream before each refusal fails three cases; a splitter without the look-behind fails the white-space case), `tests/process-state.test.ts`, `tests/realworld-corpus.test.ts` (a pool that ignores a job's deadline fails), `tests/mobi-book-structure.test.ts` (a reader that scans to the end for each unclosed picture or MOBI tag fails two cases), `tests/palette-quantizer-quality.test.ts`, `tests/image-peak-memory.test.ts` and `tests/bzip2-bwt.perf.test.ts`, the first five of them 20 of 20 on the Linux test VM in strict mode beside 12 busy processes (the base rows are in the pull request).
- **Revisit when**: a runner measures the block sort above 0.6 in CPU time or the peak memory within 100 MiB of the bound, a plain case of a file here fails on a count it did not change, or the `tests` job sets `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` (then the case sets nothing of its own).

## 113. An `.xls` is the office suite's BIFF8 export of a typed XLSX workbook, XLSX cells keep their types, and a table that is not well formed or does not fit a sheet is refused

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #444, epic #760), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request: write real workbooks before launch instead of withdrawing the target).
- **Decision**:
  - **Every `.xls` output is a BIFF8 workbook in a Compound File, written by the office suite's `MS Excel 97` export** (`soffice --convert-to xls`, the filter the suite picks for the extension). Every source reaches the export as an XLSX workbook that was checked against the BIFF8 sheet (`convertXlsTarget`, `src/worker/office-suite-route.ts`): an XLSX or XLSM source is checked as it is and exported in one pass; ODS and Numbers are first written as XLSX by the suite itself, which holds what the suite loaded, and that workbook is checked and exported; a table the in-process engine reads (CSV, TSV, JSON, Parquet, Kingsoft workbooks) is written as an XLSX workbook by the engine (`writeTransientWorkbook`), checked and exported. A PDF is read as in 120. The workbook never goes to the output path of the request. With no office suite the answer is `EngineUnavailableError('soffice')` (503): the in-process engine has no BIFF8 writer, and the pairs are in `NATIVE_ENGINE_ONLY_PAIRS`.
  - **The SpreadsheetML 2003 writer (`generateXlsXmlFromData`) is deleted**, and with it the XML that was served under an `.xls` name. The reader of that XML (an `.xls` upload that is SpreadsheetML) stays. The branch that returned an `.xls` input unchanged for the `.xls` target is deleted too; the registry never offered the pair, and the engine now answers it as an unsupported target.
  - **Pages to `.xls` is withdrawn from the registry.** The `.pages` bytes were read as CSV text and the XML around that text was served as a workbook; the office suite has no export of a text document to a spreadsheet filter.
  - **XLSX cells are typed** (`src/lib/conversions/xlsx-writer.ts`, ECMA-376 Part 1, 18.3). A number is a number with no `t`, a boolean `t="b"`, text goes through `sharedStrings.xml` (`t="s"`, once for a repeated value), a date is a serial number under a date format. The shared-string layout follows xlsxwriter (BSD-2-Clause, `sharedstrings.py`): the `_xHHHH_` escape of control characters, `_x005F_` in front of a literal that reads like one, `xml:space="preserve"` around outer whitespace, `count` and `uniqueCount`. The package has `styles.xml` with one date format, and the sheet declares its `dimension`.
  - **A text field is a number only when its sheet shows the same text.** The pattern is `-?(0|[1-9]\d*)(\.\d*[1-9])?` with at most 15 significant digits (the digits a double keeps, `DBL_DIG`) and `String(Number(text)) === text`. A figure with zeros after its last digit (`20.00`, `5.50`, `0.0`) is the number it spells under a `0.00`-style format with as many decimals (custom ids from 165), when `toFixed` gives the text back and it has at most 15 decimals: a spreadsheet's CSV import stores such a field as a number (LibreOffice `ScColumn::ParseString`, `sc/source/core/data/column3.cxx` lines 2290 to 2313 at master 9f554658c082, sets a value cell for a plain decimal), and the format keeps the zeros on view, so SUM and pivots see every cell of a money column. `00004`, `007.50`, `+5`, `1e4`, `1,250`, a 16-digit identifier, `-0` and `-0.00` stay text. A field is a date only when it is an ISO calendar day (`YYYY-MM-DD`, a real day, 1900-03-01 to 9999-12-31, which avoids the days Excel numbers twice). JSON and Parquet keep the types they have: a finite number is written as the shortest text that reads back as the same double (`37.77490123456789`, `0.30000000000000004`, `1e-7`), a boolean a boolean, a string is text whatever it spells, `null` is an empty cell, an integer past the safe range and a nested value are text. A JSON array of objects takes its header from the keys of every record in the order they first appear (`fieldsInFirstSeenOrder`, the data engine's own table builder), and an item that is not an object is a `DataParseError` (400). Parquet goes to the data engine's reader for a spreadsheet target, never to the delimited reader.
  - **The date format is `yyyy\-mm\-dd` (custom id 164), not the built-in id 14.** Id 14 is the short date of the viewer's locale, so the same workbook reads `03/05/2024` in one office suite and `2024. 3. 5.` in another, and an export to CSV would not give back the field it came from.
  - **Delimited text that is not well formed is refused.** The sheet is read with `parseDelimitedRows` (`delimited-detect.ts`, the reader of the data engine): any quote error (an unterminated quote, a quote that closes inside a field) is a `DataParseError` (400) with the row. The fallback that split each line on the delimiter, and with it the one-cell sheet, is deleted, for the XLSX, ODS and XLS targets alike. `tab` sources are split on TAB, a BOM is dropped. JSON that does not parse was refused already (`parseJsonTableCells`).
  - **Nothing is cut to fit a sheet; the refusal is a 413** (`SheetLimitError`, a `PayloadLimitError`, so every route answers its `status`; `DataLimitExceededError` keeps its 400 for the YAML, XML, nesting and output caps). The bounds are in `src/lib/conversions/office/sheet-bounds.ts`: 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns for XLSX ("Excel specifications and limits"; LibreOffice `MAXROWCOUNT` and `MAXCOLCOUNT`, `sc/inc/address.hxx`), 65,536 rows and 256 columns for BIFF8 (the same page for Excel 97-2003; a `Rw` is 16 bits and a `Col` 8 bits in [MS-XLS]), 32,767 characters in a cell (the same page; xlsxwriter cuts at this length, here the table is refused). The XLSX bounds are checked on the last cell that holds something, so empty fields at the end of a row are no cells. The BIFF8 bounds are checked on the workbook before the export, because the export cuts without a word (measured with LibreOffice 24.2: a sheet of 70,001 rows came back with 65,536, and one of 300 columns with 256). `xls-limits.ts` streams every part an office suite may open as a worksheet, because the suite is what cuts the rows: the sheets the workbook lists (`discoverXlsxSheets`: the workbook is the part the root `_rels/.rels` names as the office document, else `xl/workbook.xml`; every `sheet` with a relationship id counts whatever its name, with none or an empty one, and whatever the prefix of its `id` attribute; its part is the relationship's target resolved against the workbook's directory with `resolveZipPath`, so `../xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` and `/xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` are found; a part is listed once), the parts under `xl/worksheets/`, and the parts that `[Content_Types].xml` types as a worksheet (measured with LibreOffice 26.8: a 65,537-row sheet reached through each of the first five shapes was exported cut to 65,536 rows). A tall part that nothing references is therefore refused too, a false 413 that no real producer causes and the safe side of a check that must not miss a sheet the suite opens. A workbook that lists a sheet whose part is not in the package is refused (400), never passed. The reader keeps its own rule for the name of a sheet (one without a name is skipped), and now reads a part that several sheets list once, at its first sheet, where it read the part again under each name; where it looks changes too. A package with no worksheet to check is refused with the reader's own message (400), as the reader refuses it, instead of passing the check. The count is of the cells that hold a value, a formula or an inline string, a `row` or `c` without `r` following the one before, as SheetJS does (xlsx 0.18.5, `parse_ws_xml_data`, xlsx.js lines 14851, 14854, 14880 to 14881 and 14924); the declared `dimension` is not read. The parts are charged to one decoded-byte budget for the workbook (`InflateBudget`, the 256 MiB the XLSX reader gives its sheets). A package that is not a ZIP, a part that does not inflate, a cell reference that is not A1 and a source file past the 256 MiB the check reads are refused, never passed on unchecked.
  - **The lists beside the cells of a worksheet are streamed into their final shape and bounded, never ended silently at the scanner's 50,000 and never held as element objects.** Sheets of a workbook: 10,000 (`MAXTABCOUNT`, LibreOffice `sc/inc/address.hxx` line 64, the most Calc opens), listed once each by part; the sheet past it is refused (413) at that element, so a package of millions costs the time of the bound. Merged ranges and hyperlinks together, over the whole workbook: 1,048,576, one for each row of a worksheet; neither Excel nor LibreOffice documents a bound for merged ranges, so it is taken from memory: a range is four numbers and took 66 bytes of heap (measured with Node 24, 1,048,576 in an array: 66 MiB), and a count per sheet alone would leave sheets times that. Past it the lists stop growing and the conversion goes on without the rest, which is deliberate: CSV, TSV and JSON do not use merges or links, and refusing them for lists they ignore would refuse a file that converts today. The elements counted are the ones the scan took, so the scan costs the time of the bound (3 million `mergeCell`s in a package of 177 KB: 2.0 s of CPU and 0.74 GB peak resident with the sheet read whole and checked for well-formedness, 1,048,576 kept). There is no bound per worksheet. 65,530 is what Excel lets an author add to a sheet, not what a file can hold: LibreOffice 26.8 writes 70,000 `hyperlink` elements and 70,000 relationships for a column of 70,000 URLs, and a per-sheet cap of 65,530 refused that file for every target, though most targets do not use links at all. A sheet's relationships part is read once, under the decoded-byte budget of the workbook (the 256 MiB its sheets share), and keeps only the ids that the sheet's links name, plus its drawings, so the map follows the number of links and not the size of the part. The relationship elements scanned over one read of a package are counted against an allowance of 2,097,152 (2^21: a relationship for each of the 1,048,576 links the workbook may hold, and as many again for the sheets, the drawings and the root), and the element past it is refused (413). A part is scanned in full whatever ids are asked for, and the cost is by element and not by byte, which the budget does not bound: measured, 2.1 million short `Relationship` elements cost 0.3 s of CPU, and 70 sheets of 30,001 of them in a 110 KB package are refused after the same scan as 280 sheets. `Override` elements of the content types: 100,000, the 10,000 sheets with room for the other parts. The sheet itself stays under the 256 MiB workbook budget, whatever the lists hold. The helpers that read relationships and stream elements are not specific to workbooks and live in `src/lib/conversions/office/opc-parts.ts`. The XML scanner ends a scan at an opening whose same-name nest is deeper than its bound (64 levels), where it went on to the next opening and walked the nest again: 4,000 openings of one tag took 3.8 s, 16,000 over a minute, and now cost one walk. Two other shapes cost a walk to the end of the input at every step and are linear now: one open tag with many self-closing children of its name (80,000 took 13.7 s, now 3.5 ms), and many openings after a stray closing tag of the same name (64,000 took 7.8 s, now 5.8 ms), because the search for the next opening and the next closing of a tag keeps its last answer and a miss, which hold for every later position of the scan (CPU time on this host, Node 24, `tests/safe-xml-scanner-depth.test.ts`; 36,000 random documents, well formed and not, return the same elements as the scanner before the change). Elements found before the nest are still returned; a nest this deep is not found in any real file, and the answer for one is none of its elements.
  - **The XLSX reader returns what the package says beyond the text of the cells.** `mergedRanges` (zero-based rows and columns), `hyperlinks` (the external URL of the relationship, or `#location` for a link inside the workbook), the 1904 date system (`workbookPr date1904`, serials count from 1904-01-01), and a rich-text string without its phonetic guides (`rPh` runs, in shared strings and in inline strings), as openpyxl's `Text.content` (cell/text.py lines 173 to 184) and SheetJS's `parse_si` (xlsx.js line 9470) read it; the string is rebuilt in one pass from the runs' positions, whatever their number. The reader keeps every shared string and every row: SheetJS (`parse_sst_xml`, lines 9482 to 9496) and openpyxl (`read_string_table`, reader/strings.py lines 10 to 24) read every item, so the string table is bounded by the 20 million cells the reader builds for a workbook (one more is a 413) and the rows by the 1,048,576 of a worksheet, where both stopped silently at 50,000 before (a 60,000-row table read back with 50,000 rows).
  - **Parquet to ODS, XLSX and XLS goes to the data engine's table**, not to the office engine. The office engine read the Parquet bytes as CSV text and wrote the lines as rows.
  - **The workbook the route writes is stored without deflate**, a parameter of the route's own writer call (`writeTransientWorkbook`), not a conversion option. The office suite reads it once and it is discarded, and deflating it took 18 of the 28 ms that the write takes for the 2,500-row table of the data family. A workbook that is a result is deflated as before.
  - **The benchmark's reader of cells counts a date cell equal to the ISO date it came from, and reads a number under a fixed-decimal format with its decimals.** `instant()` in `bench/reference-server.py` accepts a date as its midnight, as it already did for a timestamp ("a timestamp is a value, not a spelling"), and `sheet_cell_text` shows `20` under `0.00` as `20.00`, the text the sheet shows. Without it the data family's CSV to XLSX rows with a date column (503 and 2,922 cells) counted the typed dates as changed.
  - **The LibreOffice pool reports the registry MIME type** of the target it wrote (`getMimeType`) instead of its own table, which had no `.xls`.
- **Why**: a file called `.xls` that Excel opens with an extension-mismatch warning, and that many readers reject, is not an Excel 97-2003 workbook. The office suite is already in the worker image, runs in the sandbox with its limits, and writes the format the reference service writes. The issue's own approach (a Compound File writer and a BIFF8 record writer) would be a new parser-level risk for launch with nothing to gain over the export that every office suite accepts. Typed cells are what a formula, a sort and a pivot need; text cells made every number a string. The number rule keeps the text of a cell, which is what the quality oracle of the data family compares (`007` and `1e5` must not change). The limits are refused because a cut table is a smaller table that looks complete.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **`.xls` needs the office suite.** On a host without LibreOffice a request answers 503 where it used to answer 200 with XML under an `.xls` name. The worker image has it.
  - **A boolean is a formula cell in the BIFF8 file** (`FORMULA` with a cached boolean result, how the suite stores TRUE and FALSE), not a `BOOLERR` record. Excel shows TRUE and FALSE; the suite itself reads the cell back as 1 and 0.
  - **A date-looking field in a CSV becomes a date cell**, as in an office suite. An ISO timestamp (`2024-01-01T00:01:30Z`) stays text, because the reader of this engine writes the date part of a date-time format only.
  - **A cell of more than 32,767 characters, and a sheet past a bound, are now refused.** Before, they were written (and cut or reported as damaged by the application that opened them).
  - **ODS and Numbers to `.xls` take a second office-suite run** (the XLSX the check reads), which is the cost of not reimplementing the suite's import in process.
  - **Merged ranges and links past 1,048,576 in a workbook are left out without a word**, in every target that shows them. No producer writes that many (a worksheet has 1,048,576 rows), and a refusal would also stop the targets that ignore them.
  - **A nest of one tag deeper than 64 levels yields none of its elements** in the XML scanner every Office reader shares, where it yielded the innermost ones after a quadratic walk.
  - **A source file past 256 MiB is refused for `.xls`**, which a BIFF8 sheet of 16.7 million cells rarely needs.
  - **Typed cells change the bytes of the CSV to XLSX rows.** A figure with a trailing zero is now a number under a fixed format instead of a shared string: on the 4-core arm64 VM `data-weather.csv` writes 97,419 bytes (the reference 97,047, inside the allowance) and `class-mixed` 66,088 (the reference 68,174); the data family's 151 rows stay at or above the reference and its baseline reports no regression.
  - **DIF, SLK, DBF, WK1, WKS, FODS and PRN to CSV, XLSX and ODS still read their bytes as delimited text**: no reader of these formats exists in process and the office suite route does not take them; refusing them would withdraw 14 advertised pairs, so it is a separate backlog row.
  - **The `.xls` export costs about one office-suite start-up plus 15 ms**, which is what the reference's own CSV import saves. Measured on the 4-core arm64 VM against a cold `soffice --convert-to xls` per document, 21 interleaved pairs each: CSV of 3 rows 0.899 (range 0.84 to 0.94; 256 ms for the reference, 284 ms ours), CSV of 2,500 rows 0.926 (0.90 to 0.97; 322 and 350 ms), XLSX of 2,500 rows 0.993 (0.97 to 1.02; 342 and 345 ms). Of the 28 ms that the CSV route adds, about 14 are the office suite's read of an XLSX instead of a CSV (measured on the same workbook, stored or deflated), 12 the in-process write, and the rest the sandbox. The launch bar is 0.90 (entry 114).
  - **PDF to XLSX and XLS were refused** (`UnsupportedTargetError`) in this entry until the tables of PDF pages were extracted (#671); 120 replaces that refusal.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A Compound File writer and a BIFF8 record writer in process** (the issue's approach): a large specification, a new parser-level attack surface, and an output the suite and Excel must still be tested against, for a format that the suite writes already.
  - **SheetJS (Apache-2.0)**: it writes BIFF8 in process, but its npm copy is old and has published advisories, it adds a dependency for one format, and the office suite is the engine the reference service uses for this target.
  - **Keeping the XML writer under the `.xls` name with a warning**: the file is not the format the extension names.
  - **The built-in date format 14**: see the decision above; it depends on the locale of the viewer.
  - **Reading every numeric-looking text as a number** (`1.50` as 1.5, `007` as 7): it changes the text of cells, which the data family's oracle counts as a mismatch, and turns identifiers into numbers.
  - **Making every `DataLimitExceededError` a 413**: it would change the status of the YAML, XML and nesting caps with no reason tied to sheets.
  - **Trusting the `dimension` of a worksheet**: it may be missing or stale, and both reach the export's silent cut.
- **Verified by**: `tests/xlsx-typed-cells.test.ts` (numbers, booleans and shared strings in the sheet XML; the strings that stay text; ISO dates as serials under the date format; the escapes; JSON types; unterminated and misplaced quotes as 400; 1,048,577 rows, 16,385 columns and a 32,768-character cell as 413; a LibreOffice read-back of every cell to CSV and of the cell kinds to ODS), `tests/xls-real-binary-output.test.ts` (the Compound File signature and `file` for CSV, TSV, JSON, XLSX, ODS, Kingsoft, Parquet and PDF sources; a test-side record walker, `tests/helpers/biff8-records.ts`, that finds RK, MULRK or NUMBER records for numbers, `LABELSST` for text and a cached boolean for TRUE and FALSE; a LibreOffice read-back to the source values, a cell with a comma, a quote and a line break through xls to csv to xlsx; the pair xls to xls refused; 65,537 rows and 257 columns as 413), `tests/xlsx-reader-merges-dates-links.test.ts` (merged ranges, hyperlinks and the 1904 date system on workbooks LibreOffice wrote from flat OpenDocument text; the 1904 flag and the phonetic runs on workbooks written by hand), `tests/office-suite-route.test.ts` (the workbook route with stand-ins for the suite: the request's options, the output path, the clean-up, the missing suite, a table that cannot be read, a workbook past the BIFF8 bounds, an orphan sheet part refused, a package with no worksheet refused with the reader's message, the export filter kept off the interchange file), `tests/xls-limits-sheet-discovery.test.ts` (a 65,537-row sheet reached through a `../` target, an absolute target, a sheet with no name, one with an empty name, another prefix for the relationship id and a root relationship that names another workbook, each refused as 413 and each passing when short; a listed sheet whose part is missing refused), `tests/xlsx-element-bounds.test.ts` (3 million `mergeCell`s in a package under 1 MB cut at the bound within the CPU guard with the sheet still read and still converting to CSV, merged ranges counted for the whole workbook, links past the workbook allowance left out; a sheet of 70,000 hyperlinks and 70,000 relationships in the shape LibreOffice writes (checked once against a workbook LibreOffice 26.8 saved; the CI test builds it by hand, because the office-suite export takes over two minutes on the runner), read and converted to CSV, TSV and JSON; a relationships part of 150,000 entries read for the one id a link names; a part that no link names not read; 70 sheets of relationships past the allowance refused as 413 at the same CPU as 280 sheets; three parts of 100 MiB refused by the workbook budget; one sheet listed 100,000 times refused for the reader and for the check, 10,000 sheets accepted), `tests/safe-xml-scanner-depth.test.ts` (repeated unclosed and nested openings, self-closing children of one open tag, and openings after a stray closing tag, each linear in CPU time in their number; the elements before a too-deep nest still returned), `tests/registry-engine-conformance.test.ts` (the seven sources that write `.xls` through the office suite, csv, tsv, json, parquet, ods, xlsx and xlsm, are native-engine pairs: each answers a missing engine with the typed 503 and converts with LibreOffice to a Compound File that holds a `Workbook` stream; the ratchet of undecidable pairs stays as it was), and the touched tests on Ubuntu 24.04 with LibreOffice 24.2 under `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1`. `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity --family data --quality-only`: 151 rows, 0 regressed, parity PASS; the speed rows of the family against the base (`--speed-only --base-root`): CSV to XLSX 1.175 head against base (18 pairs), XLSX to CSV 0.983 (24 pairs, upper bound 1.021).
- **Revisit when**: QA wants BIFF8 written without the office suite (then the writer is taken from a maintained library whose output the suite and Excel read, or written from [MS-XLS] and tested against both), the worker image drops the office suite, the speed of the export row is measured below the launch bar, or Excel files with dates before 1900-03-01 or ISO timestamps need to become date cells (then the reader writes the time part of a date-time format too).

## 114. The launch pass line of a speed row is 0.90 of the reference

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #444, PR #906), decided 2026-10-30 (QA decision: launch first, then improve speed over time).
- **Decision**:
  - **A speed row passes against the reference when the lower bound of its speed-ratio interval is at least 0.90** (`SPEED_PARITY_TOLERANCE` = 0.10 in `bench/speed-config.ts`; the stub decision of `bench/ab-child-core.ts` takes the same line). It was 0.97.
  - **Unchanged**: the per-PR check that a change is no slower than its base (the A/B gate and its thresholds in `bench/ab-config.ts`), the output-correctness and quality gates, and the low-level optimisation work on the rows below the reference.
  - The gate takes `bench/speed-config.ts` from the base commit (`scripts/ci-parity-base-gate.mjs`), so the line holds for the pull requests opened after this one is merged, not for this one.
- **Why**: the launch is held by rows between 0.90 and 0.97 of the reference that need engine work of weeks (the office-suite start-up of the `.xls` export is one: 0.899 to 0.926 of the reference's own CSV import). A user does not notice a tenth of the time of a conversion; a missing or wrong output is what keeps a user away. The A/B gate still stops a change that makes a row slower than its base, so the line cannot drift down release by release.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Rows between 0.90 and 0.97 pass without a gap entry**, so they leave `bench/parity-gaps.json` and its history. Their numbers stay in every nightly report.
  - **The nightly reads fewer failures**, which hides the rows that sit just above the new line; the report still prints each ratio.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keeping 0.97 and listing every row below it as a tracked gap**: it is the same release with more entries to maintain, and a gap entry pins a row's history rather than its target.
  - **A lower line per family**: no family's users wait differently enough to justify separate lines at launch.
- **Verified by**: `tests/bench-speed-parity.test.ts` (the constant and the decisions at the new line), `tests/bench-parity.test.ts` (a row that lost parity, a tracked row and an acknowledged slowdown judged against 0.90), `tests/bench-speed-gate-rate.test.ts` (the absolute gate fails a row just above the line on a share of the runs while the A/B gate does not), and the whole `tests/bench-*.test.ts` set.
- **Revisit when**: the product has launched; then raise the line back toward 0.97 family by family, starting with the families whose rows already sit above it.
## 115. WebAssembly calls into JavaScript imports stay on V8's generic wrapper while the runtime's V8 frees a cached wrapper twice

- **Status**: Implemented (launch blocker row of issue #783), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request: fix the native crash of the real-world run of 2026-10-27).
- **Decision**:
  - Every process that converts files sets the V8 flag `--wasm-wrapper-tiering-budget=2147483647` before any WebAssembly instance exists. `src/lib/conversions/wasm-import-wrappers.ts` sets it with `v8.setFlagsFromString`, and it is the first import of `src/lib/conversions/index.ts`, which every caller that converts loads (the web routes and the queue worker through the dispatcher, and the benchmark harness and `src/worker/engines.ts` directly), and of `src/lib/conversions/dispatch.ts`. The flag is process-wide, so the PDF text threads, the OCR threads and the main thread all keep it.
  - V8 then never tiers a call into a JavaScript import up from its generic wrapper to a compiled one, so no wrapper is added to the cache that V8 shares between the threads of a process by tier-up. An import that is not a plain JavaScript function is still compiled when the instance is made, as before.
  - The module is removed when the runtime's V8 contains V8 commit 9b8ca54d5a ("[wasm] Fix lookup of wrappers marked is_dying", first released in V8 13.7.152.1; Node.js 25 ships V8 14.1 with it).
- **Why**:
  - The real-world job server for `govdocs1-001157.pdf` died with SIGSEGV on 2026-10-27 (run 40472895855, shard 5). That killed every job in flight in the process, and in the worker it would do the same to every job on that worker.
  - Core dumps from x64 runners that replay the first 335 jobs of shard 5 show the frame. Four crashes in 103 replays without the change all hit `govdocs1-001157.pdf` (three `pdf -> html`, one `pdf -> docx`), two with SIGSEGV and two with SIGTRAP. All four are in the same V8 path, on a worker thread of the job server: `Runtime_TierUpWasmToJSWrapper`, `~WasmCodeRefScope`, `WasmEngine::FreeDeadCode`, then either `WasmImportWrapperCache::Free` and a failed check in `ThreadIsolation::UnregisterWasmAllocation` (SIGTRAP), or `NativeModule::FreeCode` on a freed module (SIGSEGV).
  - Node.js 24.21 and 24.22 bundle V8 13.6.233.17. Its `WasmImportWrapperCache::MaybeGet` adds a cached wrapper to the caller's code scope before it checks that the wrapper is dying. A wrapper that wasm code GC is freeing is then freed again when the tier-up's scope ends. The upstream commit names this case and moves the check before the reference.
  - The thread logs of the crashing job servers show the condition: tesseract.js threads (OCR jobs earlier in the shard) tiered up imports of the same signature and were then terminated, and the file's own WebAssembly calls (pdf.js runs `jbig2.wasm` for its CCITT images when the job writes pictures) tiered up an import on another thread. A stress of pdf.js alone (13,000 jobs on four threads, with and without thread churn) and a synthetic module churned on terminated threads did not crash.
  - With the budget out of reach, `Runtime_TierUpWasmToJSWrapper` is never called, so the tier-up scope that frees the wrapper a second time never runs.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - A call from WebAssembly into a JavaScript import costs about 14 ns instead of about 3 ns (5 million calls: 69.7 ms against 13.7 ms, arm64). The conversions that make such calls do not show it: `govdocs1-001157.pdf -> html` took a median of 184.1 ms against 184.5 ms and a tesseract.js hOCR page 192.1 ms against 191.0 ms (Linux VM, five alternating runs per side, medians of 15 and 7 conversions per run).
  - V8 reads the same budget when it makes the data of a JavaScript-to-WebAssembly export, so the flag also keeps a call from JavaScript into an export that the engine does not inline on the generic wrapper (about 14.5 ns instead of about 5.3 ns a call, from reading V8 13.6 `wasm-objects.cc` and a micro-benchmark). The exports of this repository (xxh64, the resampler rows, HarfBuzz, tesseract.js) do work per call, so this is expected to be negligible; no speed row measures it.
  - `v8.setFlagsFromString` after start-up is documented as unsafe in general. This flag is read when an instance is made, and the module is the first import of the conversion index and of the dispatcher. A module that instantiates WebAssembly without loading either would not have it.
  - The fix is in the configuration of the runtime, not in the runtime. Another V8 fault in one thread still ends the whole process.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Node.js 25**, whose V8 has the fix: it is not a long-term support line, and moving the worker image and CI to it is a change of its own.
  - **Running the PDF text extraction in child processes**, so that a native fault fails one job: it moves a thread pool with warm-up, recycling, deadlines and memory limits into a process pool, and the OCR threads and the main thread would still share the cache.
  - **`--no-wasm-code-gc` or a stress of wasm code GC**: the stress (`--stress-wasm-code-gc`, 10 replays and 30 stress runs) did not raise the crash rate, and turning code GC off keeps dead code of every terminated thread's modules.
  - **The pdf.js decoders' JavaScript builds instead of WebAssembly**: they have no memory maximum (entry 101), and OCR would still tier up its imports.
- **Verified by**: `tests/wasm-import-wrappers.test.ts` runs a probe in a child process with `--trace-wasm-compilation-times`. The probe makes a WebAssembly instance whose import is called 20,000 times. With the module loaded, the trace has no `WasmToJS wrapper` line. Without it, the same probe prints one, so a change of V8's message fails the test instead of passing it. The replay of the first 335 jobs of shard 5 on four x64 runners: 4 crashes in 103 replays before the change and 0 crashes and no core in 43 replays after (at the rate before, 43 clean replays happen by chance about 18% of the time, so the replays support the change and the trace test is the proof that the faulting path is gone). `govdocs1-001157.pdf -> html` ran 100 times in one process on the Linux VM with 100 outputs passing the real-world output check, one size (553,252 bytes) and no core.
- **Revisit when**: the worker image or CI moves to a Node.js whose V8 contains commit 9b8ca54d5a (then the module and its test are deleted), or a WebAssembly path is found whose speed depends on calls into JavaScript.

## 116. The native xz runs on uploaded bytes only inside the process sandbox, on one thread, with address space, CPU time and the job's time and signal

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #714, launch blocker), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request).
- **Decision**:
  - `compressXz` and `decompressXz` in `src/lib/conversions/archive.ts` start the native `xz` through `executeSandboxedBinary`: network and user namespaces, a sanitized environment, no shell, and the `prlimit` limits below. Both are asynchronous. The synchronous `execFileSync` path is deleted, and `compressXzAsync` is folded into `compressXz` (its two callers in `convertArchive` call `compressXz`). The native run (one helper, `runNativeXz`), the binary lookup and the typed refusals live in `src/lib/conversions/xz-native.ts`.
  - One thread: every native run passes `-T1`. From xz 5.6 the default is all cores (xz(1): "In xz 5.4.x and older the default is 1"), and the runner stage of `Dockerfile.worker` (`node:24.20.0-trixie-slim`, Debian 13) installs `xz-utils` by name, version 5.8.1-1+deb13u2 (packages.debian.org/trixie/xz-utils). The base image does not provide it: the Node image installs `xz-utils` only to unpack Node and then purges it. Without the package the lookup returns null and every `.xz` file would be read by the in-process reader on the event loop and written by the pure encoder, with none of the limits below. `scripts/verify-worker-container.sh` (check 9; qpdf-runner stays check 8) fails when `xz` is missing, round-trips 4096 bytes through `xz -T1` and `xz -d -T1` inside the `unshare` and `prlimit` wrapper, compresses at `-9` under `--as=1073741824` and decodes under `--as=536870912` with `--memlimit-decompress=256MiB`, and the container job of CI runs it. `xz -9 -vv` of 5.8.4 on a 12-core host reports 14,990 MiB required with the default threads against 674 MiB with `-T1` (xz then lowers its own thread count to fit its 6,144 MiB limit), writes another stream (20,001,064 against 20,001,056 bytes for 20 MB of random data), and `RLIMIT_CPU` adds the CPU time of every thread. The address-space caps below were measured on a single-threaded 5.4.5, so they hold only with `-T1`.
  - Limits of a run. Address space is 1 GiB to compress (`xz -9 -T1` needs 674 MiB by the xz(1) memory table; measured with `prlimit --as`, level 9 fails at 500 MiB and passes at 700 MiB) and 512 MiB to decode (the 256 MiB `--memlimit-decompress` the reader already used, plus 256 MiB for the C library, the stack and the buffers). CPU time is the stage limit in seconds. The output is a pipe, so no file size limit applies and `maxBuffer`, the 500 MB output cap, is its limit. The stage limit is `stageTimeoutMs(options, CPU_POOL_TASK_TIMEOUT_MS)`: 10 minutes, held to the time the job has left. The job's `AbortSignal` is passed to the run, and an abort is rethrown as it is.
  - A run that outruns the stage limit is a `CpuTaskTimeoutError` (422), the type `dispatch.ts` and `cad-dwg.ts` give other tools, for compression and for decoding alike. Neither falls back to the in-process engine after it. Before, the call had no time limit, and a compression that timed out was written again by the pure encoder.
  - With `STRICT_SANDBOX=true` and no namespace sandbox, both calls throw `SandboxUnavailableError` before any spawn (503, retried on another worker) and `convertArchive` lets it through. Before, `compressXzAsync` ignored the refusal and wrote the stream with the in-process encoder.
  - A stream the native decoder ran on and refused is refused, not decoded again by the in-process reader on the event loop. Output past the byte cap and a decoder past its memory limit (exit 1 with "Memory usage limit reached" or "Cannot allocate memory", or a kill under the address-space cap) are a 413 (`DecompressionLimitError`). Any other exit 1 whose first stderr line xz itself wrote is a `CorruptStreamError` (400), "Unsupported options" included: the pinned image ships xz 5.8.1, which knows every filter the reader knows, and a stream it rejects that way (a block after the first with a dictionary byte above 40) would otherwise make the reader decode the blocks before it on the event loop. The trade-off: on a host whose xz predates a filter the file uses, `Unsupported options` is a 400 where the reader would have decoded the file, and a filter the reader does not know changes from a 422 to a 400. An exit 1 or 2 where any line xz itself wrote reports an unsupported integrity check (xz prints that warning at the stream header, before a later error in a damaged stream) (`xz: (stdin): Unsupported type of integrity check; not verifying file integrity`) is an `UnsupportedArchiveMethodError` (422), the answer the reader gives for a reserved check type: an upload chooses the check, and the reader would first decode every stream before the bad one on the event loop. The decode runs without `-q` for this reason: `-q` hides warnings, so with it the same stream exits 2 with an empty stderr and cannot be told from any other exit 2. A death by a crash signal (SIGABRT, SIGBUS, SIGILL, SIGFPE) is a `CorruptStreamError` that names the signal and is not decoded again. Any other signal says nothing about the stream and falls back. There is no SIGXCPU branch: `prlimit --cpu=N` sets the soft and the hard limit to the same value, so the kernel sends SIGKILL, and the wall timer of the run fires first. Only stderr that xz wrote is classified: xz starts its diagnostics with the name it was started under and a colon (`/usr/bin/xz: (stdin): Compressed data is corrupt`, or `xz: ...` where the C library keeps the base name), so the first line must start with the binary's path or base name and a colon. The client message is that first line without the program name and the `(stdin): ` that names the input. A failure of the `unshare` or `prlimit` wrapper (`unshare: unshare failed: No space left on device`, `prlimit: failed to set the AS resource limit: Cannot allocate memory`) says nothing about the stream, so it is not classified, and the stream is decoded by the in-process reader as before the wrappers could fail. The in-process reader decodes only when the binary is missing or cannot judge the stream: any other exit 2, a signal that is not a crash, a wrapper's failure, and a process that could not start. A compression whose native run fails for another reason (for example the 1 GiB cap) still falls back to the pure encoder, which writes a stream of its own and never a placeholder.
  - The binary is located with `resolveBinaryPath` like the other tools: `XZ_PATH`, then `/usr/bin`, `/usr/local/bin` and `/opt/homebrew/bin`, then the directories of `PATH`. The `which` child process and the cache of the answer are gone.
- **Why**:
  - A crafted `.xz` reached a native parser with the privileges and the network of the worker and with no memory or time limit. Every other native parser of the archive path already runs in the sandbox (7-Zip, `unrar`, `zip`, `lbzip2`).
  - The synchronous call also held the event loop for the whole decode, and its callers could not pass the job's signal or deadline.
  - Without `-T1` the measured caps would have failed on the shipped image: level 9 would exceed 1 GiB of address space and every normal compression would have come from the slower pure encoder.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - The library functions `compressXz` and `decompressXz` return promises. The only caller in `src` of the decoder was already asynchronous, and the encoder had no caller in `src`.
  - A start through the sandbox costs the `unshare` and `prlimit` execs: a 256 KiB decode took a median of 5.98 ms against 5.63 ms (+6%, 0.35 ms), and a 16 MiB decode 150.8 ms against 149.4 ms (+1.0%). Compression was already sandboxed and is unchanged (41.8 ms against 41.8 ms, 4,539 ms against 4,532 ms).
  - `-T1` gives up the speed of a threaded compression on a worker with several cores. It writes the stream that xz 5.4 and older write by default, the one the oracle test of the compression level compares against.
  - A stream whose dictionary needs more than the 256 MiB decoder limit (only `--lzma2=dict=` above the 64 MiB of the presets can ask for it) is a 413 where the in-process reader used to decode it. The 256 MiB limit and the 512 MiB address space are the ones of the native run, not new ones.
  - `-T1` gives up the parallel decoding of a stream with several blocks. On a 12-core host with xz 5.8.4, a 229 MiB stream of 10 blocks decodes in 6.15 s with `-T1` against 0.75 s with the default threads. The pin is what keeps the 512 MiB address-space cap valid: the threaded decoder allocates a dictionary per thread.
  - The remaining gap: every stream is decoded by the in-process reader on the event loop with no deadline when the wrapper fails after the capability probe passed or the binary is missing, and so is a stream with an exit 2 that is not an unsupported check (an upload has no other way to choose an exit 2). A wrapper failure or a missing binary needs a failure of the host and not of the upload.
  - The open-file limit that the issue lists is not applied: the process runner has no `nofile` option, and the worker containers set it for the whole process (`docker-compose.yml`).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **`resolveSandboxedCommand` with `execFileSync`**, the pattern of the 7-Zip tar steps: it confines the child but keeps the call synchronous, so it holds the event loop for the whole run and cannot take the job's signal.
  - **Dropping the native `xz` for the in-process codec**: the native encoder is the reference for size and speed on the compression family, and the decoder is faster on large streams.
  - **Leaving the thread count to the tool and raising the cap**: a threaded level 9 needs gigabytes, so any cap that admits it admits a crafted job the same memory.
  - **Falling back to the in-process reader after every native refusal**: it decodes on the event loop with no deadline, so a stream the native tool refused after a long decode cost the loop the same time again.
- **Verified by**: `tests/archive-xz-sandbox.test.ts`. A spy binary at `XZ_PATH` records its argv, network namespace, `ulimit -v`, `ulimit -t` and environment: under `STRICT_SANDBOX` both calls pass `-T1`, run in another network namespace than the test, with address space at most 1 GiB, a CPU limit and none of the test's variables. With the sandbox unavailable both calls reject with `SandboxUnavailableError` and the spy log is empty. A job deadline of 300 ms stops a decode and a compression that would take 30 s with a `CpuTaskTimeoutError`, and a signal fired during a compression rejects with its reason. Spies that write like the wrappers (`unshare: unshare failed: No space left on device`, `prlimit: failed to set the AS resource limit: Cannot allocate memory`, both with exit 1) leave the stream to the in-process reader (counter 1, the bytes decoded); a spy that writes `xz: (stdin): Compressed data is corrupt` and a second line, as its base name and as its path, gives a 400 with the first line only (counter 0); a spy that kills itself with SIGABRT gives a 400 that names the signal (counter 0) and one with SIGTERM leaves the stream to the reader (counter 1). With the installed `xz`, a small stream whose dictionary byte is patched to 512 MiB (header CRC refreshed) is a 413, a truncated stream a 400, a two-block stream whose second block has dictionary byte 41 is a 400 ("Unsupported options"), and none calls the in-process reader (a counter on its entry point; with the binary missing the same counter shows one call); a reserved check type exits 2 and is a 422 from the native run (counter 0), also when a valid stream with 8 MiB of output comes first. One Linux test runs the installed `xz` under the real namespaces and `prlimit` at level 9: the output equals the bytes of `xz -T1 -9` and decodes natively with no call of the in-process reader. The real stderr was read on the Linux VM: `/usr/bin/xz: (stdin): File format not recognized` (the name it was started under), and `unshare: write failed /proc/self/uid_map: Operation not permitted` from the wrapper as a user without namespaces. With the stderr check removed, the two wrapper tests fail on the host. `tests/archive-xz-sandbox.test.ts` and `tests/archive-xz-hardening.test.ts` pass on the Linux VM as root at the round 3 head (52 of 52, xz 5.4.5; a 5.8 build was not installed there, so `-T1` is checked by the argv and by the 5.8.4 memory figures above), and with `tests/archive-library-compression-level.test.ts` and `tests/phase-6-zstd-and-archive-parity.test.ts` on the macOS host (xz 5.8.4). Speed: `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity --speed-only --family compression --base-root` on the Linux VM as root (the sandbox is active; xz 5.4.5; the cases limited to the xz ones; 24 to 36 interleaved pairs per row) passed with head against base 1.0056 on `mixed.xz->tar` (upper bound 1.0395; the base is below the reference there as well, at 0.947), 0.986 on `silesia-xml.xz->tar` (a tracked gap, issue #685) and 1.0029 on `silesia-ooffice.xz->tar` (upper bound 1.0293). The encoder has no row (the registry offers no xz output target), and `-T1` is the default of the VM's xz, so it cannot show on that host.
- **Revisit when**: the process runner gains a `nofile` limit (then add it here), the native decoder stops being faster than the in-process reader on large streams, the in-process reader gains a deadline (then exit 2 and the wrapper failures can be answered by it without a bound on the loop), or a measurement of `-T0` with `--memlimit-mt-decompress` on a 5.8 host shows that the decoder can keep the 512 MiB address-space cap while using the cores (then the multi-block decode cost of `-T1` can go).

## 117. Archive entry names are refused, never repaired, in tar, 7z and RAR, and a compressed tar converted on disk yields the members of the tar inside it

- **Status**: Implemented (launch blockers #674 and #712, area: archives), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request). The refusal is a behaviour change that QA aligned: two tests that pinned the rewrite of unsafe names were replaced by tests that pin the refusal.
- **Decision**:
  - **An entry name that is not a plain relative path refuses the archive.** The tar, 7z and RAR readers of the in-process engine call `assertSafeArchiveEntryName` (`src/lib/conversions/archive-extraction-safety.ts`) on every stored name, as the ZIP reader has since it was rewritten to read the central directory (#711). Refused: an empty name, a control character (C0, DEL, C1, U+2028 and U+2029, the set a message writes out), an absolute path, a drive path (a letter and a colon that end the first component, `C:/x`, `C:\\x` or a bare `C:`, tested on the stored name and again on the canonical form, so `./C:/x`, `.\\C:\\x` and `.//C:/x` are refused too), a backslash-rooted path, a `..` component with either separator, a name nested deeper than 256 levels, and a name that becomes a traversal after Unicode compatibility folding (fullwidth full stops and solidus). The folding is applied only to the traversal checks, not to the drive test, so `Ｑ：回答.txt` and `a:b.txt`, which no operating system reads as a drive, are ordinary names in tar, 7z, RAR and ZIP. The invariant is that a name a desktop OS can store and that neither escapes the root nor names a Windows drive converts unchanged. The answer is an `UnsafeArchiveError` (HTTP 400) whose message quotes the entry as it is stored, cut to 200 characters and with control characters written out.
  - **The function that gives an entry's canonical spelling no longer repairs, and is named for what it does.** `validateEntryPath` (`src/lib/conversions/archive-entry-path.ts`) is the one function that validates a stored name and returns its canonical spelling or its `UnsafeArchiveError`; the tar reader, ZIP repair and the two wrappers below use it. `canonicalEntryPath` (before, `sanitizeArchivePath`) throws the same error for such a name and, for a safe one, only gives its canonical spelling (backslashes as separators, empty and `.` components dropped, so `./a` stays `a` as before). It returns null for the root (`.`, `./`). It is for the readers of an archive. The encrypted ZIP and 7z writer names an upload by its canonical spelling, or by its leaf when the name is not a plain relative path (`../x.png` is stored as `x.png`, `..\\..\\evil.txt` as that literal leaf on a POSIX host, as the unencrypted writers store it); an upload named `Ｑ：回答.txt` or `a:b.txt` converts as before. A name that cannot be written as a file (empty, NUL or another control character, `..`) is refused with an `UnsafeArchiveError` (HTTP 400), not an untyped error. The native 7z staging does not repair at all: when a name would be rewritten it returns null and the pure writer, which stores names as given, builds the archive.
  - **ZIP repair skips a record with a garbled name.** A local record whose name is empty or holds a control character is left out of the salvage like any other unreadable record, so the good entries of a damaged file are still recovered. The repair returns only the archive, so the skipped record is dropped without a report, as any unreadable record is; a record that climbs out of the directory or is absolute still refuses the repair.
  - **A stored RAR 4 name with the Unicode flag is decoded before it is checked.** The name field holds the OEM name, a NUL and the encoded Unicode name; `decodeRar4FileName` (`src/lib/conversions/archive-rar4-name.ts`) decodes it as libarchive does (`read_header` in `archive_read_support_format_rar.c`, the `FHD_UNICODE` branch; BSD-2-Clause), writing at most one unit per byte of the field and stopping at the end of the data. The production image has no `unrar`, so this reader serves RAR archives with CJK names. A decoded name that holds a NUL is refused by the name check.
  - **Inspection and conversion agree.** `summarizeInspectionSafety` takes `archiveEntryNameError` as its verdict, so a name that conversion refuses (fullwidth lookalikes included) is reported unextractable in tar and 7z. The tar reader's report mode returns an unsafe name as stored and neither resolves nor tracks its links, so a symlink followed by a traversing name is reported, not thrown. A 7z entry that is a skipped link or a special entry is classified before its name is checked, as before the refusal.
  - **The disk route applies the selection of entries to a plain compressed file** (to the member name; a selection that leaves nothing is the existing "no files" error) and decides by the single file the wrapper unpacked to; any other shape is refused.
  - **The listing policy of the native route folds names too.** `assertSafeArchiveListing` calls `assertSafeArchiveEntryName`, so a lookalike name is refused whichever route reads the archive. Plain ASCII is its own folding and is checked once.
  - **RAR with `unrar`**: the stored names are listed with `unrar lb` before `unrar x` runs, because `unrar` writes an entry that climbs out of its directory below the directory, and the extracted tree then shows nothing. The listing is bounded by the entry cap. The stored-RAR reader in process reads the names itself and takes the same check.
  - **tar inspection** reports an unsafe name as it is stored and marks the archive unextractable, as the 7z and ZIP inspections do; before, the tar reader rewrote the name and the report said the archive was extractable.
  - **A compressed tar converted to another archive on disk is unpacked to its members.** The pipeline that extracts to a directory (a zero-heap request, an output past the in-memory budget, a selection of entries) took the file a compression wrapper unpacks to for the payload and packed it as one member named `input`. It now decides what the file is with the test the streamed route applies to its bytes (`classifyUnpacked` on the first 512 bytes, `src/worker/archive-source-extraction.ts`). A tar is extracted as the archive it is, through the listing, vetting, extraction and re-verification of every tar source, with the request's `skipLinks`, `collisionPolicy` and selection of entries (the selection names members of the tar). Any other file is the one member, named after the source without its last extension (`memberNameFor`), as the streamed and the in-process route name it.
- **Why**:
  - **libarchive refuses these names when it extracts.** `ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NODOTDOT` refuses a path with a `..` component and `ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NOABSOLUTEPATHS` refuses an absolute path (`libarchive/archive_write_disk_posix.c`). GNU tar removes the leading `/` and skips `..` entries with a message. Both leave the caller to see that the archive was hostile; the old rewrite (`a/../b` to `a/b`, `/etc/x` to `etc/x`, `C:\x` to `x`, `../evil` to `evil`) changed where a file landed and hid the archive from the caller.
  - **The refusal is the verdict the other routes already gave.** The native route and the ZIP reader refused these names, so the same archive was converted or refused by the route that happened to serve it. The fuzz of 400,000 generated names (an alphabet of separators, dots, a colon, NUL, a line break, fullwidth lookalikes, and names past the depth cap) gave the same verdict, the same reason, before and after the rewrite of the checks.
  - **The tar inside a wrapper was repackaged as one file.** `tar -tvf` of a `.tar.xz` converted to `.tar` on the disk route listed one member holding the inner tar, where the streamed route listed the inner members. A zero-heap request or a large archive, the requests that most need the disk route, got the wrong shape.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **An archive that held an unsafe name used to convert and is now refused.** The old output had no such file; the caller now learns why. A name that is legal on Linux and unsafe elsewhere (a drive path, a name with a control character, a `..` component spelled with a backslash) is refused with the same message the native route gives; `a:b` is not a drive and converts.
  - **The disk route holds the tar and its members at once.** The payload is removed once the members are extracted, so the peak is the payload plus the members, each within the size and ratio caps (the ratio against the upload). Before, only the payload was on disk and the members were never made.
  - **One more 7-Zip extraction** for a compressed tar on the disk route (the tar itself), and one `unrar lb` process for a RAR read in process with `unrar`. Measured on the Linux VM (arm64, Node.js 24.22, seven alternating pairs of fresh processes, the median of five conversions in each; head against base): an 18.3 MB tar in an 8.3 MB `.tar.xz` to tar with `zeroHeap` took 275.1 ms against 261.5 ms (+5.2 %); a stored RAR of 5,000 entries to tar in process took 230.1 ms against 217.9 ms (+5.6 %, the `unrar lb` run); a 7z of 5,000 entries to tar in process 29.0 ms against 26.7 ms (+8.6 %, runs from 23 to 35 ms on both sides); a tar of 5,000 entries to tar in process 17.1 ms against 16.8 ms. The streamed routes did not move: `.tar.xz` to tar 241.3 ms against 241.1 ms, 7z to tar 209.0 ms against 211.2 ms.
  - **The check of a name costs less than it did.** On 50,000 entries (host, medians of 15) `assertSafeArchiveListing` takes 22 ms where it took 28 ms, because the path checks no longer split every name into an array; `readTarEntries` takes 36 to 39 ms where it took 32 to 33 ms, which is the check it did not make before. The new checks give the verdict of the old ones for 400,000 generated names.
  - **The order of the members** of a tar written by the disk route is the order of the tree 7-Zip walks, not the order of the tar that was read; the streamed route keeps the order. The member list, modes and bytes are the same.
  - **A RAR name that `unrar` prints in another spelling** (a backslash as a separator, a non-ASCII name as the locale prints it) is checked as printed. The names in the stored-RAR reader are checked as stored.
  - **The 7z and tar inspection fallbacks** that run without a 7-Zip binary read names with the same functions; a hostile 7z is refused there, where the 7-Zip listing reports it.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keep rewriting and report it.** The name the caller sees would not be the name in the archive, and a file the archive named elsewhere would be written to a place of the reader's choosing.
  - **Skip the unsafe entry and convert the rest.** The output would differ from the archive without the caller knowing, and the native route and ZIP refuse.
  - **Read the payload tar into memory on the disk route and reuse `readVettedPayloadTar`.** A zero-heap request must never buffer the unpacked bytes, and a payload over the in-memory budget cannot be held; the disk route extracts the tar with the pipeline every tar source takes, and shares the decision of what the file is.
  - **Charge the payload and the members to one byte budget** (as an rpm or a deb package is). It would refuse a 300 MB tar the streamed route converts, because the payload and the members together pass the 500 MB cap.
  - **Check RAR names after `unrar x`.** `unrar` has already placed the entry below the directory, so the tree shows a safe name for a hostile entry.
- **Verified by**: `tests/archive-unsafe-entry-names.test.ts` (tar with the name in the header, in a GNU long-name record and in a pax `path` record, 7z and RAR, for each class above; the names are read back by `tar -tf` or Python's `tarfile`, `7z l -slt` and `unrar lb` before the conversion is run; every refusal names the entry; the bytes of the tar written for an ordinary tar, 7z and RAR are pinned by SHA-256 and equal what the code wrote before the change) and `tests/archive-wrapper-unwrap-on-disk.test.ts` (`.tar.xz`, `.tgz` and `.tbz2` to tar with `zeroHeap` and past the in-memory budget list the same mode and name for every member as the original tar under `tar -tvf`; the streamed and the disk route give the same list for one input; a compressed text file is the one member `notes`, `data.csv` for `data.csv.xz`; a link and a traversing name in the payload are refused on both routes with their reasons; a selection names members of the inner tar). Names that look like a drive but are not (`Ｑ：回答.txt`, `a:b.txt`) are converted in tar, 7z, RAR and ZIP, read back by `tar -tf`, Python's `tarfile` and `7z l -slt`, and the dotted drive forms, control characters and the empty and NUL upload names of the encrypted writers are refused with a typed error; the drive test fails on these tests when it is put back to the folded name. A zip uploaded as `.gz` is refused by the disk unwrap. The two tests that pinned the rewrite in `tests/oracle-integrity-and-security-audit.test.ts` and `tests/phase-1-archive-and-media-fidelity.test.ts` pin the refusal.
- **Revisit when**: a reader of these formats stores names as something other than text that can be checked as written (a RAR 5 name that `unrar` lists in a spelling the policy cannot see), or the disk route no longer needs the payload and the members at the same time.

## 118. E-book targets written by calibre: MOBI, AZW3, PDB, LRF and OEB through `ebook-convert`, with no writer of our own

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #443 of epic #760), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request: ship these five targets as real writers instead of withdrawing them, and launch with them). It replaces the plain-text writers of `office.ts` for these targets and the choice not to put calibre in the worker image (entries 40 and 96).
- **Decision**:
  - **The writer is calibre's `ebook-convert`, an unmodified separate program** in the process sandbox (entry 11): GPL-3.0, started with no shell, no network (a network namespace where the host allows one, and proxy variables that point nowhere), an address space of 4 GiB, an output file of at most 512 MiB, at most 100 MiB printed, the job's time limit (120 s when the request names none, 600 s at most) and the whole process group killed on a timeout or an abort. The route has one deadline: the time limit counts from the start of the route, and the second run of a PDB book gets the time the first left, so a PDB conversion never takes twice the limit. No calibre code is copied or linked. The worker finds it through `EBOOK_CONVERT_PATH` (an absolute path, as the rule of the setting says; a bare command name is rejected at start-up) or in `/usr/bin`, `/usr/local/bin` and `/opt/homebrew/bin`, and the health report lists it as the advisory component `ebook-convert`.
  - **The image gets the Debian package `calibre`** (8.5.0 in trixie) with `qt6-image-formats-plugins` and `qt6-svg-plugins`, which the package only recommends and the books' WebP and SVG pictures need. The build converts a text file to each of the five targets with the options of the route (`QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen`, each run under `timeout 120`) and fails if the program does not start or a book lacks its signature (`BOOKMOBI` type and creator for MOBI, MOBI header version 8 for AZW3, `TEXtREAd` for PDB, the LRF magic, an OPF package in the OEB folder), and `scripts/verify-worker-container.sh` runs the same five conversions and checks inside the sandbox of the running container. CI keeps the pinned upstream archive (9.15.0) it already installs for the ebook benchmark; the tests read it through `EBOOK_CONVERT_PATH` or `PATH`.
  - **The route** (`src/worker/ebook-calibre.ts`, called first by `convertWithOfficeSuiteRoutes`, after the spoof check): a source that calibre reads itself (MOBI, AZW, AZW3, PDB, LRF) is handed over as it is, under a name with its extension, because calibre picks its reader by the extension. Every other source is first written as EPUB by the worker's own conversion of the pair (`source` to `epub`: the in-process converters, and LibreOffice's interchange file for the formats only the office suite reads), and calibre converts that EPUB, taken from the file the converter left when there is one and not read into memory. An e-book handed over as it is, and the EPUB of another source, above 256 MiB are refused (413). EPUB and FB2 are not handed over as they are: the registry offers them as sources of no calibre target, and an EPUB reaches calibre's reader with hrefs that nothing here confines to the package (the worker has no mount namespace), so that path is not shipped until it has containment and a probe (see Revisit when).
  - **Options per target**, from the manual page https://manual.calibre-ebook.com/generated/en/ebook-convert.html:
    - **MOBI**: `--mobi-file-type old`, section "MOBI Output Options" ("by default calibre generates MOBI files that contain the old MOBI 6 format. This format is compatible with all devices"). `both` would add the KF8 half to the same file, which the AZW3 target already offers, and `new` is AZW3 under another extension. The default is passed explicitly so that a calibre release that changes it does not change this target.
    - **AZW3**: the defaults of the AZW3 writer (KF8).
    - **MOBI and AZW3**: `--no-inline-toc` ("don't add Table of Contents to the book"). The navigation is the NCX and the KF8 index; a contents page written into the text would add words that the source does not have, and the text of the book would no longer equal the text of the source.
    - **PDB**: `--format doc`, section "PDB Output Options" (`doc`, `ereader`, `ztxt`). PalmDOC is the format the registry names ("Palm OS Database Doc"), the one every Palm-family reader opens (type `TEXt`, creator `REAd`, LZ77 records of 4096 bytes), and the one this issue specifies; eReader keeps headings and pictures but few readers still open it. See the encoding rule below.
    - **LRF** and **OEB**: the defaults of their writers.
  - **PDB text is written in Windows-1252 when it fits, and in UTF-8 when it does not.** PalmDOC has no encoding field, and calibre's writers (`doc`, `ereader` and `ztxt` alike) encode in Windows-1252 and write `?` for every character that code page lacks: measured with calibre 9.15.0, a book of Hangul, kana and Latin text read back as `????` from all three. `--pdb-output-encoding utf-8` keeps the text of `doc` and `ztxt` (not of `ereader`), and calibre reads it back. A UTF-8 book would show mojibake for every accented letter in a reader that assumes Windows-1252, so the route asks calibre for the plain text of the source first (one more run, 0.2 s), and chooses UTF-8 only when a character is outside Windows-1252 (the 27 characters of bytes 0x80 to 0x9F included, a character past U+FFFF excluded). A western book keeps calibre's default; a Korean, Japanese or Chinese book is written in UTF-8, which Calibre, and the readers that detect UTF-8, read.
  - **OEB is delivered as one ZIP file** of what calibre writes into the output folder (the OPF package, the XHTML, the NCX and the style sheets), with the media type `application/zip` and the name `<name>.zip`, so that `/api/convert` (which names the download from the result) and `/api/v1/convert` (which names it from the media type) agree, because calibre's OEB output is a folder and no registered type names a zipped OEB package. The registry still lists `application/x-oeb1-package+xml` for the `oeb` format.
  - **Failures are typed and nothing is made up.** A run that outlasts its limit is `CpuTaskTimeoutError` (422); a DRM-protected book (calibre's `DRMError`) is the 422 encrypted-document error; any other failure of the program is `ConversionFailedError` (400) with the last line it printed and the job directory replaced by `<tmp>`; its output or memory limit is a `ConversionFailedError`. The file calibre wrote is checked before it is handed out (PalmDB type and creator `BOOKMOBI` for MOBI and AZW3, `TEXtREAd` for PDB, the LRF magic, an OPF in the OEB folder; a link or a device in the folder is refused), and a mismatch is `InvalidConversionOutputError`.
  - **A worker without `ebook-convert` answers `EngineUnavailableError` (503) for every pair that ends in one of the five targets**, before it converts, and the retry on another worker applies. `requiresNativeEngine` is true for these pairs, the in-process `convertOffice` throws the same error, and `generatePalmDoc`, `generateOebPackage`, `generateLrf` and the `Extracted content from` string are deleted (`git grep "Extracted content from" src` finds nothing). The five targets are no longer "text only" targets: `TEXT_ONLY_TARGETS` keeps XPS, HWP and HWPX.
  - **calibre reads a configuration, a cache and a temporary directory that belong to the job** (`CALIBRE_CONFIG_DIRECTORY`, `CALIBRE_CACHE_DIRECTORY`, `CALIBRE_TEMP_DIR`, `HOME` and the XDG directories, all inside the job directory that is deleted afterwards), so no plug-in, setting or earlier job reaches it; the environment is the sanitized one of every native program (no secret of the worker).
  - **The helper `officeInputWithoutMacros` and the two input checks that stood in `engines.ts` moved to `src/worker/office-input-checks.ts`**, so that `engines.ts` does not grow past its entry in the code smell baseline (entry 32); the behaviour is the same.
- **Why**:
  - **The files the old writers made were not books.** Measured on the base with calibre 9.15.0 (arm64): the MOBI and AZW3 output has PalmDOC compression 1 and no EXTH record, and calibre reads it back as an empty text; calibre refuses the LRF ("has an invalid LRF header") and the OEB ("No plugin to handle input format: oeb"); only the PDB read back, as uncompressed UTF-8 that the PalmDOC format does not define. A reader of a real device would fare no better.
  - **calibre is the reference converter for these formats.** The reference service writes them with calibre (entry 40), the ebook benchmark already compares against its `ebook-convert` (the `ebook` family and its pinned CI install), and its writers are the ones device makers test against: a MOBI 6 book with the EXTH title and language, an AZW3 with the FDST, index and end records, an LRF with the BBeB object tree.
  - **A writer of our own was the alternative that carries the cost.** The issue first proposed PalmDOC, KF8 and LRF writers; KF8 (skeleton and fragment indexes, FDST, NCX) and BBeB are large, little documented and falling in use, and every reader quirk of every device would be ours to find and track. A GPL program run unmodified out of process is the boundary entry 11 already allows.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The image grows.** Computed from the Debian trixie `Packages` index (amd64, no recommends): the dependency closure of `calibre` and the two Qt plug-in packages is 207 packages beyond what the runner stage installs today, about 698 MiB installed and 203 MiB to download (calibre 8.5.0). This is an estimate and no image was built for this change: no container runtime was available. Of it 258 MiB is Qt WebEngine (six packages) and 128 MiB the scientific Python packages (scipy, numpy, sympy, mpmath), which none of the five targets load; `ebook-convert` itself is in the `calibre` package (`calibre-bin` holds only the compiled modules, 5.5 MiB), so there is no smaller package route. For comparison the upstream archive is 182 MB to download and 609 MB unpacked (calibre 9.15.0, arm64), and entry 96 measured 623 MB for 9.17.0.
  - **The first measure to cut it is known and not taken.** With the Qt WebEngine libraries and Python modules taken out of the upstream archive on the test machine, all five targets still convert (PDF output is the only part that needs them). The Debian package declares the dependency, so removing the libraries would leave the package manager in a broken state; the cut belongs to a later change that either builds the image from the archive or holds the package back, with the size measured on a built image.
  - **The image runs calibre 8.5.0, the tests 9.15.0.** The options used exist in both. The image build and `verify-worker-container.sh` convert a book to each of the five targets on 8.5.0 and check each signature; the structure tests of this entry were run on 9.15.0 only.
  - **The text of a PDB book in UTF-8 is read by fewer readers** than a Windows-1252 one; the choice is made per book and only for text that Windows-1252 cannot hold, where the alternative is to lose it.
  - **LRF, MOBI and AZW3 books do not carry the layout of the source**: calibre re-flows the EPUB (LRF text blocks run paragraphs together in calibre's plain-text export, although the file keeps them as `P` elements with `CR` between). A PDF source reaches calibre as the EPUB that the in-process PDF reader writes, so its quality is that reader's.
  - **One more process per conversion**: 0.2 to 0.4 s per book on a warm VM, and one more run (0.2 s) for a PDB book.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Hand-written PalmDOC, KF8 and LRF writers** (the first proposal of issue #443): high effort, and a reader quirk we would find on a customer's device.
  - **Withdrawing the five targets**: QA decided to ship them.
  - **The upstream archive in the image**: 609 MB unpacked, outside the distribution's security updates and its package tracking; the Debian package is updated with the image.
  - **Linking or embedding calibre code** (a library, a port): GPL-3.0 propagates to what links it.
  - **`ereader` or `ztxt` for PDB**: the first is read by few programs, the second by fewer; neither keeps Hangul in Windows-1252.
  - **Always UTF-8 for PDB**: mojibake for every accented letter in a reader that follows the PalmDOC code page.
  - **Refusing a PDB whose text Windows-1252 cannot hold**: keeps the file honest, but a Korean user then gets no PDB at all; MOBI is the offered format for such books, and the UTF-8 file is readable where the reader detects it.
- **Verified by**: `tests/ebook-calibre-writers.test.ts` (calibre present: the structure of each target read by `tests/helpers/palmdb-reader.ts`, written from the MobileRead layout of the Palm database, PalmDOC and MOBI headers and sharing no code with the converter: MOBI 6 with PalmDOC compression 2, UTF-8, the title in the full name and EXTH 503; AZW3 with version 8 and its FDST, FLIS, index and end records; PDB type `TEXt` and creator `REAd`, LZ77 of 4096-byte records; the text of every book equal to the source after NFC and white space collapse, Hangul, kana and a decomposed `e` with an accent included, read by that parser, by `ebook-convert` to text, by `lrf2lrs` for LRF and from the XHTML for OEB; the titles by `ebook-meta`; six direct pairs between books; a damaged book; nothing left in a temporary directory of the test's own after a MOBI, PDB or OEB conversion, which is also how it keeps other test files that run at the same time from being counted), `tests/ebook-calibre-route.test.ts` (no calibre: the unavailable engine for each target through the dispatcher before it converts, the in-process engine's refusal with its message, every registry pair ending in a target marked native-only, the string `Extracted content from` absent from `src`, and the text writer of the e-book sources refusing a target it does not list; against stand-in programs: the arguments of each target, the encoding rule on four texts, one time limit for the two runs of a PDB book, the job's own directories and the missing secrets, the OEB ZIP and its `.zip` name, DRM, the last line of a failure, five wrong outputs, a file above the input limit, the EPUB of another source taken from the converter's file and bounded, and a program and its child killed by the time limit, checked by pid), and the missing-engine suite of `tests/registry-engine-conformance.test.ts` for all 77 pairs that end in a target, from an input of each source. Red on the base (calibre 9.15.0 on the arm64 Linux VM): all 15 tests of the first version of the writers file fail there, and a MOBI of the base reads back empty. Timing, one sample per target on the 4-core arm64 Linux VM (a text file of 615,000 bytes of repeated Latin, Hangul and kana paragraphs through `dispatchConversion`, load average 0.5): MOBI 936 ms, AZW3 584 ms, PDB 897 ms, LRF 661 ms, OEB 375 ms. The ebook family of the parity gate (`ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity --family ebook` on the VM with calibre 9.15.0, EPUBCheck 5.2.1 and Poppler; it measures the EPUB, TXT and PDF outputs of EPUB, MOBI and FB2 books, none of the five targets) passed: 174 rows evaluated, 0 failing. Its gate step lists two PDF word-F1 rows (one book, one class) as baseline metrics missing from the report; the cause was not investigated, and the calibre PDF run that serves as the reference for the same book sat idle in Qt WebEngine until the tool's 300 s limit on the VM. On the host (Apple silicon, no calibre) `npm run lint`, `guard:anti-cheat`, `guard:code-smells`, `guard:policy-decisions` and `ci-parity-families` are clean and the tests that need no calibre pass; the ones that need it are skipped there and run on the VM and in CI.
- **Revisit when**: an image has been built and its size is known (trim the WebEngine and scientific packages or build from the archive); the image's calibre is run through the writers test (the package is 8.5.0, the test run is on 9.15.0); EPUB, DOCX, ODT and FB2 are offered as sources of these targets (the registry lists them for no calibre target today, and `tests/parity-audit.test.ts` records the gap; an EPUB or FB2 then needs the hrefs inside the book confined to the package, with a probe on the VM that a crafted spine item cannot read `/proc` first); the `oeb` source reads the ZIP this target writes (its reader still reads only the single-file package of the old writer); a CBC (a ZIP) passes the spoof check of the worker, which refuses it today for every target; a PDB reader of the audience is found not to read UTF-8; or Debian ships a calibre whose options differ.

## 119. FFmpeg and ffprobe open an upload only with the demuxer of its detected format and the file protocol, run in the namespace sandbox, and need FFmpeg 8.1.3 or later

- **Status**: Implemented (issues #715 and #618), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request: launch blockers of the media path).
- **Decision**:
  - `src/lib/conversions/media-process.ts` is the only module that starts ffmpeg or ffprobe. Every process runs in the namespace sandbox (`resolveSandboxedCommand` or `executeSandboxedBinary` with `networkIsolated: true`, the sanitized environment, a timeout and an output limit). Under `STRICT_SANDBOX` a host without network namespaces refuses before any process starts (`SandboxUnavailableError`, 503), ffprobe included.
  - Every input gets `-protocol_whitelist file` and a demuxer choice, decided once where the conversion starts and the file and its declared source format are both known (`openMediaInput`, in the in-process media path, the packaging path and the worker's native route). The argument builders and every ffprobe call take that opened input; they no longer read the file to choose. The demuxer is the container the file's signature shows (MP4 and QuickTime, Matroska and WebM, AVI, WAVE, FLAC, Ogg, ADTS), or else the one of the declared source format of the request, which the upload check compared with the bytes. The file's name is never read: a queued job reads `<sha256>.bin` or `<uploadId>.bin`. One demuxer is forced with `-f`. A format whose files come in several containers or bitstreams (AC-3 and E-AC-3, DTS and DTS-HD, Musepack SV7 and SV8, AV1 as OBU, IVF or Annex B) gets `-format_whitelist` of those, and FFmpeg's own probe picks among them.
  - A file that opens like a reference format is refused with `RefusedMediaInputError` (422) before any engine reads it: an HLS playlist (`#EXTM3U`), a concat list (`ffconcat version 1.0`), a DASH manifest (`<MPD` with a DASH profile), an IMF composition playlist, an SDP description, a VobSub index (the 20-byte prefix `# VobSub index file,`) and an XBIN picture.
